papers.title: Comparative assessment of benzyl alcohol and m-cresol as preservatives in maropitant injectable formulation: implications for pain & tolerability.
papers.authors: Pawar V, Trivedi J, Muchhara J, Dharvadiya N, Patel S, Patel R, Shah M, Sundar R, Kannan ME, Ukawala M, Laddha R, Jain M
papers.abstract: The selection of an optimal preservative in multi-dose injectable veterinary formulations requires antimicrobial efficacy with local tissue compatibility. While m-cresol provides potent broad-spectrum efficacy in multi-dose veterinary injectables, subcutaneous administration causes acute injection-site pain and distress, compromising compliance despite recommended low-temperature management. We hypothesized that a benzyl alcohol-preserved maropitant formulation (BAF) would result in lower acute injection-site pain scores than a m-cresol preserved formulation (MCF), regardless of storage temperature. Thirty-two adult healthy beagle dogs were enrolled in this study. Under blinded, randomized crossover design, each dog received subcutaneous maropitant using both formulations maintained at refrigerated and room temperature conditions. Pain was assessed by two independent assessors using a visual analog scale, simple descriptive scale, and clinical observation. Cerenia ® was used as a meta-cresol-based formulation and benzyl-alcohol formulation was provided by ZyVet, USA. The BAF produced significantly lower Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and Simple Descriptive Scale (SDS) scores than the MCF ( P < 0.0001). Log VAS values for BAF were 1.94 ± 0.14 at 25 °C and 2.33 ± 0.14 at 4 °C, vs. 3.43 ± 0.11 at 25 °C and 3.38 ± 0.11 at 4 °C for MCF. Treatment with MCF increased the odds of elevated SDS scores up to 10.32-fold compared with BAF ( P < 0.0001). Observer agreement was excellent. Restlessness and head shaking occurred more frequently with the m-cresol formulation. The benzyl alcohol-based maropitant formulation appears better-tolerated than meta-cresol containing formulation in terms of injection-site pain and irritation.

papers.title: Decision tree models to guide endotracheal tube selection in dogs.
papers.authors: Ngamlertwong N, Punyapornwithaya V, Siriyakhun S, Seymour C, Seki S
papers.abstract: Choosing an endotracheal tube (ETT) of an appropriate size is critical for effective airway management in dogs undergoing anesthesia or emergency care. Conventional methods often rely on body weight (BW), palpation of external tracheal diameter, nasal septum width, or subjective clinician experience. However, these approaches are frequently imprecise and lack well-established guidelines. Therefore, this study aimed to develop a machine learning-based decision tree model to standardize ETT size using measurable anatomical parameters in dolichocephalic, mesocephalic, and brachycephalic breeds. A retrospective analysis was conducted on data from dogs undergoing anesthesia or emergency care at the Northern Regional Veterinary Healthcare and Learning Center, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Chiang Mai University, (NOVEL CMU) Thailand between January and December 2024. We investigated the relationship between the internal diameter (ID) of the ETT used and multiple patient variables, including BW, sex, age, breed, and internal tracheal diameter (ITD) measured at the thoracic inlet on radiographs. Decision tree analysis was used to determine the ETT selection. We hypothesized that a decision tree model integrating BW and ITD would accurately predict appropriate ETT sizing in dogs, but that upper airway anatomical differences would necessitate separate models for non-brachycephalic breeds (Group DM, including dolichocephalic and mesocephalic conformation) and brachycephalic breeds (Group B). The results demonstrated that Group B required ETTs with a significantly smaller ID compared to Group DM of the same BW. Variable importance analysis identified BW and ITD as the primary predictors of ETT size in both groups. Conversely, sex and age demonstrated negligible predictive value and were not significant factors in the selection process. Hence, the decision tree model successfully generated distinct algorithmic pathways for Group DM and Group B. The developed decision tree models offer a practical, non-invasive method for standardizing ETT sizes in clinical practice, thereby enhancing skilled veterinary human capital. This algorithmic approach accounts for individual anatomical variations in the respiratory tract, particularly in brachycephalic dogs. For clinical application, clinicians should prepare tubes within ±0.5 mm of the predicted size to ensure optimal airway management and patient safety.

papers.title: Precision nutrition in companion animals: a response-based framework linking dietary strategies, metabolic function, and measurable clinical outcomes.
papers.authors: Du X, Zhang H, Tian W, Chen J, Wen M, Fan W
papers.abstract: Population-level nutrient recommendations provide the foundation for complete and balanced diets in dogs and cats, but they do not fully account for inter-individual variation in nutritional requirements, metabolic phenotypes, and dietary responses. Precision nutrition provides a response-guided framework that integrates individual characteristics with monitored dietary responses to refine nutritional management through repeated reassessment. This review examines the conceptual framework, host determinants, clinical applications, and translational challenges of precision nutrition in companion animals. Obesity, chronic enteropathy, chronic kidney disease, and urolithiasis are discussed as representative clinical models in which dietary interventions can be linked to measurable outcomes and adjusted according to individual response. Current clinical implementation is informed primarily by phenotypic assessment, dietary history, routine clinical and biochemical measures, and longitudinal monitoring, with biomarkers such as serum phosphate providing direct guidance in specific clinical contexts. Microbiome and metabolomic profiles, selected molecular biomarkers, and digital monitoring tools, such as smart feeders and activity monitors, may provide complementary information, whereas multi-omics integration and AI-assisted prediction remain largely exploratory. Further progress will require standardized species-specific datasets, prospective validation of predictive biomarkers, reliable digital measurements, and externally validated, interpretable models that demonstrate added value beyond established clinical assessment. Overall, precision nutrition represents an iterative, response-guided framework in which individual characteristics and monitored outcomes inform dietary selection and adjustment over time.

papers.title: Metabolomic and lipidomic signatures of aging in cats reveal shifts in energy metabolism and inflammation: an 11-year longitudinal study.
papers.authors: Hartvigsson O, Ross AB, Moesta A, Heiser A, Lee E, Butowski CF, Thomas DG, Laxalde J, Bermingham EN, Moniot D
papers.abstract: Aging encompasses multiple biochemical changes, some of which may be associated with the development of age-related diseases. The dynamics of aging in relation to metabolism in cats has not been established and understanding this could identify targets for early intervention. The aim of this longitudinal study was to identify changes in the plasma and fecal metabolome and lipidome of cats from 1 to 11 years of age. Twenty-one cats from a research colony had plasma and fecal samples collected yearly between one and 11 years of age. Clinical biomarkers were measured in serum, while plasma and fecal metabolomics and lipidomics were measured using mass spectrometry. Data were analyzed using repeated measures-ANOVA Simultaneous Component Analysis. Two metabolic trajectories were observed: one linear, suggestive of progressive accumulation of metabolic alterations with aging, and a U-shape, suggestive of more complex metabolic changes over time. Three themes emerged: inflammaging (linear decrease of plasma albumin:globulin ratio, increase in fecal inflammatory mediators), mitochondrial dysfunction (linear increase of plasma long-chain phosphatidylcholines, U-shape for plasma hydroxy-butyric acids and lactic acid, inverse U-shape for fecal coenzyme Q), and a possible link to an aging gut microbiome (tryptophan pathway with linear increase of plasma kynurenine versus decrease of fecal anthranilic acids). Metabolic changes in plasma and feces support the inflammaging hypothesis for cats, alongside mitochondrial dysfunction, and possible changes to gut microbial metabolism. Clear metabolic shifts between 6 and 8 years of age suggest that early intervention could help to support a healthy aging trajectory in cats.

papers.title: Wound healing complications after tooth extraction in dogs.
papers.authors: Šparaš L, Pavlica M, Lukanc B, Nemec A
papers.abstract: This prospective clinical study aimed to assess incidence of wound healing complications associated with extraction sites following permanent tooth extractions in healthy dogs. Eighty-seven client-owned healthy adult dogs undergoing clinically indicated closed or open dental extractions, comprising 404 extraction sites, were included in the study. No perioperative and immediate postoperative antibiotics or antiseptics were used in any of the dogs. All dogs were discharged on the day of the procedure with pain management as clinically indicated and underwent a routine (non-sedated) follow-up examination 10 days later. Sites with incomplete epithelial healing and wound edge separation were classified as dehisced. Weekly in-person or telemedicine follow-up examinations were performed until complete healing was confirmed. Dehiscence was the most common postoperative complication, diagnosed in 19.5% (17/87) of the dogs and 4.2% (17/404) of the extraction sites within 10 days after the procedure. Most affected sites involved large, functionally important teeth, and 76.5% (13/17) of cases were mild. None of the dehisced sites required surgical revision, and only 23.5% (4/17) dogs required additional medical management with antibiotics and/or analgesia. All dehisced sites healed by second intention within one month. Increasing body weight was associated with higher odds of dehiscence, with a 13% increase in odds for each additional kilogram of body weight. Removal of at least 50% of the alveolar bone, extraction in the rostral mandibular region, and the use of triangular flaps during open extraction were also significantly associated with increased odds of dehiscence. Traumatic dentoalveolar injury was the only indication for tooth extraction significantly associated with increased odds of dehiscence. Extraction wound dehiscence was uncommon at the individual-site level, but remained a clinically relevant postoperative complication when assessed per treated dog. Most affected sites healed uneventfully by second intention within one month, without surgical revision or prolonged medical management. This finding supports conservative management of extraction wound dehiscence in uncomplicated cases.

papers.title: Determination of reference intervals for symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA) in Lacaune sheep.
papers.authors: Kiene F, Wagener MG, Röhrig P, Ganter M
papers.abstract: Traditional biomarkers such as serum creatinine and urea often fail to reflect early renal dysfunction, particularly in emaciated animals, as they depend on muscle mass or dietary protein intake. Symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA), a novel renal biomarker, has shown promise in other species for earlier and more sensitive detection of kidney disease. However, reference intervals for SDMA in ovine species remain undocumented. This study aimed to establish reference intervals for serum SDMA in clinically healthy Lacaune sheep. A reference population of 143 healthy sheep, stratified by age (juvenile < 1 year, adult ≥ 1 year), was selected based on clinical health, body condition score, and serum creatinine concentration. Serum SDMA was quantified using an ELISA validated for cats and dogs. Reference intervals were calculated as 0.59-1.72 µmol/l for all sheep, 0.59-1.56 µmol/l for adults, and 0.59-1.83 µmol/l for juveniles, with juveniles exhibiting significantly higher concentrations (p < 0.001). No sex-related differences were observed. In a retrospective analysis of 51 deceased sheep with histopathological renal assessments, SDMA concentrations were significantly elevated in animals with severe renal lesions compared to those with no, mild or moderate lesions (p = 0.005). Creatinine by contrast did not show significant differences. Notably, in animals with poor body condition, SDMA remained effective in identifying individuals with severe renal lesions, whereas creatinine levels remained within or below the reference interval. These findings suggest that SDMA is a more sensitive indicator of renal dysfunction in sheep than creatinine, particularly in emaciated individuals. The established reference intervals provide a foundation for clinical application. The economic feasibility of SDMA testing remains a limitation, but its potential to improve early diagnosis of renal disease in sheep justifies further investigation.

papers.title: Comparative epidemiology of multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli ST131 across human, poultry, and companion animal hosts in Iran.
papers.authors: Hafiz M, Askari Badouei M, Hashemi Tabar G, Nemati A
papers.abstract: Escherichia coli ST131 is a globally prevalent multidrug-resistant pathogen, mainly linked to human infections but increasingly found in animals. Its spread is largely driven by the O25b-ST131 sublineage carrying the CTX-M-15 ESBL. However, limited data exist on its prevalence, transmission, resistance, and genetics in Iran. A total of 360 E. coli isolates from human urinary tract infections (UTIs), poultry colibacillosis, and fecal samples from companion animals were collected (2021-2024). Molecular typing identified ST131 clones and determined phylogenetic groups. Antimicrobial agent susceptibility was tested using the CLSI disk diffusion method. Key resistance genes (e.g., bla CTX-M , bla OXA , aac(6')-Ib-cr) and plasmid replicon types were investigated. Among 360 isolates, 21 (5.8%) were identified as ST131, with significantly higher prevalence in human UTIs 19/120 (15.8%) compared to poultry 1/120 (0.83%) and companion animal 1/120 (0.83%) sources (p < 0.001). Among ST131 isolates, 94.7% (18/19) from human sources belonged to the O25b clonal group, while 5.3% (1/19) were O16. Both animal-derived ST131 isolates 2/2 (100%) were O25b clonal group. All ST131 isolates 21/21 (100%) belonged to phylogroup B2 and demonstrated multidrug resistance. High resistance rates were observed against ciprofloxacin 18/21 (85.7%), cefotaxime 20/21 (95.2%), and ampicillin 21/21 (100%). ESBL genes were detected in 61.9% of ST131 isolates, and bla CTX-M-15 was identified in 47.4% of urinary strains. Half of the UTI isolates 9/19 (47.4) harbored bla CTX-M-15 , bla OXA , and aac(6')-Ib-cr simultaneously. IncFIA (78.9%) and IncFIB (73.6%) plasmids were predominant in human isolates, while HI2 replicon was more common in non-human sources 2/2 (100%), including one dog sample and one poultry sample. ST131 poses a significant public health concern in Iran, particularly in human UTIs, due to its multidrug resistance and ESBL production. The predominance of O25b clonal group and differential resistance patterns between human and animal sources suggest distinct evolutionary pressures. Importantly, this study provides the first report of ST131 in poultry and companion animals in Iran (representing a critical surveillance gap previously undocumented in the Iranian veterinary literature), thereby establishing a foundational baseline for future comparative genomic studies to elucidate interspecies transmission dynamics and resistance evolution.

papers.title: Evaluating plasma renin activity as a monitoring parameter for mineralocorticoid treatment in dogs with primary hypoadrenocorticism.
papers.authors: Arrigoni S, Harburger LA, Neubert E, Riond B, Evans H, Unterer S, Boretti FS, Sieber-Ruckstuhl N
papers.abstract: In human medicine, plasma renin activity (PRA) is used to assess mineralocorticoid treatment adequacy in hypoadrenocorticism, with elevated levels indicating under-replacement and suppressed levels over-replacement. In dogs with primary hypoadrenocorticism, PRA is increased before treatment and decreases with treatment, but its value as a monitoring parameter remains uncertain. The objective of this study was to evaluate PRA as a marker to guide mineralocorticoid dosing in dogs with primary hypoadrenocorticism. A total of 52 PRA measurements were collected from 28 dogs during scheduled desoxycorticosterone pivalate (DOCP) treatment visits. All dogs had received DOCP and prednisolone for at least five months. PRA was measured by ELISA detecting angiotensin I. Median PRA was 1.6 ng/mL/h (range, 0-19.2), with 19 values above, 17 within, and 16 below the reference interval. PRA showed moderate correlations with potassium (p = 0.009, 𝛒 = 0.36), sodium (p = 0.02, 𝛒 = -0.33), the sodium-to-potassium (Na/K) ratio (p = 0.006, 𝛒 = -0.38), and DOCP dose (p = 0.02, 𝛒 = -0.34), while urine specific gravity correlated with DOCP dose (p = 0.01, 𝛒 = -0.50). Compared with visits with decreased PRA, visits with increased PRA had a significantly lower Na/K ratio (p = 0.048). Increased PRA occurred more frequently during visits with concurrent disease (p = 0.005); concurrent disease was also associated with higher creatinine concentrations (p = 0.023) and lower DOCP doses (p = 0.004). In subgroup analyses, chronic enteropathy was associated with higher potassium concentrations (p = 0.003), lower Na/K ratios (p = 0.009), and higher DOCP doses (p < 0.001), whereas chronic kidney disease was associated with higher creatinine concentrations (p < 0.001) and lower DOCP doses (p < 0.001). Clinical assessment and PRA status were concordant in 48% of visits. PRA may provide additional information for monitoring mineralocorticoid treatment in dogs with hypoadrenocorticism treated with DOCP. However, its interpretation can be challenging, as it often does not match electrolyte results and both PRA and electrolytes may be affected by other diseases. Therefore, PRA should be interpreted as a supportive parameter within the clinical context.

papers.title: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor in a 9-year-old male neutered mixed-breed dog with gastrointestinal signs; a case report.
papers.authors: Vafaei R, Nassiri SM, Mirani AH
papers.abstract: A 9-year-old male neutered mixed-breed dog was presented with chronic diarrhea and vomiting. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a mass in the jejunum, which was surgically excised. Histopathological examination and immunohistochemistry confirmed the diagnosis of an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT). This case report discusses the clinical presentation, diagnostic approach, and management of IMT in this dog.

papers.title: Dietary taurine mitigates waterborne arsenic trioxide toxicity in Nile tilapia: effects on growth performance, intestinal health, stress biomarkers, and immune-related genes.
papers.authors: Radwan M, Ragab AM, Bashar MAE, Al Malki JS, Al-Megrin WAI, Moussa MA
papers.abstract: Chronic arsenic contamination can compromise fish performance and health, yet practical nutritional approaches to limit its effects remain poorly defined. This 60-day study tested whether dietary taurine (TA; 10 g kg⁻¹ diet) mitigates waterborne arsenic trioxide (As₂O₃; AS; 10 µg L⁻¹, nominal) toxicity in Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) using a 2 × 2 factorial design (with or without AS and TA; four aquaria per treatment, 15 fish per aquarium). AS exposure significantly reduced growth, feed efficiency, digestive enzyme activities, intestinal health, blood indices, innate immunity, and antioxidant responses, while increasing markers of hepatorenal stress, lipid peroxidation, intestinal injury, tissue DNA fragmentation, and IL-1β, HSP70, and Casp3 gene expression (P < 0.05). Observed survival was 70.00% in the AS group compared with 98.33% in the control group. In AS-exposed fish, TA improved growth and feed conversion, preserved villus architecture, restored most haematological, biochemical, immune, and antioxidant variables, enhanced SOD, CAT, GPx, and Nrf2 transcript abundance, and lowered MDA, DNA fragmentation, and inflammatory, stress, and apoptotic gene expression. Most responses in the AS + TA group approached control values. Significant AS × TA interactions for most statistically analysed variables indicated that TA conferred marked benefits during the AS challenge. In conclusion, dietary TA improved the physiological resilience of Nile tilapia to chronic exposure to waterborne As₂O₃ by supporting intestinal function and redox-immune balance.

papers.title: Antimicrobial peptides for companion animals: research advances, translational challenges, and opportunities.
papers.authors: Pan S, Wei Y, Sun M, Yu H, He P, Zhang G, Qiao S, Wu Y, Yang Q
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a growing global threat to public health, necessitating the development of novel antimicrobial strategies. Companion animals, particularly dogs and cats, are increasingly integrated into human lives, and their close interactions with humans facilitate the transmission of antimicrobial-resistant pathogens. Therefore, the use of contemporary antimicrobials in these animals raises significant concerns for both animal and human health. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), a class of naturally occurring peptides, play a critical role in host innate immunity through dual antimicrobial and immunomodulatory activities. Due to their pleiotropic mechanisms of action and lower selective pressure for resistance, AMPs are emerging as promising alternative candidates to conventional antimicrobials. Notably, accumulating evidence has also highlighted the promising antitumor capacity of AMPs, expanding their therapeutic potential beyond microbial infection control. Despite their potential, research on AMPs in companion animals remains limited, with most available evidence derived from in vitro assays and pre‑clinical in vivo experiments, while well‑controlled clinical studies are sparse. This review overviews recent advances in AMP research in dogs and cats, discusses major challenges in their development, and outlines future directions for their application in veterinary medicine. The adoption of AMPs in small animal practice has the potential to improve animal health while contributing to the mitigation of AMR. Collectively, this review offers new insights into the development of multifunctional novel therapeutic strategies in companion animals.

papers.title: Survival time and prognostic factors in cats with suspected acute pyelonephritis.
papers.authors: Fletcher JR, Gal A, Dill-Macky E, Cook EK, Harris LM, Mackie JT, Malikides N
papers.abstract: Although acute pyelonephritis (APN) is considered to have a better prognosis than other causes of acute kidney injury (AKI) in cats, survival time and prognostic factors are poorly defined. To determine survival time and prognostic factors influencing survival time in cats suspected of APN. Fifty-four client-owned cats with suspected APN. A retrospective cohort study was designed to review medical records between June 2017 and December 2025 for clinical data and survival time. Overall survival time was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Cox proportional hazard regression univariable screening then multivariable modeling identified factors associated with survival. Clinical features of survivors and non-survivors to 30-days after presentation were compared. Median survival time (MST) was 390 days (95% CI, 153-774 days). Cats that experienced less than 50% reduction or any increase in percentage change in serum creatinine concentration between hospital admission and discharge or euthanasia (sCrΔ%) had significantly higher hazards of death than cats experiencing greater than 50% reduction in sCrΔ%, after adjusting for International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) AKI grade and admission temperature (adjusted hazard ratios [HRs], 8.4 × 104-1.1 × 106; 95% CIs, 4.9 × 102-3.1 × 108; P < .001). No other factors, including pre-existing chronic kidney disease, infecting bacterial isolate, or antimicrobial regimen used, were independently associated with overall survival time. Cats suspected of APN have favorable long-term prognosis. Less reduction or any increase in sCrΔ% was associated with shorter survival time, with the prognostic effect strongly influenced by IRIS AKI grade and temperature at admission. Acute pyelonephritis (APN), a bacterial infection of the kidneys, is an important cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) in cats. Although APN is generally considered to have a better prognosis than other causes of AKI, the prognosis and factors associated with survival time in cats are poorly defined. This study followed 54 cats with suspected APN to evaluate survival time and factors associated with survival time. MST was 390 days, although individual survival times varied. Cats whose kidney function improved less or worsened during hospitalization had shorter survival times than cats with a greater improvement in kidney function. The severity of AKI and body temperature at admission influenced this association. In contrast, pre-existing chronic kidney disease, type of bacteria implicated in the infection, and the antimicrobial treatment used were not independently associated with survival time. Therefore, less improvement in kidney function, higher AKI grade, and decreased body temperature during hospitalization together indicate a less favorable prognosis in cats suspected of APN and may offer pet owners a stronger decision-making foundation.

papers.title: Elimination kinetics of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs during carbon hemoperfusion in 19 dogs with toxicosis.
papers.authors: Her J, Labato MA, Langston CE, Butty EM
papers.abstract: To describe the elimination kinetics of NSAIDs during carbon hemoperfusion (cHP) in dogs with toxicosis, specifically the apparent elimination rate constant, half-life, and plasma reduction. 19 client-owned dogs (median age, 2.5 years; median body weight, 22 kg) with ibuprofen (n = 10), carprofen (5), or naproxen (4) toxicosis treated with cHP at 2 academic veterinary teaching hospitals from November 30, 2022, through July 7, 2024. Dogs were presented after known or suspected ingestion at median estimated maximum doses of 720, 200, and 325 mg/kg for ibuprofen, carprofen, and naproxen, respectively. The median interval from ingestion to cHP was 6.8 hours. Plasma concentrations were measured by LC-MS-MS in-serial samples collected during and, when available, after cHP. The median total plasma reduction was 58% (IQR, 51 to 80). The overall half-life during cHP was 1.3 hours (IQR, 1.1 to 1.8) by the 2-point method, concordant by regression (1.4 hours), and approximately 3.7-, 5.4-, and 52.0-fold shorter than respective therapeutic-dose half-lives. Among 5 dogs with posttreatment samples, plasma concentration rebounded after cHP in 1 naproxen-treated dog. The cHP-associated rate constant exceeded the intrinsic rate constant 11- to 40-fold in 4 of 5 dogs. Carbon hemoperfusion was associated with substantial reductions in plasma NSAID concentrations during treatment in dogs with severe ibuprofen, carprofen, or naproxen toxicosis. Most of the decline occurred early in the session. Further studies are warranted to optimize treatment protocols. Carbon hemoperfusion markedly shortened NSAID elimination half-lives in dogs with severe toxicosis, accelerating removal well beyond endogenous elimination.

papers.title: Comparison of the pharmacokinetics and sedative effects of Zenalpha (medetomidine and vatinoxan) administered intramuscularly and oral transmucosally in dogs.
papers.authors: Lathan AW, Smith CK, Kleine SA, Smith JS, Ng Z, Hampton CE, Bussieres G, Sun X, Rust MR, Knych H, Seddighi R
papers.abstract: To evaluate the sedative effects and pharmacokinetic profile of medetomidine and vatinoxan (Zenalpha) administered via the oral transmucosal (OTM) route. We hypothesized that sedation scores obtained from Zenalpha OTM (ZOTM) would not differ from Zenalpha IM (ZIM). Dogs received 20 µg/kg ZIM or 80 µg/kg ZOTM. Sedation, anxiolytic, and handling scores were collected at 0, 15, 30, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 120, 150, and 180 minutes after administration of Zenalpha. Normality was tested using the Shapiro-Wilk test, and data were presented as median and range. Physiologic data were collected at 0, 5, 10, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 240, 360, and 480 minutes. Plasma samples were collected at 0, 3, 5, 8, 8, 10, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 240, 360, 480, 720, and 1,440 minutes and analyzed for concentration of medetomidine and vatinoxan using LC-MS-MS. 8 healthy adult Beagles participated in this study. Dogs in ZIM and ZOTM showed significant increases in sedation, anxiolysis, and handling scores compared to baselines. Medetomidine OTM was associated with a time to maximum concentration and relative bioavailability of 86 minutes (6 minutes ZIM) and 26.4%, respectively. Vatinoxan OTM was associated with a time to maximum concentration and relative bioavailability of 216 minutes (15 minutes ZIM) and 55.2%, respectively. ZOTM (80 μg/kg) provided effective sedation, anxiolysis, and improved handling in healthy dogs comparable to ZIM (20 μg/kg) administration. Zenalpha administered OTM, at higher doses, may provide an attractive alternative to IM injection to achieve similar sedation.

papers.title: A case-case-control study of cefovecin use and third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Escherichia coli infections in cats.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Frye A, Kim H, Rosenthal C, Angel CC, Chikara Y, Cummings KJ, Guarino CMB, Cazer CL
papers.abstract: To determine if cefovecin administration increased the risk of third-generation cephalosporin (3GC)-resistant Escherichia coli infections in cats. In this retrospective case-case-control study, cases were cats with 3GC-susceptible or 3GC-resistant E coli infections at the Cornell University Hospital for Animals from 2009 to 2023; controls were randomly selected from all feline patients seen during the study period. Exposure data were collected via review of medical records. Direct acyclic graph-driven multivariable regression models of each potential exposure were built for each case-control grouping. 36 susceptible cases (3% cefovecin treated), 14 resistant cases (21% cefovecin treated), and 72 controls (6% cefovecin treated) were identified. Resistant cases had a higher proportion of cefovecin use (21%) than susceptible cases (3%) and controls (6%), but case numbers were too low to evaluate whether cefovecin use was associated with either infection type. Most of the cats that received cefovecin (75%) were underdosed. The overall frequency of cefovecin administration was low (7%) compared to previous studies. Cefovecin use was less frequent than previously reported, resulting in too few cases to determine whether cefovecin use is associated with 3GC-resistant E coli infections in cats. The sample size was too small to evaluate association between cefovecin and 3CG resistance. Based on prudent antimicrobial stewardship, veterinarians should limit cefovecin use to cases where oral antimicrobial treatment is impossible and, ideally, its use is supported by antimicrobial susceptibility testing to avoid selecting for antimicrobial resistance in treated cats. When using cefovecin, veterinarians should ensure they are administering the label-recommended 8-mg/kg dose.

papers.title: Laryngeal paralysis in 72 cats: a multicenter study on epidemiology and treatment.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Gobbetti M, Rossanese M, Tremolada G, Pisani G, Cinti F, Montinaro V, Cantatore M
papers.abstract: To describe the etiology, treatment, and outcomes of cats with laryngeal paralysis (LP) and identify factors associated with survival. Retrospective, multicenter, observational study. Medical records from 7 referral hospitals (Italy, UK, US) were reviewed to identify cats with LP (2003 to 2024). Survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses. 72 cats were included. Primary idiopathic LP was diagnosed in 49 cats (68%) and secondary LP in 17 (24%), most commonly associated with pulmonary neoplasia, trauma, or surgery. Six cats (8%) had comorbidities without a confirmed causal relationship. Bilateral LP was diagnosed in 44 cats (61%), and unilateral LP was diagnosed in 26 cats (36%). Arytenoid lateralization was performed in 53 cats (74%); 93% of cats with bilateral LP and 38.5% of cats with unilateral LP underwent surgery. Complications occurred in 13 cats (24%), including 8 major complications (15%) and 3 deaths from aspiration pneumonia. Estimated 1-, 2-, and 3-year postoperative survival rates were 88%, 85%, and 85%, respectively. Major postoperative complications were the only independent predictor of decreased survival (hazard ratio, 99.42; 95% CI, 8.50 to 1,161.77). Primary idiopathic LP was the most common diagnosis, although secondary causes, particularly neoplasia, were frequent. Unilateral LP may require surgical treatment. Arytenoid lateralization provided good long-term outcomes, although major complications markedly reduced survival. Thorough investigation should be considered in cats with LP to identify underlying neoplasia. Treatment decisions should be based on clinical severity rather than laterality, and owners should be informed of the risk of serious postoperative complications.

papers.title: Functional peptide therapeutics for veterinary osteoarthritis: mechanisms, delivery systems, and translational priorities.
papers.authors: Choi SC, Song MG, Yi SY, Lee SH, Lee IA
papers.abstract: Veterinary osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic whole-joint disorder that causes pain, gait impairment, reduced activity, and diminished quality of life in companion and performance animals. Current multimodal management includes weight control, rehabilitation, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, prostaglandin E2 EP4 receptor antagonists, anti-nerve growth factor monoclonal antibodies, intra-articular therapies, and nutraceuticals. Although these interventions improve pain and function, they generally do not restore the cartilage extracellular matrix or provide sustained disease modification. Functional peptides have emerged as promising candidates because of their potential to suppress inflammation, inhibit matrix degradation, promote chondrogenesis, target damaged cartilage, and support sustained or targeted delivery. This narrative review evaluated the pathobiological rationale, veterinary evidence, peptide classes, delivery technologies, pharmacological requirements, and translational barriers relevant to veterinary OA. Targeted literature searches and qualitative evidence appraisal focused on clinical relevance, peptide mechanisms, delivery strategies, species-specific limitations, and the distinction between nutritional collagen hydrolysates and sequence-defined therapeutic peptides. Oral bioactive collagen peptides currently provide the most direct clinical evidence in naturally occurring canine and equine OA. However, the principal canine trial was limited by modest sample size and duration, predominantly symptomatic rather than structural outcomes, and manufacturer support. Thus, the available evidence supports potential adjunctive clinical benefit rather than a disease-modifying claim. Sequence-defined hyaluronan-binding, bone morphogenetic protein receptor-mimetic, collagen-binding, collagen-hybridizing, and cartilage-targeting peptides have demonstrated mechanistic or delivery advantages in cell, tissue, rodent, and selected large-animal studies, but target-species pharmacokinetic and clinical validation remains limited. A credible development pathway should integrate target-specific activity, protease stability, immunogenicity, manufacturability, species-appropriate delivery, joint exposure, repeated-dose safety, objective gait and activity outcomes, and structural endpoints. Functional peptides are unlikely to replace multimodal care in the near term but may become valuable adjunctive platforms and contribute to future disease-modifying strategies when biological activity is supported by demonstrated joint exposure, structural protection, and rigorous comparative trials.

papers.title: Seroprevalence of anti-Leptospira antibodies in unvaccinated hunting and guard dogs from Tiaret, northwestern Algeria: a cross-sectional study.
papers.authors: Bia T, Korba AA, Slimani KM, Villanueva-Saz S, Manseur H, Mekhloufi OA, Degui D, Khames M, Lafri I, Györke A, Benameur Q
papers.abstract: Leptospirosis is a globally important zoonotic disease caused by pathogenic Leptospira species and represents a public health concern, particularly for people in close contact with infected companion animals. As the seroprevalence of canine leptospirosis in Algeria remains unknown, this study aimed to estimate seroprevalence and identify potential risk factors in dogs from Tiaret Province. A total of 82 dogs of both sexes, aged 6 months to 10 years, were sampled between January and December 2022 and underwent a general clinical examination, general health status was recorded as good or poor, and the absence of clinical signs compatible with leptospirosis ( collapse, jaundice, difficulty breathing, heamaturia) was noted. Serum samples were tested using the Microscopic Agglutination Test, the international reference serological method. Overall seroprevalence was 29.3% (95% confidence interval (CI): 20.5-39.9). The most frequently detected reactions were to Patoc (8.5%; 95% CI:4.2-16.6; 7/82), Bratislava (8.5%; 95% CI:4.2-16.6; 7/82), Autumnalis and Copenhageni (7.3% each; 95% CI: 3.4-15.1; 6/82), Icterohaemorrhagiae (6.1%; 95% CI:2.6-13.5; 5/82), Canicola (4.9%; 95% CI:1.9-11.9; 4/82), and Pyrogenes (1.2%; 95% CI:0.2-6.6; 1/82). Among the 24 seropositive dogs, 66.7% (95% CI: 46.7-82.0) reacted to a single serovar, whereas 33.3% (95% CI: 18.0-53.3) reacted to two or three serovars, indicating exposure to diverse leptospiral antigens. Two dogs reacted simultaneously to Copenhageni and Icterohaemorrhagiae, both belonging to the Icterohaemorrhagiae serogroup. None of the investigated variables - sex, age, breed group, function (hunting vs. guard), geographical area, or health status - was significantly associated with leptospiral seropositivity (p > 0.05). These findings demonstrate a previous exposure to multiple Leptospira serovars among unvaccinated hunting and guard dogs in Tiaret and highlight a potential zoonotic risk to humans, particularly dog owners and other individuals in close contact with dogs.

papers.title: Clinical leptospirosis in a cat presenting with severe hypokalaemia and glucosuria.
papers.authors: Jagdhane R, Cattin R
papers.abstract: A 1.5-year-old, female spayed domestic mediumhair cat presented for lethargy, inappetence, weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia and severe generalised muscle weakness with cervical ventroflexion. She was noted to be severely hypokalaemic and to have severe glucosuria without significant hyperglycaemia. PCR and serological tests suggested a diagnosis of leptospirosis serovar Pomona. The cat was treated with doxycycline, potassium supplementation and spironolactone, after which the hypokalaemia improved and glucosuria resolved when assessed 2 weeks later. Cats are generally considered to be resistant to clinical infection with leptospirosis, and reports of clinical disease are rare. To the authors' knowledge, there have been no reports of hypokalaemia or severe glucosuria in clinically affected cats. In addition, this report highlights the importance of considering leptospirosis as a differential diagnosis in cats who are exposed to various risk factors reported for this disease.

papers.title: Long-term, longitudinal companion dog research at a nationwide scale.
papers.authors: Creevy K

papers.title: Primary Erythrocytosis (Polycythaemia) in a Neutered Male Dog Presenting With Right Hindlimb Lameness.
papers.authors: Belch R, Henry P, Ferreira M, Padros AA, Munoz ML, Lloyd-Bradley B, Isaac I, Llewellyn E, Nagendran A
papers.abstract: A 2-year-old male entire Cocker Spaniel was referred for investigation of progressive right hindlimb lameness and polyuria and polydipsia. Investigations conducted by the primary care veterinary surgeon revealed erythrocytosis (haematocrit of 78%, reference interval: 37%-55%) and urine concentration consistent with polyuria and polydipsia (specific gravity 1.014). Upon referral, physical examination revealed a dark red oral mucosa and right hindlimb lameness, characterised by intermittent non-weight bearing of the limb when standing. Neurological examination only revealed a mild short-strided gait, and orthopaedic examination was unremarkable. Secondary causes of erythrocytosis were excluded by normal arterial blood gas, low erythropoietin levels and normal thoracic and abdominal imaging, resulting in a diagnosis of primary erythrocytosis (PE). Focal ultrasonography identified a right external iliac venous thrombus, suspected to be the cause of the right hindlimb lameness and presumed to be associated with the PE. Initial management involved repeated phlebotomies, followed by long-term treatment with hydroxyurea (31 mg/kg twice weekly) and rivaroxaban (2 mg/kg once daily). At the 5-month recheck, the dog was asymptomatic, with resolution of the iliac thrombus and a normal haematocrit. This case highlights an unusual presentation of PE in a dog, not previously described in the veterinary literature, and re-examines the discussion on the optimal management of this rare condition, with a focus on the necessity of antithrombotic therapy.

papers.title: Surgical Site Infection and Antimicrobial Resistance After Mastectomy in Dogs and Cats: A 615-Case Multicentre Cohort and Infection-Control Audit.
papers.authors: Hedayatinia M, Gorjian F, Pato M, Maadi MA, Ahmadi R, Abdous A
papers.abstract: Surgical site infection (SSI) is an important complication after mastectomy and antimicrobial resistance may complicate treatment. To estimate 30-day SSI incidence after mastectomy in dogs (Canis lupus familiaris Linnaeus, 1758) and cats (Felis catus Linnaeus, 1758), evaluate patient- and procedure-related factors, describe perioperative antimicrobial use and microbiology and assess clinic infection-control practices. This multicentre retrospective cohort included 615 mastectomy procedures from 12 veterinary clinics in Tehran Province, Iran, between 2020 and 2025. SSI-positive records were independently re-reviewed by two investigators using contemporary veterinary SSI terminology. Clinic-stratified conditional logistic regression evaluated seven clinically selected predictors. SSI occurred after 54/615 procedures (8.8%; 95% CI, 6.8%-11.3%); 50 infections were superficial and four deep. Surgical duration per 30 min (aOR, 2.37; 95% CI, 1.61-3.49), intraoperative hypothermia (aOR, 3.66; 95% CI, 1.39-9.62), body condition score per point (aOR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.05-2.42) and previous major surgery (aOR, 3.57; 95% CI, 1.49-8.55) were associated with SSI. An MDR isolate was identified in 16/33 cultured SSI cases and antimicrobial-isolate discordance was present in 15/30 assessable comparisons. Mean clinic infection-control audit score was 4.6 ± 1.7/10. Longer surgery, intraoperative hypothermia, higher body condition score and previous major surgery were associated with SSI in this predominantly canine cohort of intact animals undergoing mastectomy without concurrent ovariohysterectomy. These associations were not independently demonstrated in cats. The findings support standardised surveillance, perioperative risk reduction, culture-guided treatment and antimicrobial stewardship. Not applicable. This was a retrospective observational study and clinic-level audit and was not a clinical trial.

papers.title: Toxoplasma gondii in Ethiopia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Infection Prevalence and Associated Risk Factors in Humans and Animals.
papers.authors: Wubaye AM, Shitu BF, Delie AM, Haimanot AB, Ayicheh YW, Mulugeta AM, Enawgaw AS, Ambaw YG, Bitewa MD, Wondie SG, Kassie TD, Mengie ZA, Kallu SA, Tafere BA, Mekonnen TS, Molla MG, Eshetu DM, Yewodiaw TK
papers.abstract: Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan parasite with significant animal and public health implications. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of toxoplasmosis in ruminants and humans in Ethiopia and to determine the major risk factors associated with the disease. Five databases were used to search for all articles published between 2012 and 2025. The pooled prevalence of toxoplasmosis was calculated using a random-effects model. I 2 statistics were used to assess heterogeneity among the included studies. Publication bias was assessed through a meta-analysis Egger regression asymmetry test. The overall pooled prevalence of T. gondii was 42.0% (95% CI: 35.0%-49.0%) in ruminants and 61.0% (95% CI: 49.0%-74.0%) in humans. Female animals have higher odds of acquiring T. gondii (OR = 1.76; 95% CI: 1.56-2.00) than males. Similarly, adult animals were more likely to be exposed to the disease (OR = 2.39; 95% CI: 2.10-2.74) than young age groups. In humans, rural residence (OR = 1.23; 95% CI: 1.07-1.42) and cat ownership (OR = 2.04; 95% CI: 1.79-2.32) were significantly associated with T. gondii seropositivity. These results highlight the necessity of targeted monitoring and preventative measures to reduce T. gondii exposure in both animal and human populations in Ethiopia.

papers.title: Partners or tools? Ethical framings shape welfare research on dogs and horses in animal-assisted services.
papers.authors: Zenker F, Thodberg K, Sandøe P
papers.abstract: The welfare of dogs and horses involved in animal-assisted services (AAS) has received increasing scholarly attention, reflecting growing recognition of the ethical complexity of human-animal interactions in these settings. However, ethical framings of animal welfare in research on AAS vary substantially, ranging from an emphasis on avoiding harm to animals while pursuing human benefit to the view that AAS should create mutual benefits for both humans and animals. This critical review examines how ethical framings shape AAS welfare research and aims to make underlying assumptions more transparent to support more consistent research and policy. To this end, we analyzed 116 peer-reviewed papers (2000-2025), focusing on conceptual frameworks (e.g., One Health) and their implications for the interpretation of results and conclusions. Included papers covered direct welfare measures in dogs and/or horses, indirect welfare assessments, and conceptual welfare analyses. We identified three key findings. First, ethical frameworks in AAS welfare research are highly diverse and at times insufficiently specified. Second, studies may combine multiple ethical framings, reflecting a pluralism of ethical perspectives. Conceptual conflation may arise, however, when positive and negative welfare perspectives are combined without acknowledging their fundamentally different understandings of welfare. Third, a recurring pattern across the literature is a relational framing of ethical considerations, highlighting the need for greater attention to different understandings of good or justified human-animal relationships. Overall, greater transparency about ethical framing is needed to improve the interpretation, comparability, and communication of welfare findings.

papers.title: Development of a sandwich ELISA for recombinant feline GM-CSF and determination of its serum half-life.
papers.authors: Yu C, Wang M, Chen L, Wang T, Zhao Y, Song H, Jin M
papers.abstract: Feline granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) is a key cytokine involved in the regulation of myeloid immune responses and represents an important therapeutic target for leukopenia. However, the rapid in vivo clearance of native GM-CSF requires frequent administration, which limits its clinical translation. To overcome this limitation, a recombinant GM-CSF-Fc protein was constructed using Fc fusion technology. Pharmacokinetic evaluation of GM-CSF-Fc, however, is constrained by the lack of analytical approaches capable of simultaneously quantifying differently engineered forms of recombinant GM-CSF. In this study, recombinant feline GM-CSF was expressed in a CHO eukaryotic expression system and used to immunize rabbits to generate high-affinity polyclonal antibodies. Based on these antibodies, a sandwich ELISA was established. The assay exhibited excellent linearity within 7.8-2000 pg/mL (R 2  = 0.993), and its validated quantitative range was 50-2000 pg/mL, covering the expected concentration fluctuations of recombinant GM-CSF under physiological and immune-activated conditions in cats. The assay demonstrated good precision and accuracy, and no cross-reactivity with related feline cytokines (IL-3, IL-5, M-CSF, and G-CSF) was observed. Notably, the system efficiently quantified differently engineered forms of recombinant feline GM-CSF (His-tagged and Fc-fused) with comparable recovery, overcoming the limitations of conventional assays optimized for a single protein format. Pharmacokinetic analysis following subcutaneous administration in cats showed that Fc fusion substantially prolonged the apparent terminal elimination half-life of immunoreactive GM-CSF from 5.05 ± 0.91 h to 40.89 ± 3.41 h, supporting the improved pharmacokinetic profile of the Fc-fused construct. In conclusion, this study provides a versatile and sensitive analytical platform for the preclinical evaluation of Fc-fused feline GM-CSF formulations and serves as an important methodological reference for the quantitative assessment of Fc-fused veterinary biologicals.

papers.title: Clinically relevant hypomagnesemia during recovery from severe leptospirosis-associated acute kidney injury in a dog treated with continuous renal replacement therapy: a case report.
papers.authors: Cho J, Kang S, Kim S, Kim M, Park C
papers.abstract: Leptospirosis is an important cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) in dogs and commonly induces renal tubular dysfunction. Although electrolyte abnormalities are frequently recognized during the course of leptospirosis, clinically relevant hypomagnesemia associated with neurological manifestations has rarely been reported in dogs. This report describes a dog that developed severe symptomatic hypomagnesemia during recovery from severe leptospirosis-associated AKI treated with continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). A 9 year old, 12 kg spayed female mixed-breed dog was referred for severe leptospirosis-associated AKI complicated by anuria, hyperbilirubinemia, thrombocytopenia, and pulmonary involvement. Blood and urine polymerase chain reaction assays confirmed Leptospira spp. Because of persistent anuria and progressive azotemia despite intensive medical management, the dog underwent two continuous renal replacement therapy sessions approximately 15 and 18 h, respectively. Urine production subsequently recovered, and the dog entered a polyuric recovery phase with progressive improvement in azotemia. On day 13 after admission, generalized tremors, hypersalivation, and altered mentation developed concurrently with severe hypomagnesemia (ionized magnesium, 0.24 mmol/L; total magnesium, 1.4 mg/dL). Fractional excretion of magnesium (FEMG) was markedly increased (38.8%), suggesting inappropriate renal magnesium loss despite improving renal function. Intravenous magnesium sulfate administered as a bolus followed by continuous rate infusion resulted in rapid resolution of the neurological signs. At follow-up evaluations performed 11 and 23 days after the hypomagnesemic episode, fractional excretion of magnesium remained increased at 30.2% and 28.4%, respectively, despite improvement in serum creatinine concentration, supporting persistent impairment of renal tubular magnesium handling during recovery. This case demonstrates that clinically significant hypomagnesemia may develop during the polyuric recovery phase of severe leptospirosis-associated AKI in dogs, even after apparent improvement in renal function. Serial measurements of fractional excretion of magnesium supported continued renal magnesium loss during recovery and emphasized the importance of monitoring magnesium concentrations in dogs with leptospirosis, particularly when neurological abnormalities develop.

papers.title: Isolation, identification and antifungal resistance profile of toxigenic Aspergillus species from marketed dog foods in Ibadan, Nigeria.
papers.authors: Adeyemo IA, Ahmed AO, Isola TO, Aremu A, Odetokun IA, Raufu IA, Raji MA
papers.abstract: Mycotoxin-producing fungi that contaminate dog food have effects on the feed's nutritional value, organoleptic characteristics, and overall quality. Animals and humans may experience both short-term and long-term harmful effects by consuming fungi and mycotoxin-contaminated feeds. In dogs, high morbidity and mortality are observed as a result of immunosuppressive, hepatotoxic, nephrotoxic, and carcinogenic effects from the mycotoxins. This study investigated the occurrence, antimicrobial resistance profile and mycotoxins produced by toxigenic Aspergillus species, with the potential aim of providing baseline information on the quality and safety of commercial dog feeds. Eighteen brands/types of dog food samples were obtained from pet and veterinary stores in Ibadan, Oyo State. Two main species of presumptive toxigenic Aspergillus were isolated and identified by using both macroscopic examination and standard microbiological procedures. Antifungal susceptibility test (AFST) was carried out using the disc diffusion method to determine resistance profiles of these presumptive isolates (n=14). The GC-MS analytical method was used to screen 10 selected dog foods for 16 different mycotoxins. Sixteen (88.9%) samples were presumptively positive for Aspergillus species. All (100%) crunchies (imported), noodles and mash types of dog food samples were positive for Aspergillus species. While two out of the three local crunchies and one out of the spaghetti types of the dog food were positive for Aspergillus species. Seven (39%) and 16 (89%) isolation rates were recorded for presumptive Aspergillus parasiticus and Aspergillus flavus, respectively. A varying degree of resistance was observed among the selected isolates to Miconazole, Ketoconazole, Clotrimazole and Nystatin. However, 100% of the 14 isolates showed resistance to Flucytosine and Fluconazole, while 100% of the selected isolates were sensitive to Econazole. Seven different resistance patterns were observed for the 14 isolates of both Aspergillus parasiticus and Aspergillus flavus, with 85.7 % Multiple drugs resistance (MDR). Nine mycotoxins (Aflatoxins B1, G1, G2, M1, M2, Fumonisin B2, Ochratoxin A, T2-toxin and H2-toxin) were detected and higher levels for seven of the mycotoxins (Aflatoxins B1, G1, G2, M1, M2, Ochratoxin A and T2-toxin) were observed. This study isolated toxigenic Aspergillus spp that are resistant to standard antifungal drugs with high mycotoxin contamination in dog foods marketed in Ibadan.

papers.title: Monitoring of oxidative stress and acute phase proteins following testes exposure with ultrasound waves in cats.
papers.authors: Hashempur Z, Mogheiseh A, Nazifi S, Divar M, Ahmadi N, Derakhshandeh N, Ahmadi E, Bastani M, Shaikhzadeh A, Hassani A
papers.abstract: Ultrasonic therapy has harmfully effects on the structure and function of the testis. Various mechanisms are involved in the impact of ultrasound waves on testes tissue. This study aimed to investigate the effects of ultrasound exposure on cat`s testes by monitoring acute phase proteins, oxidative stress indices, histopathology, and epididymal sperm evaluation over a period of 60 days. Ten adult domestic short hair (DSH) male cats were divided into two equal groups: one exposed to ultrasound and one control groups. The testes were exposed to ultrasonic therapy using 1 MHz, 1.5 W/cm 2 , three times with a 48-hour interval. Blood samples were taken before treatment and at days 1, 3, and 6 after treatment. Histopathology of the testes and epididymal sperm evaluation were performed at day 60. The results showed that acute phase proteins, serum amyloid (SAA), C-reactive protein (CRP), and alpha-1 glycoprotein (AGP), significantly increased in the first three days after treatment and decreased significantly by day 6 in the treatment group. The increase in acute phase proteins was significantly higher in the treatment group compared to the control group. Malondialdehyde (MDA) and total antioxidant capacity (TAC) did not show significant change in the first week after treatment in the ultrasound exposure group compared to the control group. Testosterone concentration was significantly decreased in the ultrasound exposure group compared to the control group. The epididymal sperm and histopathology evaluation indicated no harmful effect of ultrasound in the treatment group compared to the control group. Ultrasound exposure of cat`s testes induced an acute phase inflammatory response and decreased testosterone concentration in the first week after treatment, but it did not have harmful effect on testis tissue and epididymal sperm quality.

papers.title: Dose-response effects of dietary luteolin-loaded chitosan nanoparticles on growth and physiological responses of post-weaning rabbits reared under summer heat stress.
papers.authors: Thagfan FA, Al-Hoshani N, Mohamed RAEH, Ahmed KAE, Abdelnour SA, Abd-Elkarim MM
papers.abstract: Applying nanotechnology to promote sustainable livestock production and mitigate the adverse impacts of rising global temperatures on animal health has received critical attention. In the existing research, we synthesized luteolin-loaded chitosan nanoparticles (NLU) and evaluated their efficacy in mitigating heat stress (HS) in growing rabbits by investigating growth performance, immune response, oxidative stress, tissues integrity, antioxidant defenses, inflammatory markers, and apoptotic cascades. A total of 120 weaned growing rabbits (New Zealand white breed) were randomly assigned to four experimental groups (30 rabbits per group, with 30 replicates per group) and raised under summer condition during a 9 weeks trial. Treatments consisted of a basal control diet (HS group) or the basal diet fortified with 25 (NLU25), 50 (NLU50), or 100 (NLU100) mg/kg of NLU. The temperature-humidity index (THI) was 30.65, calculated from ambient temperature and relative humidity, confirming that the rabbits experienced severe HS. The prepared NLU nanoparticles exhibited a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 138.5 nm, a polydispersity index of 0.380, and a positive zeta potential of + 54.5 mV. Dietary NLU supplementation exhibited a significant quadratic dose-response effect on growth performance (P < 0.05), with the NLU50 and NLU100 treatments eliciting the most pronounced protective effects relative to the HS group. Dietary NLU supplementation significantly decreased serum lipid profiles, liver enzymes, and renal function markers (P < 0.05). Specifically, NLU quadratically increased glutathione peroxidase (GPx), catalase (CAT) levels, and total antioxidant capacity (TAC, linear effect), alongside immunoglobulin concentrations (IgM and IgG) (P < 0.05). Conversely, oxidative stress indicators (myeloperoxidase and MDA) and cell death biomarkers (caspase-3 and CK-18) were markedly reduced (P < 0.001) in quadratic manner. Furthermore, NLU supplementation quadratically attenuated the inflammatory response by decreasing the serum inflammatory makers including nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-4 (IL-4), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-8 (IL-8) alongside significant increase of nitric oxide levels (P < 0.001). Consequently, dietary NLU effectively preserved the histoarchitectural integrity of both hepatic and intestinal tissues under heat-stress conditions. Overall, dietary inclusion of 50 or 100 mg/kg NLU effectively showed beneficial effects on growth indices in rabbits exposed to heat stress by preserving tissue histoarchitecture, remodeling metabolic and redox homeostasis, boosting immune competence, and suppressing inflammatory and apoptotic signaling cascades.

papers.title: Prevalence and clinical relevance of hypocobalaminaemia and hypercobalaminaemia in cats.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Casas C, Dye C
papers.abstract: The aim of the present study was to investigate the prevalence of hypo- and hypercobalaminaemia in a cohort of cats with diverse disease pathologies and to assess associations with signalment and disease characteristics. Residual blood from cats presented to a large veterinary referral hospital during a 24-month period was used for serum B12 quantification. All cats requiring blood collection as part of diagnostic investigations were eligible for inclusion regardless of clinical presentation. Serum B12 concentration was assessed according to signalment, body weight, body condition score, primary affected body system and type of disease pathology as derived from the clinical notes. A total of 229 cats were enrolled: 128 male (119 neutered, 9 entire) and 101 female (88 neutered, 13 entire). Of these, 176 were domestic shorthair or longhair, and 53 were purebred. The median age was 9.9 years and median body weight 4.1 kg. Of the 229 cats, 80 (34.9%) had high serum B12, 86 (37.6%) had normal, 18 (7.9%) had borderline and 45 (19.7%) had low serum B12. Median serum B12 concentration was higher in cats aged <8.0 years than ⩾8.0 years, and there was a weak but significant negative correlation between age and serum B12. Median serum B12 concentration was lower in cats weighing <3.0 kg than in those ⩾3.0 kg, and a weak but significant positive correlation was found between body weight and serum B12 concentration. No associations were found between serum B12 and sex, breed, body condition score, affected body system or pathology type. Vitamin B12 aberrations were common in this cohort of cats, with approximately one-third and one-fifth having abnormally high and low serum concentrations, respectively. Serum vitamin B12 concentration declined with advancing age, and hypocobalaminaemia was more prevalent in cats with body weights <3.0 kg. Hypo- and hypercobalaminaemia were documented in cats with a wide variety of clinical presentations, and no specific disease associations were elucidated.

papers.title: A case of pseudo-obstruction in a cat associated with amebiasis.
papers.authors: de Sousa Filho RP, Lopes Neto BE, Ferreira CB, Sampaio KO
papers.abstract: This report describes a 9-year-old, spayed female domestic shorthair cat presenting with a 7-day history of anorexia and previous chronic constipation. Clinical examination revealed abdominal distension and discomfort. Radiographic and ultrasonographic imaging showed severe, generalized gaseous distension of the entire gastrointestinal tract without evidence of mechanical obstruction. An exploratory celiotomy confirmed severe, non-obstructive dilation of the stomach and intestines, with aperistalsis of the ileum and large intestine. Histopathological analysis of intestinal biopsies revealed neuritis and necrosis of the myenteric plexus, along with the presence of protozoan trophozoites consistent with Entamoeba histolytica . These findings led to a diagnosis of intestinal pseudo-obstruction secondary to amebiasis-associated ganglionitis. Treatment was initiated with pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, and metronidazole. The cat responded favorably, with resolution of clinical signs and normalization of defecation. This case documents a rare instance of intestinal pseudo-obstruction in a cat, uniquely associating it with amebiasis and demonstrating a successful therapeutic outcome with pyridostigmine. To our knowledge, this is the first report of intestinal pseudo-obstruction associated with amebiasis in a feline patient. Furthermore, it adds to the limited literature on the successful use of pyridostigmine for treating severe gastrointestinal dysmotility in cats, offering a potential therapeutic option for this challenging condition.

papers.title: Feasibility of Shallow Whole-Genome Sequencing-Based Circulating Tumour DNA Analysis in Canine Multicentric Lymphoma: A Pilot Study.
papers.authors: Kim GH, Jang JH, Kim SH, Ryu MO, Kwon CH, Seo KW
papers.abstract: Lymphoma is a common canine malignancy with high morbidity and variable prognosis. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a minimally invasive biomarker for tumour burden, treatment response and prognosis in human lymphoma. However, the feasibility of applying shallow whole-genome sequencing (sWGS)-based ctDNA analysis to canine lymphoma remains unclear. In this pilot study, plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) was quantitatively assessed and additional genomic features were evaluated using sWGS in dogs with multicentric lymphoma. cfDNA concentration was significantly higher in dogs with lymphoma (n = 13) compared with healthy controls (n = 24) (median 3.18 vs. 0.25 ng/mL; Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.004). However, total cfDNA concentration was not significantly associated with time to progression (TTP) (p = 0.055). Tumour fraction (TF), a surrogate for ctDNA, showed preliminary association with clinical outcome, with a shorter median TTP in the high-TF group than in the low-TF group (77 vs. 302 days; p = 0.006). Genomic analysis further revealed copy number aberrations (CNAs); notably, gains on chromosome 13 containing the MYC locus were identified in three dogs, all of which belonged to the high-TF group. Dogs with lymphoma also displayed distinct cfDNA fragmentation profiles, characterized by an enrichment of shorter fragments within the analysed size range and a shift in the highest mean-profile peak compared with healthy controls. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of sWGS-based cfDNA analysis in canine lymphoma and suggest that TF may provide clinically relevant information beyond total cfDNA concentration. Validation in a substantially larger, independent cohort is warranted.

papers.title: Bendamustine induces peripheral lymphodepletion in dogs with relapsed lymphoma.
papers.authors: Lenz JA, Upton L, Ma J, Talone MM, Peng B, Jiang L, Ghanian A, Didehvar D, Yang E, Fraietta JA, Atherton MJ
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has improved outcomes for many human patients with B-cell lymphoma and provides a rational template for analogous canine patients. To date, the expansion, persistence, and activity of CAR T cells in dogs have been limited. Lymphodepletion supports CAR T-cell engraftment and antitumor activity. In human medical oncology, bendamustine has emerged as a well-tolerated lymphodepleting agent. However, prospective use of bendamustine for dogs with lymphoma has not been characterized. To determine the lymphodepleting activity and tolerability of bendamustine in dogs with relapsed lymphoma. Secondary objectives included monitoring serum cytokines and short-term changes in peripheral tumor burden. Eleven client-owned dogs with relapsed lymphoma. Luminescent assays were used to assess the direct cytotoxic activity of bendamustine against canine lymphoid cell lines. A prospective rapid dose-escalation pilot trial was undertaken in 11 dogs with relapsed lymphoma to evaluate tolerability while tracking peripheral lymphocyte counts, serum cytokine concentrations, and lymph node measurements. Bendamustine induced concentration-dependent cytotoxicity in all cell lines tested. Two-dose bendamustine regimens up to 90 mg/m2 were generally well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities observed, and resulted in peripheral lymphodepletion (pretreatment median, 880 cells/μL; posttreatment median, 310 cells/μL), an exploratory decrease in circulating interleukin-6 (pretreatment median, 5.32 pg/mL; posttreatment median, 1.33 pg/mL), and a short-term decrease in peripheral nodal burden in 8 of 11 dogs. Bendamustine was generally well tolerated and induced lymphodepletion in our cohort. These findings support further evaluation of bendamustine as a preconditioning agent before autologous canine CAR T-cell infusion.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Hyperammonemia in cats with acute (on chronic) kidney disease: associations with urea cycle amino acids, azotemia and acid-base status.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: McFadden K, Labato MA, Linder DE, Webster CR
papers.abstract: ObjectivesHyperammonemia occurs in cats with kidney disease although the pathophysiology is poorly understood. The objective of this study was to determine if hyperammonemia in cats with kidney disease is associated with decreased concentrations of plasma amino acids involved in the urea cycle and more severe acid-base derangements.MethodsTwenty cats presenting with acute kidney injury (AKI) and acute on chronic kidney disease (AoCKD) were prospectively enrolled. Fasting blood samples were analyzed for ammonia, pH, anion gap, electrolytes, lactate, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine and phosphorus. Plasma was frozen at -80 o C and shipped for amino acid analysis.ResultsFive of 20 cats had an AKI and 15/20 had AoCKD. Median age and weight were 12 years (range 3-14) and 4.5 kg (range 3-5.6), respectively. Seven cats were hyperammonemic (median 252 µmol/l, range 113-886) and 13 were not (median 23 µmol/l, range 11-49). Creatinine, BUN and phosphorus were significantly higher in hyperammonemic cats. BUN and phosphorus correlated with ammonia. Fifteen of 20 cats (75%) were acidotic but there was no difference in lactate or blood and urine pH between the cats with and without hyperammonemia. The anion gap was higher (29.6, range 27-40 vs 25.1, range 11-34) and serum bicarbonate lower (9 mEq/L, range 4.8-13.5 vs 11.9, range 8-24.2) in hyperammonemic cats. Median plasma citrulline (47 nMol/mL, range 31-128 vs 22, range 12-37) and ornithine (20 nMol/mL, range 12-33 vs 10, range 7-35) but not arginine concentrations were significantly higher in hyperammonemic cats (p<0.05). Plasma citrulline concentrations were positively correlated with serum creatinine (r = 0.621, p = 0.003).Conclusions and relevanceHyperammonemic cats with AKI/AoCKD do not have deficiencies in urea cycle amino acid concentrations but do have more severe azotemia with accompanying high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Increases in citrulline may reflect decreased kidney function.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Elbow luxation treatment in cats using external fixation.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Yener K, Hurma MS, Karadağ MS, Dikmen Ilginoğlu K, Hünerli H, Bayir ÖY, Yavuz Ü, Hayat A
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo describe outcomes and complications of open reduction, collateral ligament repair and temporary epoxy resin Type Ia transarticular external skeletal fixation (TaESF) in cats with traumatic lateral elbow luxation after failed closed treatment.MethodsTen cats were referred 3-4 days after injury. Closed reduction failed in four cats and reluxation occurred in six after reduction and Robert Jones bandaging. All underwent open reduction, apposition of identifiable collateral ligament ends and four-pin epoxy resin Type Ia TaESF. Clinical and orthogonal radiographic examinations were performed weekly until frame removal at 3 weeks and at 6 weeks. Lameness was graded 0-3, and Campbell's test was performed after frame removal and at 6 weeks. At 6 months, three cats underwent orthopaedic examination and seven were assessed by structured owner telephone interview. Complications were classified according to Cook et al.ResultsReduction was maintained in all cats through 6 weeks. Grade 0/1 lameness was recorded in seven/three cats at 3 weeks and eight/two cats at 6 weeks (Cases 3 and 9). Functional outcome was full in eight cats (80%) and acceptable in two (20%). A contralateral proximal ulnar fracture contributed to residual lameness in Case 3. Case 1 required unplanned intervention for proximal humeral pin migration and seroma. The pin was repositioned under sedation without replacement or additional epoxy resin. Radiolucency and periosteal reaction surrounded the distal ulnar pin. The seroma resolved without recurrence, and the frame was removed as scheduled. No comparable pin-site radiographic abnormalities were identified in the other cats. At 6 months, all cats had normal owner-reported walking, running and jumping without observable lameness.Conclusions and relevanceIn this small retrospective series, open reduction and collateral ligament repair protected by epoxy resin Type Ia TaESF maintained reduction and yielded satisfactory short-term outcomes after failed closed treatment. One cat required unplanned intervention for a pin-related complication. Comparative studies with objective long-term clinical and radiographic follow-up are warranted.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Feline granulocytic anaplasmosis in Europe: anamnesis, clinicopathological abnormalities, bacterial DNA load, treatment, and outcome.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Meyer L, Moritz A, Baneth G, Strube C, Jindal K, Müller E, Schäfer I
papers.abstract: Feline granulocytic anaplasmosis (FGA) is caused by Anaplasma ( A. ) phagocytophilum . Fever and thrombocytopenia are the most common clinicopathological abnormalities.ObjectivesThe aim was to investigate regionality, seasonality, clinicopathological parameters, treatment, and outcomes in cats with FGA.MethodsThe database of a commercial laboratory was retrospectively screened for A. phagocytophilum -polymerase chain (PCR)-results on EDTA-blood submitted by European veterinarians from 01/2022 to 12/2025. Hematological data and bacterial DNA loads quantified by digital droplet-PCR were analyzed. Questionnaires were sent to the veterinarians asking for underlying diseases, anamnesis, clinicopathological abnormalities, treatment, and outcome in cats with FGA.Results43/702 cats (6.1%) tested positive by A. phagocytophilum -PCR in Europe. Questionnaires were available for 29/43 cats (67.4%), all of which had outdoor access. Lethargy (23/29; 79.3%), anorexia (22/29, 75.9%), and fever (>39.5°C, 18/29, 62.0%) were the most reported findings. Thrombocytopenia was detected in 14/18 cats (77.8%) without concurrent diseases, anemia and leukopenia in 2/20 cats each (10.0%), eosinopenia in 10/17 (58.8%), and lymphopenia in 8/17 cats (47.1%). The bacterial DNA load was available for 27/43 cats (25 x 10 2 -87 x 10 6 , median 124 x 10 5 /ml EDTA-blood), revealing no significant correlation with hematological parameters. 20/21 cats (95.2%) were treated with doxycycline and one (4.8%) with enrofloxacin. Uncomplicated course of disease was reported in 19/21 cats (90.5%). In one cat treated with doxycycline for 10 days, another positive PCR was recorded one month later. Clinical signs recurred immediately in another cat treated with doxycycline for five days only.Conclusions and relevanceFGA should be considered in cats with outdoor access, lethargy, inappetence, and most often mild thrombocytopenia and/or anemia, regardless of fever. Infected cats usually responded well to doxycycline with individual relapses if treated for 10 days or shorter. Treatment for 14 days to clear the infection, and PCR monitoring after finishing treatment are recommended.

papers.title: Intraoperative Indocyanine Green Fluorescence for Assessment of Suspected Venous Invasion in a Dog With Thyroid Carcinoma.
papers.authors: Kim M, Kim Y, Lee S
papers.abstract: Accurate intraoperative assessment of vascular involvement in canine thyroid carcinoma remains challenging when preoperative imaging findings are equivocal. This case describes the use of intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence imaging to assist real-time assessment of suspected venous involvement during canine thyroidectomy. A 5-year-old spayed female Maltese dog was presented with a cervical mass and clinicopathological findings consistent with hypothyroidism. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography identified a left thyroid mass with suspected external jugular vein compression but no definitive evidence of vascular invasion. During left thyroidectomy, dilation and distal tapering of the thyroid veins raised concern for venous involvement. Indocyanine green (0.5 mg/dog) was administered intravenously for intraoperative near-infrared fluorescence imaging. Diffuse fluorescence of the thyroid mass and segmental intraluminal fluorescence within the dilated thyroid vein were observed, with signal loss at the tapering point. Based on these findings, en bloc resection including a short segment of the involved vein was performed. Histopathology confirmed thyroid carcinoma without evidence of regional lymph node metastasis. This case illustrates that intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence imaging may provide adjunctive real-time information for assessing suspected venous involvement during canine thyroid carcinoma surgery and may complement preoperative imaging when vascular invasion is uncertain.

papers.title: Effects of violet light exposure on aging dogs: a pilot study.
papers.authors: Miyamoto K, Ono N, Kondo S, Miwa Y, Tsubota K, Ozawa M, Kikusui T
papers.abstract: Aging in dogs is known to induce various physical and brain alterations similar to dementia in humans. Concurrently with the recent extension of canine life expectancy, these age-related changes have imposed growing burdens on both dogs and their owners, emerging as a significant social issue. However, no curative treatment has yet been established, and the current mainstay of management focuses on improving the quality of life through symptomatic therapies, such as environmental modifications and pharmacotherapy. This study focused on violet light, which has suggested efficacy against such age-related changes. We developed a novel violet light irradiation device and evaluated its efficacy and safety in elderly dogs as a pilot study. An intra-individual comparison using an ABA design was employed with geriatric dogs aged 14 to 16 years housed in a senior dog care facility (two of which discontinued midway). The study design consisted of a one-month violet light exposure phase preceded and followed by two-week non-exposure periods. Physical activity levels were measured using accelerometers and cognitive function was assessed using the DISHAA and CCDR. To evaluate the safety, general physical and ophthalmic examinations were conducted by veterinarians. As a result, no significant overall effect was found on activity levels (Daytime: x 2  = 4.22, p  = 0.12; Nighttime: x 2  = 1.58, p  = 0.45). Similarly, no significant overall effects were observed for either the DISHAA or the CCDR (DISHAA: x 2  = 1.60, p  = 0.45; CCDR: x 2  = 1.56, p  = 0.46). However, a trend toward cognitive improvement was observed in six out of seven dogs and an upward trend in activity levels-indicating physical function improvement-was noted in two out of seven dogs. Regarding safety, no overt clinical abnormalities associated with violet light irradiation were identified.
