This pilot study demonstrated no clear overall effect, though some individuals showed signs of improvement. Future research should consider large-scale trials controlling for various variables.

papers.title: Case Report: 18 F-FDG PET/CT findings and SUVmax characterization in a dog with apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Shim B, Kim Y, Lee S
papers.abstract: Apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA) is a malignant epithelial tumor in dogs that commonly metastasizes to regional lymph nodes. Although 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18 F-FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) has been mentioned as a staging modality for this tumor, detailed imaging findings and maximum standardized uptake values (SUVmax) have not previously been reported. A 10-year-old castrated male Maltese was referred for a right anal sac mass and suspected lymph node metastasis. Preoperative 18 F-FDG PET/CT revealed increased uptake in the primary mass (SUVmax 7.3), the internal iliac lymph node (SUVmax 6.35), and the lumbar aortic lymph node (SUVmax 4.3), with no evidence of distant metastasis. Therefore, the dog was therefore classified as Stage IIIa. Based on these findings, intra-abdominal lymphadenectomy and right anal sacculectomy were performed. Histopathology confirmed AGASACA in the primary mass and morphologically similar metastatic adenocarcinoma in the resected lymph nodes. To our knowledge, this is the first report of 18 F-FDG PET/CT findings and SUVmax values in a dog with AGASACA and histologically confirmed lymph node metastases. These findings suggest that PET/CT may provide complementary metabolic information for preoperative nodal staging.

papers.title: Sarcocystis sp. infection associated to encephalomyelitis and myositis in a Brazilian dog.
papers.authors: do Nascimento Iara ÍH, Martins AFG, de Sousa Ribeiro L, Boabaid FM, de Oliveira LGS, da Silva EMS, Driemeier D, Torres BBJ
papers.abstract: Sarcocystis sp.-induced disease is known especially in horses, in which S. neurona is the primary causative agent of Equine Protozoal Myeloencephalitis in the Americas. While horses are aberrant hosts, the range of susceptible species includes marine mammals, raccoons, and cats. Reports of clinical disease in dogs are rare, remaining unreported in South America. This study describes the clinical, pathological, and immunohistochemical findings of a naturally occurring, fatal case of meningoencephalomyelitis and myositis caused by Sarcocystis sp. in a dog in Brazil. A 5-year-old mixed-breed bitch presented with acute non-ambulatory tetraparesis, generalized muscle atrophy, and blindness. Despite supportive therapy, the patient deteriorated and was euthanized. Gross findings included enlarged lymph nodes, moderate splenomegaly and hepatomegaly, with multifocal mild fibrin deposition on the liver capsule, accompanied by multifocal mild hemorrhages in the pancreas. Histopathology demonstrated severe, multifocal necrotizing meningoencephalomyelitis, myositis, splenitis, lymphadenitis and interstitial pneumonia, associated with intralesional protozoal schizonts. Immunohistochemistry supported immunolabelling consistent with Sarcocystis sp. while excluding Toxoplasma gondii and Neospora caninum. To the authors' knowledge, this represents the first report of clinical canine sarcocystosis with this severity in South America supported by histopathological and immunohistochemical findings. These findings support that Sarcocystis sp. should be considered a differential diagnosis for canine progressive neurological disease, highlighting the potential role of wildlife reservoirs in the disease's epidemiology.

papers.title: Characterization and in Vitro Radiation Response Analysis of Patient-Derived Heterogeneous Cells From Canine Oral Melanoma.
papers.authors: Hwang G, Oh SJ, Hong IH, Choi MY, Lee SL, Lee HC, Hwang TS
papers.abstract: Conventional cancer cell lines often fail to capture tumour heterogeneity, limiting their translational relevance for radiation response studies. This study aimed to establish a low-passage, patient-derived heterogeneous culture and to evaluate its radiation response characteristics. Tumour tissue obtained from a canine oral melanoma patient was used to generate the culture. Cellular heterogeneity was confirmed by morphological features and the expression of stem cell-associated markers (CD133 + CD44 + : 50.53% ± 5.05%, CD133 - CD44 + : 30.93% ± 7.21%). Tumorigenicity was validated using a xenograft model. Radiation responses to 2 and 10 Gy were assessed using clonogenic survival, viability, proliferation, apoptosis, DNA damage, migration, and invasion assays. The culture demonstrated morphological heterogeneity, expression of stem cell-associated markers, and tumorigenic potential in vivo. Compared with the 0 Gy control, 10 Gy irradiation significantly reduced cell viability, proliferative activity, and migration, while increasing early apoptosis and DNA damage (all p < 0.006). These effects were generally more pronounced after 10 Gy than after 2 Gy. Notably, clonogenic survival curves deviated from the linear-quadratic model, indicating non-classical radiation response behaviour in heterogeneous cell populations. This proof-of-concept study suggests that a low-passage, patient-derived heterogeneous culture may serve as a practical and biologically informative in vitro platform for investigating radiation responses in canine oral melanoma. Further validation using additional patient-derived cultures and comparisons with corresponding clinical radiation responses is needed.

papers.title: Novel liquid biopsy based on comprehensive small RNA profiling for screening of cancer in dogs utilizing machine learning.
papers.authors: Harako S, Yuki M, Noguchi S, Ohno T, Nozaki N, Nishida R, Hojo H, Horikawa R, Kawata D, Noda Y, Miura N, Mizuno T, Momoi Y
papers.abstract: Recent investigations have demonstrated the relevance in cancer of a variety of small RNAs, beyond microRNAs (miRNAs). However, the comprehensive application of these RNAs to cancer detection in dogs remains unexplored. We investigated whether combining miRNAs and other small RNAs using a custom database improves the accuracy of machine learning cancer screening in dogs compared with models using only miRNAs. A total of 389 dogs were enrolled: 85 with cancer, 77 with nonmalignant diseases, and 227 healthy controls. Small RNAs in blood samples were sequenced, and miRNAs (via miRBase) and other small RNAs (via a custom database) were profiled. Based on these profiles, 2 datasets were prepared: one with only miRNAs and another combining miRNAs with other small RNAs. For each dataset, 12 classification models were constructed using identical methods to enable paired comparisons of performance, with 5-fold cross-validation and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as the primary metrics. The model that integrated both miRNAs and other small RNAs yielded a significantly higher AUC compared with the miRNA-only model (median AUC: 0.926 [95% CI, 0.911-0.944] vs 0.881 [0.860-0.897]; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P < .001), indicating enhanced capability in discriminating malignant tumors in dogs. We investigated the comprehensive integration of diverse small RNA species, beyond miRNAs, using a machine learning approach for cancer screening in dogs. Although further prospective validation in independent cohorts is needed, our results indicate that this strategy improves the performance of cancer classification models in dogs.

papers.title: Letter regarding "Pancreatic lymphangioma and concurrent intestinal lymphangiectasia in a dog:" long-term follow-up and necropsy findings.
papers.authors: Hifumi T, Ishikawa T, Kozuma C, Kozuma M, Kuramoto T, Takahashi M, Miura N, Miyoshi N

papers.title: A newly derived formula outperforms published formulae for estimating urine osmolality in healthy dogs receiving intravenous fluids.
papers.authors: Jeong Y, Qu Y, Kim MS, Her J
papers.abstract: To derive a formula to estimate urine osmolality (Uosm) in dogs with urine sodium, potassium, glucose, and urea nitrogen and to compare the performance of the derived formula with published formulae. A prospective observational study was conducted using purpose-bred Beagles housed at a university research facility. Healthy dogs, confirmed by physical examination and laboratory testing, received isotonic or hypotonic IV fluids in a randomized sequence for 48 hours, with a 10-day washout period between treatments. Urine samples were collected through indwelling urinary catheters at baseline and every 12 hours. Urine osmolality and urinary osmolytes were measured. Linear mixed models were used to derive formulae, and agreement was assessed using the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), Bland-Altman analysis, and Passing-Bablok regression. Performance was compared with published formulae. 9 dogs provided 89 urine measurements. The proposed formula was Uosm = 2 X sodium + 1.8 X potassium + urea nitrogen2.5 (mg/dL) + glucose3.9 (mg/dL). The CCC was 0.96 (95% CI, 0.94 to 0.97), and the fixed bias was +7.99 mOsm/kg. Passing-Bablok regression revealed no proportional or constant bias. Compared with the published formulae, the proposed formula had the highest CCC and lowest fixed bias. The proposed formula provided a simple and reliable method to estimate Uosm in healthy dogs receiving isotonic and hypotonic IV fluids and outperformed the published formulae. Further validation in pathologic states is warranted. This formula improves the assessment of renal water handling, fluid balance, and kidney concentration ability when measuring Uosm is unavailable.

papers.title: Clinical presentation, computed tomographic findings, treatment, and outcome of traumatic jaw fractures in domestic rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus): 21 cases (2014-2025).
papers.authors: Charrasse M, Hahn H, Phillips K, Boutoille F, Sanchez-Migallon Guzman D, Huynh M
papers.abstract: To present clinical features, CT findings, treatment, and outcome for traumatic jaw fractures diagnosed via CT. Medical records from 2014 through 2026 were reviewed, and 21 rabbits with traumatic jaw fractures diagnosed by CT were selected. Among the 21 rabbits that fit the inclusion criteria, trauma sources included involuntary owner-inflicted trauma (n = 10), sofa-related falls or entrapment (3), dog bites (2), post-dental trimming issues (1), trauma with a table (1), fall of cardboard onto the head (1), fall of a folding table onto the head (1), and unknown (2). Fractures of the mandibular ramus were identified in 85.7% cases (unilateral, n = 14; bilateral, 4). Concurrent fractures were common (intermandibular suture (n = 5), body of the mandible (4), zygomatic arch (5), frontal bone (1), presphenoid bone (1), tympanic bulla (1)). A recurrent mandibular fracture pattern was seen in 47.6% of cases (n = 10). Complications in 13 rabbits that had a follow-up included dental malocclusion of incisors (n = 8) and cheek teeth (6), chronic dacryocystitis (2), hyperthermia (2), mandibular abscess (1), and persistence of vestibular syndrome (1). Notably, 11 rabbits were still alive 581 days after the trauma. Traumatic jaw injuries in rabbits frequently involve multiple concurrent fracture sites and associated craniofacial lesions. Computed tomography allowed detailed anatomical characterization of fracture configurations and associated injuries, supporting its value for comprehensive lesion assessment. Mandibular ramus fractures were the most common injuries and were generally associated with favorable survival, although long-term dental complications were frequent.

papers.title: Fixation of proximal humeral Salter-Harris type 1 fractures in a 3-dimensionally printed skeletally immature canine bone model: a biomechanical assessment of fully threaded headless cannulated screws.
papers.authors: Hwang TW, Kang E, Kim JM, Kim HY
papers.abstract: To compare the biomechanical stability of 4 fixation techniques for proximal humeral physeal fractures in skeletally immature canines using 3-D-printed models. This experimental in vitro study was conducted from September 25, 2025, through April 22, 2026. To strictly control biological variability, identical 3-D-printed models of juvenile canine proximal humeral Salter-Harris type 1 fractures (CT-derived from a 6-month-old 26-kg Labrador Retriever) were evaluated across 4 groups: pin and tension band wire (group A), partially threaded cannulated screw (group B), fully threaded headless cannulated screw (FTHCS) alone (group C), and FTHCS with a 1.6-mm Kirschner (K)-wire (group D). Tensile loading was applied at 10 mm/min at 105° to simulate supraspinatus traction. Outcomes included loads at 1- and 2-mm displacements, maximum failure load, and failure modes. Twenty-four models were tested (n = 6/group). Group D exhibited significantly higher resistance at 1-mm (663.95 N) and 2-mm (1,080.33 N) displacements than other groups. At 1-mm displacement, group D outperformed groups C, A, and B (mean differences [MD]: 206.2 N, 380.6 N, and 405.7 N, respectively; P < .0083). Maximum failure load did not differ significantly. Group B failed via localized proximal crushing and subsidence, whereas FTHCS groups (C, D) preserved proximal integrity, failing distally. In this 3-D-printed model, FTHCS combined with a K-wire provided superior resistance to tensile displacement compared with other tested constructs. FTHCS augmented with a K-wire may offer a biomechanically robust alternative mitigating subhead bone collapse, providing sufficient standalone stability for early rehabilitation in immature canines.

papers.title: Most dogs transported to a veterinary teaching hospital are unrestrained during vehicular travel.
papers.authors: Steinolfson C, Odunayo A, Ng Z, Stone A, Domaracki C, Mandese W, Wuerz J, Griffin F, Schaub J, Rooks J, Okafor C
papers.abstract: To evaluate the frequency and type of vehicular restraint use in dogs transported to a veterinary teaching hospital and to identify factors associated with restraint use. This prospective, survey-based study was conducted at a veterinary teaching hospital from May 28 to August 2, 2024. Dog owners presenting their dog for emergency, sick, or wellness visits completed a questionnaire regarding transportation practices, including restraint use, type of restraint, travel duration, anxiety level, and administration of previsit pharmaceuticals. Logistic regression analysis was performed to assess associations between patient and transport variables and restraint use. A total of 195 of 533 (36.6%) dogs were transported using a restraint system, whereas 338 of 533 (63.4%) were unrestrained. The most common restraint type was a seat belt-based device. Each 1-kg increase in body weight was associated with a 3.3% decrease in the odds of restraint use (OR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.95 to 0.98). Administration of previsit pharmaceuticals (OR, 1.8; 95% CI, 1.02 to 3.01) and having pet insurance (OR, 1.5; 95% CI, 1.01 to 2.34) were associated with restraint use. Age, reason for visit, travel duration, anxiety level, and mode of transportation were not associated with restraint use. Most dogs in this population traveled unrestrained during vehicular transport. Restraint use was not associated with visit type, travel duration, anxiety level, or transportation mode. Increased veterinary client education may improve safe transport practices and reduce the risk of injury during vehicular travel.

papers.title: Targeted quantitative polymerase chain reaction-based bacterial and fecal metabolite markers show early stability in healthy puppies after 8 weeks of age.
papers.authors: Birk D, Weidinger AK, Schmidt T, Bachmann S, Spring I, Felten S, Meunier SM, Blake AB, Suchodolski JS, Unterer S
papers.abstract: To assess longitudinal stability of targeted quantitative PCR (qPCR)-based fecal microbial and metabolomic markers in healthy puppies from 8 weeks to 1 year of age. This prospective longitudinal cohort study was conducted at the Clinic for Small Animal Internal Medicine, Vetsuisse Faculty, University of Zurich, Switzerland, from August 2023 to January 2025. Clinically healthy client-owned puppies were sampled at 8 to 12 weeks, 16 weeks, 6 months, and 1 year. Eligible dogs had no gastrointestinal signs, no previous systemic antibiotics, and negative parasitology. Primary outcomes were the qPCR-based dysbiosis index, selected qPCR-targeted bacterial taxa, fecal bile acids, long-chain fatty acids, and sterols, quantified by mass spectrometry. Mixed-effects models assessed time point associations. 23 dogs contributed 62 fecal samples. Dysbiosis index values and most targeted bacterial taxa remained within reference intervals, with no significant longitudinal changes. Bacteroides spp abundance was lower at 8 to12 weeks than at 6 months (difference, -0.73 logDNA copies/g feces; 95% CI, -1.40 to -0.06; Tukey-adjusted P = .028). Secondary unconjugated bile acids dominated at all ages. The concentration of 12-oxo-lithocholic acid was lower at 16 weeks than at 1 year (ratio, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.14 to 0.79; Tukey-adjusted P = .007) but not after multiple-testing adjustment. Long-chain fatty acid and sterol profiles showed no age-related changes. The qPCR-based dysbiosis index and targeted microbial and metabolomic markers were largely stable from 8 weeks to 1 year, supporting early functional maturation of measured markers. These findings establish age-specific baseline information for fecal bacterial and metabolite markers, supporting interpretation in young dogs with gastrointestinal disease.

papers.title: Intramuscular tranexamic acid results in lower peak plasma concentrations but comparable systemic absorption to intravenous administration in healthy dogs.
papers.authors: Kwak EJ, Zersen K, Tucker C, Lavender C, Talbot C, Gustafson D, Hendry-Hofer T, Hall K
papers.abstract: To determine the pharmacokinetics of IM and IV tranexamic acid (TXA) in healthy dogs. There were 6 healthy client-owned dogs that received TXA (20 mg/kg) in a randomized crossover study design with a 6-week washout period between IM and IV administration. Venous blood samples were collected from baseline to 8 hours after injection. Plasma TXA concentrations were measured using LC-MS-MS. For IM administration, mean ± SD maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) was 46.8 ± 26.6 μg/mL, total area under the curve was 173.8 ± 25.0 μg/mL·h, time to Cmax was 1.6 ± 1.4 hours, half-life (t1/2) was 2.8 ± 2.1 hours, and bioavailability was 120.9 ± 10.0%. For IV administration, Cmax was 119.8 ± 17.6 μg/mL, total area under the curve was 143.3 ± 10.5 μg/mL·h, and t1/2 was 2.1 ± 1.8 hours. IM Cmax reached approximately 39% of IV Cmax and exhibited a 33% longer t1/2, consistent with slower absorption. Despite the lower Cmax, bioavailability was 120.9%, suggesting that IM TXA maintained a higher plasma concentration for a longer duration. Although the prolonged time to Cmax associated with IM administration may limit its use in patients requiring rapid intervention, it offers practical advantages when IV access is delayed, allowing prehospital treatment prior to definitive veterinary care. Further investigation into IM dosing protocols is needed before it can be recommended in clinical patients.

papers.title: A randomized controlled trial of intravenous magnesium sulfate shows no analgesic or anti-inflammatory benefit in dogs undergoing thoracolumbar disk herniation surgery.
papers.authors: Mallet G, Gaitero L, Sanchez A, James FMK, Wood G, Monteith G, Samarani F
papers.abstract: To investigate the analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects of intraoperative IV magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) continuous rate infusion in dogs undergoing thoracolumbar hemilaminectomy for intervertebral disk extrusion (IVDE). 30 client-owned dogs presented at the Ontario Veterinary College Health Sciences Centre were enrolled from October 2022 through October 2023. Prospective, randomized, double-blind, controlled clinical trial dogs received either MgSO4 (magnesium group) or an equal volume of saline (control group) intraoperatively. All dogs followed standardized anesthesia and analgesia protocols. The primary outcome measures were postoperative pain assessed using the Glasgow Composite Measure Pain Scale-Short Form at recovery and 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours after surgery and serum IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α concentrations measured preoperatively and 1 hour postoperatively to assess anti-inflammatory effects. Serum magnesium concentrations were measured as a secondary outcome to monitor for potential toxicity. There were no significant differences in the pain scores and the IL-6 levels between the 2 groups. Tumor necrosis factor-α levels were undetectable in most dogs and were not analyzed statistically. The placebo group did not significantly require additional pain medication. Magnesium sulfate administration provided smoother anesthesia recoveries. Serum magnesium concentrations were significantly higher in the magnesium group immediately and 1 hour postoperatively but not at 24 hours. Intraoperative IV MgSO4 did not significantly improve postoperative analgesia or decrease inflammation compared to placebo in dogs undergoing surgery for IVDE. There was no significant evidence to use intraoperative IV MgSO4 to improve postoperative analgesia or decrease inflammation in dogs undergoing surgery for IVDE. However, no adverse effects were reported.

papers.title: Changes in metabolomic profile in dogs with hepatic encephalopathy secondary to congenital portosystemic shunt suggests mitochondrial homeostasis disturbances.
papers.authors: Fernandez Gallego A, Marques J, Kurian D, Diez F, Mellanby RJ, Gow AG, von Kriegsheim A, Faller KME
papers.abstract: To identify specific metabolomic changes in dogs showing signs of hepatic encephalopathy (HE) compared to those not showing obvious neurological signs and to follow these changes following medical treatment. In this prospective observational study, we recruited 10 client-owned dogs diagnosed with congenital portosystemic shunt (from March 2021 through October 2022). The sera of dogs with or without signs of HE at the time of diagnosis of congenital portosystemic shunt and following medical treatment for more than 4 weeks were analyzed by UPLC-MS. Dogs showing signs of HE at the time of diagnosis (n = 6) had significantly lower serum concentrations of taurine (fold change [FC], 0.44), creatine (FC, 0.32), and guanine (FC, 0.45) and higher serum concentrations of 3-hydroxybenzaldehyde (FC, 2.51) than their counterparts not showing signs of HE (4). A marked albeit nonsignificant decrease in serum stearate concentrations was also observed in the HE group (FC, 0.12). Following medical treatment, which improved neurological signs, the concentrations of these metabolites, particularly taurine, normalized to concentrations similar to the non-HE group. Dogs with HE exhibit a different serum metabolomic profile compared to dogs without signs of HE. The main changes are suggesting disturbances in mitochondrial homeostasis in dogs suffering from HE. Supporting mitochondrial function could form the basis of new therapeutic strategies in HE and merits further investigations in future studies.

papers.title: Tendotonometry allows noninvasive in vivo biomechanical evaluation of the patellar tendon in sedated dogs in a study assessing intrauser variability.
papers.authors: Caturay KC, Amato NS, Stewart SD, Khanna C, Wilson-Robles H, Schmidt DM, Roske MT, Schulz K
papers.abstract: To describe the use and determine the feasibility and user reliability of a commercially available digital palpation device, a myotonometer, on the canine patellar tendon (PT). In this prospective clinical feasibility study, client-owned dogs with no history of pelvic limb lameness were eligible for study enrollment from September through December of 2025 and included if their stifles were considered normal based upon physical examination and radiographic findings. Dogs were sedated, and a myotonometer was used to measure tone, stiffness, elasticity, relaxation, and creep of the PT. For each PT, a single user obtained 2 measurement series consisting of 5 individual measurements. 20 dogs were enrolled, and 400 total tendotonometric measurements were collected. No adverse events were observed. There were no statistically significant differences for any of the 5 biomechanical parameters between series within each side nor between left and right groups. There was good to excellent intraobserver repeatability between series and moderate to poor repeatability between sides. This clinical study demonstrated feasible myotonometer use as a novel method to obtain biomechanical data for the canine PT in a cohort of sedated dogs with normal stifles. This study introduces tendotonometry into the clinical setting as a novel modality for in vivo evaluation of orthopedic soft tissues using the PT as a test case. Beyond the canine PT, future tendotonometry studies may allow for the generation of noninvasive, rapid, and objective biomechanical data in tendon repair and healing, soft tissue reconstruction for orthopedic conditions, and treatment response in neuromuscular disorders.

papers.title: Transcatheter arterial embolization for massive hepatocellular carcinoma in 18 dogs (2020-2025).
papers.authors: Kadowaki K, Nishimura S, Toyoda A, Yamamoto R
papers.abstract: To report tumor response, complications, outcomes, and extrahepatic collateral arterial supply presence in dogs with massive hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treated with transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE). 18 dogs diagnosed with massive HCC. All dogs underwent contrast-enhanced CT and pretreatment histopathologic confirmation by laparoscopic biopsy (n = 1) or ultrasound-guided needle core biopsy (17). Tumor response was assessed using percentage of change in tumor volume on CT before TAE and 1 to 3 months after TAE. Post-TAE tumor response was classified as partial response in 9 of 18 (50.0%), stable disease in 6 of 18 (33.3%), and progressive disease in 1 of 18 (5.6%). Two dogs (11.1%) died within 2 weeks after TAE. The median percentage of change in tumor volume, excluding those 2 dogs, was -32.6%. Extrahepatic collateral arterial supplies to tumors were identified in 13 of 18 (72.2%), including the gastroepiploic (22.2%), right phrenic (22.2%), left phrenic (27.8%), pancreatic (16.7%), and mesenteric (5.6%) arteries. Collateral supply from 2 and 3 vessels was observed in 3 of 18 (16.7%) and 1 of 18 (5.6%), respectively; second TAE was performed in 2 of 18 (11.1%) and hepatic lobectomy after TAE in 4 of 18 (22.2%) cases. Postoperative complications included mild diarrhea (77.8%), anorexia (61.1%), mild anemia (16.7%), and acute gallbladder infarction (11.1%) etc. Both cases of gallbladder infarction were asymptomatic with good clinical outcomes. Median survival time was 447 days, including all 18 dogs. Transcatheter arterial embolization achieved disease control in most dogs and often involved extrahepatic collaterals. TAE may be a useful option in selected dogs with massive HCC.

papers.title: Needle bevel orientation does not affect the cranial spread of injectate in a lumbosacral epidural in canine cadavers.
papers.authors: Harris O, Ferreira TH, Loeber S, Hughes S, Bartholomew KJ
papers.abstract: To investigate the cranial and circumferential spread of iohexol (240 mg/mL) diluted 1:3 with saline injected at the lumbosacral junction in canine cadavers using 0.1- and 0.2-mL/kg volumes administered with a cranial- or caudal-facing Tuohy bevel direction. Lumbosacral epidurals were performed with a cranial- or caudal-facing needle bevel. The median vertebrae reached and the estimated percentage of the spinal cord surrounded with injectate were assessed via CT after administering two 0.1-mL/kg aliquots of injectate. Contrast medium was diluted to achieve physical properties closer to local anesthetics. 5 cadavers in each group were assessed in August of 2024. The median vertebrae reached with a 0.1-mL/kg volume using a cranial bevel and 100%, ≥ 50%, and ≥ 1% circumferential epidural coverage contrast medium were 1, 7, and 10 bodies compared to a caudal bevel direction of 1, 7, and 9 bodies. For 0.2-mL/kg total volume using a cranial bevel and having 100%, ≥ 50%, and ≥ 1% circumferential epidural coverage, there were 2, 9, and 14 bodies compared to a caudal bevel direction being 2, 11, and 15 bodies. The findings in this cadaveric study suggest that needle bevel direction does not affect the cranial epidural spread of injectate performed at the lumbosacral space. While no benefit to performing a lumbosacral epidural with a caudally facing bevel in limiting cranial spread was found, further studies in live patients are required to adjust clinical recommendations.

papers.title: Improvements in knowledge and detection of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales transmission in companion animals will strengthen prevention across the One Health spectrum.
papers.authors: Frey E, Alroy KA, Beaudoin A, DeStefano I, Diaz-Campos D, Curren E, Fellman C, Funk M, Granick J, James AE, Kollmann L, KuKanich K, McDermott D, Stull JW, Surendran-Nair M, Wagner R, King C, Louis S, Stapleton GS, Cole SD
papers.abstract: Carbapenemase-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CP-CRE) represent a growing threat to veterinary patients. Although CP-CRE infections in companion animals remain relatively rare, outbreaks in veterinary hospitals are increasingly being reported. Case reports and epidemiologic studies also support CP-CRE transmission between people and animals, making emergence in companion animals both an animal health and public health problem. However, substantial knowledge gaps limit understanding of the human and animal health impacts of CP-CRE in companion animals and of effective prevention and control interventions. For example, the true prevalence of CP-CRE colonization in companion animals is unknown, longitudinal dynamics of carriage remain poorly defined, and specific risk factors for acquisition in veterinary hospitals and community settings require further study. There are also unique structural and cultural challenges to implementing veterinary infection prevention and control practices, and evidence-based best practices tailored to veterinary settings are lacking. Diagnostic and surveillance infrastructure for companion animals is also highly fragmented, with inconsistent carbapenemase testing availability, limited mandatory reporting, and minimal capacity to rapidly detect and respond to outbreaks. This review synthesizes current clinical and molecular epidemiology of CP-CRE in companion animals; identifies critical gaps in diagnostics, surveillance, and veterinary infection prevention and control implementation; and outlines research priorities needed to mitigate and control CP-CRE within veterinary facilities. The companion Currents in One Health by Granick et al, JAVMA, 2026, addresses the clinical implications of the emergence of CP-CRE in companion animals and strategies for veterinary practitioners to mitigate spread.

papers.title: Reference intervals for myocardial T1, T2, and extracellular volume in clinically normal dogs and cats at 3-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging: a single-center study.
papers.authors: Fries RC, Kadotani S, Toborowsky C, Javery EA
papers.abstract: To establish species-specific reference values for myocardial native T1, native T2, and extracellular volume fraction (ECV) in clinically normal dogs and cats using a 3-Tesla (3-T) cardiac MRI (CMRI) and to provide a description of image acquisition and analysis suitable for veterinary clinical and research applications. Cardiac examinations were performed between 2015 and 2024 using a 3-T system with ECG gating under general anesthesia on clinically normal client-owned dogs and cats. Native T1 and T2 maps were acquired at the midventricular short-axis level using validated mapping sequences adapted from human CMRI protocols. Calculated ECV values were obtained from native and postcontrast T1 measurements in conjunction with Hct values. Reference intervals were determined using parametric methods and expressed as 95% prediction intervals with 90% CIs around the lower and upper reference limits. In dogs (n = 54), native T1, native T2, and ECV reference intervals (95% prediction intervals) were 1,057 to 1,152 ms, 42.0 to 60.9 ms, and 19.3% to 25.7%, respectively. In cats (n = 60), corresponding reference intervals were 1,066 to 1,172 ms, 34.2 to 61.6 ms, and 21.8% to 30.3%. Age was not a significant predictor of myocardial ECV in either species. This study establishes clinically applicable reference values for myocardial T1, T2, and ECV in dogs and cats at 3 T and provides imaging methodology to facilitate reproducibility. Species-specific reference intervals established in this study enable objective quantification of myocardial composition and support clinical implementation of CMRI tissue characterization in dogs and cats.

papers.title: Serum iodine concentrations in euthyroid dogs and dogs with autoimmune thyroiditis and hypothyroidism.
papers.authors: Egbert RJ, Buchweitz JP, Godfrey MA, Petroff BK
papers.abstract: To characterize the total and inorganic serum iodine concentrations of canines with varying thyroid disease status. Leftover serum samples submitted to the Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory for diagnostic thyroid panel screening between January and June 2023 were utilized for this retrospective study. Thyroglobulin autoantibody was used as a marker for autoimmune thyroiditis. Inorganic and total iodine were measured via an inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometer. An estimated reference interval was calculated for inorganic and total iodine using results from euthyroid dogs. Iodine concentrations were measured in dogs with autoimmune thyroiditis (n = 101) and hypothyroidism (97) and euthyroid dogs (86). Serum iodine concentrations ranged widely but were not increased in dogs with autoimmune thyroiditis or hypothyroidism in comparison to euthyroid animals. Concentrations of both total and inorganic iodine were statistically different between dogs suffering from autoimmune thyroiditis and those with hypothyroidism. Elevated serum iodine is not associated with autoimmune thyroiditis or hypothyroidism in dogs. The concentration of iodine alone in canine serum is not a marker for thyroid disease in dogs.

papers.title: Poor quality of life and recent veterinary consultation are associated with increased owner-perceived pain and/or suffering prior to euthanasia in dogs.
papers.authors: Mann AM, O'Brien J, Dog Aging PC, Ruple A, Parker RL
papers.abstract: To examine the influence of age, quality of life, illness, and recent veterinary consultation on an owner's perception of pain and/or suffering and consequently end-of-life decision-making for dogs. This retrospective cohort study examined Dog Aging Project end-of-life survey data. Owner and dog demographic characteristics were analyzed by whether pain and/or suffering were listed as a reason for euthanasia. A multivariate logistic regression model assessed associations. Owner surveys from 2020 through 2024 were included. Overall, 7,764 of 8,955 owners (87%) reported pain and/or suffering as a reason for euthanasia, with older owners, smaller dogs, and dogs < 5 years of age as factors that had lower frequency of pain as a reason for euthanasia. A multivariate logistic regression showed that the presence of a chronic condition and number of lifetime diagnoses were not associated with pain as a reason for euthanasia (OR, 1.02; 95% CI, 1.0 to 1.03 and OR, 1.11; 95% CI, 0.96 to 1.28, respectively). Recent veterinary consultation was positively associated with pain or suffering (OR, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.50 to 2.05), and better quality of life was negatively associated with pain or suffering (OR, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.86 to 0.93). Owners should be educated regarding the signs of pain and/or suffering to promote awareness of the high prevalence of pain and/or suffering and inform end-of-life care and decision-making. Veterinary visits influence owner perception of pain and/or suffering. Future studies could evaluate the best way to educate dog owners during end-of-life care.

papers.title: Serum erythropoietin concentration is higher in healthy brachycephalic dogs than nonbrachycephalic dogs acclimated to 1,535 meters altitude.
papers.authors: Cook M, Moore AR, Goldblatt BH, Cavanagh A, Zersen KM
papers.abstract: To assess the relationship between PaO2 and erythropoietin (EPO) concentrations and between PaO2 and hemoglobin (Hgb) concentrations in healthy brachycephalic (BRACHY) and healthy non-BRACHY dogs acclimatized to an altitude of 1,535 m. The third objective was to validate a human ELISA EPO kit for canine EPO measurement. Dogs were enrolled prospectively from January 2025 through September 2025. Venous samples for CBC, serum biochemistry, and EPO measurement were collected from a peripheral vein, and arterial samples were collected from the dorsal pedal artery. A human EPO quantitative ELISA was validated via spiking with recombinant canine EPO and establishment of linearity under dilution with 18 convenience samples. 22 healthy adult BRACHY dogs and 32 healthy adult non-BRACHY dogs were enrolled. There was no correlation between PaO2 and EPO in any group. A moderate negative correlation was identified between PaO2 and Hgb among all dogs and for BRACHY dogs alone. Erythropoietin concentrations were significantly higher in BRACHY dogs compared to non-BRACHY dogs. Analytical performance of the ELISA kit was deemed acceptable. The results of this study highlight that more research is required to better elucidate the physiologic adaptations of dogs in conditions of hypobaric hypoxia or with chronic hypoxia due to BRACHY conformation. EPO concentrations are significantly different between BRACHY and non-BRACHY dogs; however, the relationship between EPO, PaO2, and Hgb in these groups remains unclear.

papers.title: Immediate separation and storage of serum at a refrigerated temperature for 24 to 36 hours leads to minimal alterations in circulating microRNA levels in dogs.
papers.authors: Grimes JA, Webb B
papers.abstract: To determine how microRNA (miRNA) levels are altered in serum samples under different storage conditions. Whole blood was collected from 10 healthy dogs and placed into 7 tubes: (Tube 1) a red-top tube (RTT) centrifuged for immediate serum separation and stored at -80 °C (control), (Tube 2) room temperature (RT) for 24 to 36 hours, or (Tube 3) refrigerated temperature (FT) for 24 to 36 hours; (Tube 4) an RTT stored at RT for 24 to 36 hours or (Tube 5) FT for 24 to 36 hours; and (Tube 6) a serum separator tube centrifuged and stored at RT for 24 to 36 hours or (Tube 7) FT for 24 to 36 hours. Following RNA isolation and sequencing, differential expression analysis was performed. All tubes had altered levels of miRNA compared to the control. Tube 5 was not further analyzed due to a high incidence of hemolysis. Conditions with immediate serum separation and refrigeration (Tube 3, Tube 7) had the fewest alterations in miRNA levels. Collection of serum for future miRNA analysis should be done with immediate separation of serum (via centrifugation of an RTT and removal of serum or use of a serum separator tube) and storage at FT for 24 to 36 hours prior to placement into a -80 °C freezer to have the fewest changes in miRNA levels. These findings will help facilitate collection of additional samples from secondary research sites. Researchers should be aware of specific miRNA that may be altered based on storage conditions.

papers.title: Treatment of Refractory Vomiting With Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine in Two Dogs and a Cat: A Cases Series.
papers.authors: Wang X, Yang L, Ma W
papers.abstract: Refractory vomiting in dogs and cats is a common clinical condition in small animal practice, typically characterized by recurrent vomiting, belching and related symptoms, which is a great challenge to veterinarians. According to Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine (TCVM), this condition is primarily attributed to dysfunction of the spleen and stomach in transformation and transportation, leading to the upward rebellion of stomach Qi. Derived from the Shang Han Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage), Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction functions to direct rebellious Qi downward, resolve phlegm, tonify Qi and harmonize the stomach. It is mainly indicated for conditions resulting from stomach Qi counter flow. In this report, three cases of refractory vomiting in two dogs and a cat diagnosed as stomach Qi rebellion according to TCVM were treated with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on syndrome differentiation. The results showed that all three cases achieved favourable therapeutic outcomes. These findings suggest that, for refractory vomiting caused by stomach Qi rebellion in dogs and cats, individualized treatment with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on specific clinical presentations can achieve stable and reliable efficacy.

papers.title: Neglected but Not Harmless: Characterising Nonantibiotic Antimicrobial Use in Small Animal Practices in Colombia.
papers.authors: Correa-Valencia NM, Arango-Arcila S, Mendoza NK, Sierra-Zapata DA, Guzmán-Mejía VA, Carmona Ramírez A, Restrepo Salazar JG
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global threat, yet stewardship efforts have largely overlooked nonantibiotic antimicrobials (NAAs), despite their widespread use and potential role in resistance selection and environmental persistence. Evidence on NAA use in small animal practice, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, remains scarce. To characterise patterns of NAA use and assess prescription quality in dogs, cats, and other small animal species treated at a university veterinary hospital in Colombia. A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted using veterinary prescription records from January to December 2022. A systematic sampling approach (first four prescriptions per day) yielded 1460 prescriptions, of which 731 involved NAAs. Data on animal characteristics, consultation type, and prescription details were extracted, and NAAs were classified by pharmacological group, pharmaceutical form, and route of administration. Bivariate analyses were performed to identify stewardship-relevant patterns. NAAs accounted for a substantial proportion of prescriptions, predominantly in dogs (91.5%). Topical antiseptics (49.9%), external antiparasitics (21.3%), and internal antiparasitics (17.1%) were the most frequently used classes. Cutaneous (58.7%) and oral (41.3%) routes predominated, with chlorhexidine as the most common active ingredient (22%). Dermatology consultations were more likely to involve topical antiseptics (55.0% vs. 45.5%; OR = 1.47; 95% CI 1.06-2.02), whereas general consultations showed substantially higher odds of internal antiparasitic use (OR = 5.58; 95% CI 2.93-10.62). While 67.6% of treatments adhered to standard duration, only 38% matched recommended dosing, and key prescription elements were frequently missing, including International Nonproprietary Names (7%), concentration (12.2%), and complete administration instructions (5.5%). NAAs are widely used in small animal practice but are frequently prescribed with incomplete documentation and suboptimal dosing practices. These findings highlight a critical and underrecognised gap in antimicrobial stewardship and support the need to formally integrate NAAs into surveillance, regulatory frameworks, and stewardship interventions under a One Health approach.

papers.title: A clinical case series evaluation of cross-linked gelatin foam to treat naturally occurring periodontal pockets and furcation defects in dogs.
papers.authors: Stepaniuk KS, Sievers AM, Lalonde AA
papers.abstract: This clinical case series evaluated periodontal debridement and the application of a biodegradable liquid scaffold composed of a porcine-derived crosslinked gelatin foam for the treatment of naturally occurring furcation defects and combined suprabony and infrabony defects in client-owned dogs. A total of 21 treated sites in 9 client-owned dogs were evaluated. Periodontal probing, intraoral computed radiography (CR), and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) under general anesthesia were performed. Full-mouth periodontal treatment and closed (13 sites) or open (8 sites) root planing were performed before the application of the flowable scaffold. The mean duration between treatment and recheck was 169 days (with a range of 101-388 days and a median of 167 days). The mean decrease in periodontal pocket depth was 1.9 mm. The mean furcation stage decreased by 1.4, and the treated tooth periodontal stage was reduced by a mean of 0.8.

papers.title: Clinical outcome and implant accuracy in cervical fractures stabilization using 3D-printed patient-specific drill guides for placement of bicortical screws in 16 dogs.
papers.authors: Manzanedo-Delgado A, Oxley B, Behr S
papers.abstract: To describe the clinical outcome of dogs with cervical fractures undergoing spinal stabilization surgery using 3D-printed patient-specific drill guides, and to evaluate the accuracy of pedicle screw placement with this technique. Retrospective descriptive study. Sixteen dogs. Medical records were searched between August 2015 and January 2025 for dogs with traumatic spinal fracture via CT scan causing signs of cervical myelopathy that underwent spinal stabilization surgery using 3D-printed patient-specific drill guides followed by a postoperative CT scan. Neurological status was graded retrospectively with the Modified Frankel Score (MFS) on presentation, preoperatory on the day of the surgery, postoperatively on the first day after surgery, at hospital discharge and at the follow-up examination performed 4–6 weeks after surgery, when available. A telephone questionnaire was obtained for the long-term outcome. Sixteen dogs met the inclusion criteria (3/16 grade 2 MFS, 5/16 grade 3 MFS, 7/16 grade 4 MFS and 1/16 grade 5 MFS). Two dogs showed mild minor transient intraoperative complications. Optimal pedicle screw placement was achieved in 85/90 (94.4%) of screws. Twenty-four hours after surgery, the neurological grade remained unchanged in 10/16 dogs, improved in 5/16, and transiently deteriorated in 1/16 dog, which recovered by discharge. Postoperative complications occurred in 10/16 dogs and resolved with medical management in 9/10 cases. Short term follow-up revealed a static stable (6/14) or improved (8/14) neurological grade since discharge. Among the 12 dogs with owner-reported long-term follow-up, all were reported by their owners to be ambulatory and to have improved neurologically. Long-term quality-of-life (5 = excellent; 1 = poor) was scored by the owners 5/5 in 11/12 (91.7%) dogs and 4/5 in 1/12 (8.3%) dogs. Dogs in this study overall had an improved neurological status and favorable long-term outcomes when follow-up information was available. However, postoperative adverse events, including complications, should be considered when interpreting overall clinical outcome.

papers.title: Myocardial injury in cats with acute blunt trauma: Prevalence and prognostic implications.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Dossi G, Carnevale L, Mismetti M, Borromeo V, Pocar P, Locatelli C
papers.abstract: The aim of the present study was to determine the prevalence of increased serum high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) concentrations in cats with acute blunt trauma and assess associations with trauma severity, clinicopathological variables, echocardiographic findings, and short-term outcome. A total of 39 cats presenting within 48 h of blunt trauma were prospectively enrolled. All cats underwent physical examination, Animal Trauma Triage scoring, thoracic radiography, electrocardiography, echocardiography, complete blood count, serum biochemistry, N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide testing, and hs-cTnI measurement. Associations between hs-cTnI concentrations and clinical, laboratory, echocardiographic, and outcome variables were assessed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed as an exploratory assessment of prognostic performance. Increased hs-cTnI concentrations were detected in 34/39 (87%) cats (95% confidence interval 72-96). A significant ordinal association was identified between trauma severity and hs-cTnI class (linear-by-linear association, P  = 0.036), although the overall Fisher-Freeman-Halton test was not significant ( P  = 0.088). Hs-cTnI concentrations correlated positively with urea, creatinine, neutrophil count, alanine aminotransferase, neutrophil:lymphocyte ratio, blood glucose, end-diastolic interventricular septal, and posterior wall thicknesses, and negatively with end-diastolic left ventricular internal diameter. Increased left ventricular wall thickness was identified in 10/39 cats and was associated with higher hs-cTnI concentrations ( P  = 0.033). No traumatic cardiac rupture, pericardial effusion, or pleural effusion were observed. Electrocardiographic abnormalities were detected in 6/39 cats and were not associated with hs-cTnI concentrations. Seven cats (18%) died during hospitalization. Increased urea concentration, white blood cell count, and neutrophil count were associated with non-survival. ROC analyses were considered exploratory because of the limited number of outcome events. Increased hs-cTnI concentrations were common in cats with acute blunt trauma and were associated with leukocyte variables, renal function markers, and subtle echocardiographic abnormalities. These findings suggest that hs-cTnI may reflect a multifactorial biological response involving myocardial stress or injury, systemic disease severity, altered renal handling, and possible underlying subclinical cardiac disease. Further studies are needed to clarify the relative contribution and clinical significance of these mechanisms. What happens to the heart after blunt trauma in cats? Cats who experience blunt trauma may develop damage affecting multiple organs, including the heart. Detecting heart involvement can be challenging because clinical signs are often non-specific and may be masked by other traumatic injuries. Cardiac troponin I is a protein released into the bloodstream when heart muscle cells are damaged. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) tests can detect even small increases in this biomarker and may help identify cardiac involvement in injured cats. This study investigated hs-cTnI concentrations in 39 cats examined within 48 h of blunt trauma. Each cat underwent blood testing, electrocardiography, thoracic radiography, and echocardiography. The aim was to determine how commonly hs-cTnI concentrations were increased and whether these increases were associated with injury severity, laboratory findings, heart imaging results, or short-term survival. Increased hs-cTnI concentrations were found in most cats (87%). Higher hs-cTnI concentrations were associated with more severe trauma and with several blood test abnormalities, including leukocyte-related variables and markers of kidney dysfunction. Cats with increased thickness of the left ventricular wall also had higher hs-cTnI concentrations. Severe traumatic cardiac lesions (cardiac rupture or fluid accumulation around the heart) were not detected. Electrocardiographic abnormalities were uncommon and not associated with hs-cTnI concentrations. These findings suggest that increased hs-cTnI concentrations in traumatized cats may be influenced by multiple factors, including myocardial injury, the severity of systemic illness, altered renal handling of the biomarker, and possible pre-existing heart disease. Because baseline cardiac status before trauma was unknown, the relative contribution of these factors could not be determined. Further studies are needed to clarify the causes and clinical significance of increased hs-cTnI concentrations in cats after trauma.

papers.title: Efficacy of Oral Lotilaner in Controlling Clinical Signs in Cats Naturally Infested With Lynxacarus radovskyi.
papers.authors: da Mota de Magalhães Y, Marques DM, Christ LX, Campos DR, Fernandes JI
papers.abstract: Lynxacarus radovskyi is a pilicolous mite that may cause pruritus and coat or skin lesions in cats. Evidence regarding the efficacy of oral lotilaner for the treatment of feline lynxacariasis remains limited. To evaluate the parasitological and clinical efficacy of oral lotilaner in cats naturally infested with L. radovskyi. Twenty client-owned cats naturally infested with L. radovskyi. A prospective, longitudinal, parallel-group study was conducted with 20 cats allocated to a treated group (n = 10) or an untreated control group (n = 10). Treated cats received oral lotilaner on Day (D)0 and D30. Parasitological assessment was performed every 7 days from D0 to D63 using trichograms obtained from three anatomical sites and scored using a semi-quantitative scale. Pruritus and clinical lesion scores also were recorded. Treatment with lotilaner resulted in a significant reduction in parasitological scores from D7 onwards (p = 0.0033), while untreated cats remained persistently infested. Mite-count reduction increased progressively, reaching 98.0% at D35 and 100% from D42 onwards after the second administration. Pruritus and clinical lesion scores also decreased significantly compared with baseline (p = 0.0117). Oral lotilaner administered twice (D0 and D30) was effective for the treatment of feline lynxacariasis under natural infestation conditions, resulting in rapid parasite reduction and significant clinical improvement.

papers.title: A species comparison of videofloroscopic metrics of swallowing in healthy dogs and cats.
papers.authors: Grobman M, Luciani E, Reinero C
papers.abstract: Videofluoroscopic swallow studies (VFSS) are the criterion standard for diagnosing dysphagia in veterinary species. However, a lack of normative swallowing variables in cats hinders assessment of cats with potential aerodigestive disease. Species variation in swallowing could lead to over- and under-interpretation of findings on VFSS, resulting in misdiagnosis. Compare differences in objective swallowing metrics between cats and dogs using VFSS. We hypothesize that cats will show differences in objective swallowing metrics on VFSS compared with dogs. Healthy adult cats (n = 13) and dogs (n = 12) without clinical signs (CS) of respiratory or alimentary disease. Prospective, cross-sectional study. Cats and dogs underwent standardized VFSS. All were evaluated according to 16 objective metrics and compared between species. Between group comparisons were made using Mann-Whitney-U, T-test, or Fischer's exact test with a P < .05 significance level for all comparisons. Cats had significantly longer inter-swallow intervals, shorter pharyngeal transit times, and more pharyngeal swallows to generate primary peristalsis compared with dogs (P < .05). Cats were also more likely to have esophageal volume accumulation and slowing of distal esophageal transit time compared with dogs (P < .05). Physiologic reflux was identified in 2 (15.4%) cats vs 6 (50%) dogs. Pathologic penetration-aspiration (P-A score: 7; aspiration without attempt to cough) was found in 1 cat despite a lack of respiratory or alimentary CS. Species variation should be considered when interpreting VFSS. In 1 cat, occult tracheal aspiration of contrast (P-A score 7) was detected without accompanying cough.

papers.title: Multimodal imaging characteristics and case management of intraspinal Spirocerca lupi infection in a dog.
papers.authors: Carrillo AJ, Grosso FRV, Walden HDS, Alas O, Garcia GA
papers.abstract: A 1-year-old female spayed mixed breed dog was ambulatory with paraparesis and proprioceptive ataxia, absent conscious proprioception in pelvic limbs, and spinal pain with a T3-L3 neurolocalization on presentation. Thoracic radiographs revealed caudal mediastinal mass, pneumothorax, and pleural effusion. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple mediastinal masses with vertebral canal extension, extradural compression at T5-T6, intramedullary T2 hyperintensities at T5 and T9, esophageal compression and dilation, and aortic aneurysmal dilation. Transdiaphragmatic ultrasonography was suggestive of parasitic involvement. A right T5-T8 hemilaminectomy and parasitology confirmed Spirocerca lupi. Treatment with ivermectin (400 mcg/kg SC q24h for 3 days followed by once a week for 6 weeks), prednisone (0.7 mg/kg/day), and clindamycin (10.7 mg/kg PO q12h) was initiated. Recovery of independent ambulation occurred 2 months after treatment. Computed tomography revealed resolution of mediastinal and esophageal nodules with progressive aortic aneurysmal dilation. Multimodal imaging was essential for the management of spinal spirocercosis.

papers.title: Clinical and serologic variables associated with dissemination and seasonal presentation in dogs with newly diagnosed coccidioidomycosis.
papers.authors: Chittick L, Jaffey JA, Hanzlicek AS, Kreisler R, Rayhel LH, Balaban J, Alcott C, Adams C, Gould AG
papers.abstract: Disseminated coccidioidomycosis in dogs is associated with substantial morbidity, yet distinguishing pulmonary from disseminated disease can be clinically challenging. Antibody serology might assist in predicting dissemination, but its performance across disease sites requires clarification. To identify clinical and serologic variables associated with disseminated coccidioidomycosis and to evaluate differences in antibody magnitude among common sites of infection. Two hundred fourteen client-owned dogs with newly diagnosed coccidioidomycosis. Retrospective study. Anti-Coccidioides spp. immunoglobulin (Ig)G was measured by enzyme immunoassay (EIA) and agar gel immunodiffusion (AGID) at a reference laboratory. Disease was classified as pulmonary in 148/214 (69%) and disseminated in 66/214 (31%). Higher EIA IgG concentration and AGID IgG titer were independently associated with dissemination. Enzyme immunoassay discriminated disseminated from pulmonary disease well (area under the curve [AUC]: 0.81; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74-0.87), estimate likely representing an upper bound because serology contributed to case classification. Agar gel immunodiffusion performance was not statistically distinguishable (AUC: 0.74; 95% CI, 0.67-0.82; P = .65). Exploratory cutpoints included an EIA IgG threshold of 37 enzyme immunoassay units (sensitivity 86%, specificity 63%) and an AGID IgG threshold of ≥1:32 (sensitivity 48%, specificity 86%). Pulmonary diagnoses were least common in spring and peaked in late fall and winter. Coccidioidal IgG serology might provide clinically useful adjunctive information when assessing dogs for disseminated coccidioidomycosis. However, overlap in serologic results between disease phenotypes precludes the use of serology alone to determine disease extent. Serologic results should therefore be interpreted alongside clinical findings and appropriate diagnostic evaluation.

papers.title: Utility of the ACTH/cortisol ratio for differentiating pituitary microadenomas from macroadenomas in dogs with pituitary-dependent hypercortisolism.
papers.authors: Stylianou G, Vassallo F, Nishii N, Diana A, Tardo AM, Del Baldo F, Fracassi F
papers.abstract: No simple, blood-based biomarker to estimate tumor size in dogs with pituitary-dependent hypercortisolism (PDH) has been evaluated. Determine whether the adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)/cortisol ratio differentiates pituitary microadenomas from macroadenomas in dogs with PDH and correlates with pituitary size. Seventy privately-owned dogs with PDH (microadenomas, n = 30; macroadenomas, n = 40). Retrospective multicenter observational study. Endogenous ACTH and cortisol concentrations obtained at the same time point before treatment were used to calculate the ACTH/cortisol ratio. Pituitary tumor size was classified using the pituitary-to-brain (P/B) ratio. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis and multivariable logistic regression. Dogs with macroadenomas had significantly higher ACTH/cortisol ratios than dogs with microadenomas (median, 9.12; IQR, 6.46-14.28 vs median, 4.90; IQR, 3.08-8.10; P < .001). The ratio showed moderate discrimination for differentiating macroadenomas from microadenomas with an area under the curve of 0.77 (95% CI, 0.66-0.89; P < .001). A cutoff >5.69 yielded 85% sensitivity and 60% specificity (positive likelihood ratio 2.13), whereas a higher ratio >11.74 achieved 90% specificity and 35% sensitivity (positive likelihood ratio 3.50). The ACTH/cortisol ratio showed moderate positive correlation with pituitary size (Spearman's ρ = 0.48; 95% CI, 0.26-0.64; P < .001) and remained independently associated with macroadenoma classification in multivariable analysis (OR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.05-1.40). The ACTH/cortisol ratio is associated with pituitary tumor size in dogs with PDH and may support clinical risk stratification, particularly when advanced imaging is unavailable.

papers.title: Serum fibroblast growth factor-23 concentration in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease.
papers.authors: Iwasa N, Shimizu M, Okamoto T, Kosuga H, Morikita N, Kawabe M, Iwata M, Watanabe K, Kobatake Y, Takashima S, Nishii N
papers.abstract: Circulating fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF-23) is primarily a kidney-related biomarker, but also may be influenced by cardiovascular remodeling and hemodynamic load. Verify whether serum FGF-23 concentration increases with myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) severity. Forty-two client-owned dogs with MMVD without overt kidney disease. Retrospective cross-sectional study to evaluate serum FGF-23, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine (Cr), and symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA) concentrations. Imaging variables included vertebral heart score (VHS), vertebral left atrial size (VLAS), left atrial-to-aortic root ratio (LA/Ao), normalized left-ventricular internal diameter in diastole (LVIDDN), and diastolic transmitral E-wave velocity (E-vel). Differences among American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine stages were analyzed using the Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Correlations were analyzed using Spearman's correlation. Multivariable linear regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with serum FGF-23 concentration. Dogs with ACVIM stages C and D had higher serum FGF-23 concentrations than those with stages B1 and B2 (P < .05). Serum FGF-23 concentrations were positively correlated with VLAS (rs = 0.500, P < .01), ANP (rs = 0.455, P < .01), LA/Ao (rs = 0.384, P < .05), E-vel (rs = 0.372, P < .05), and NT-proBNP (rs = 0.366, P < .05). ACVIM stage was significantly associated with serum FGF-23 concentration after adjustment for serum Cr concentration and loop diuretic use. The potential influence of MMVD should be considered when interpreting increased circulating FGF-23 concentrations in dogs with MMVD.

papers.title: Case Report: Presumptive subdural hemorrhage as a rare neurological manifestation of primary immune-mediated thrombocytopenia in a dog.
papers.authors: Hong HP, Kei TG, Gagnon NA, Scrivani PV
papers.abstract: A 10-year-old female spayed mixed-breed dog was presented with a history of seizures and acute progressive intracranial signs. The neurological examination was consistent with multifocal brain disease. Clinical examination revealed ecchymoses, petechiae, and bilateral retinal hemorrhage. Clinicopathological evaluation identified severe thrombocytopenia [a platelet count of 9 × 10 3 /μL without clumps on manual smear evaluation] with an increased mean platelet volume. Coagulation testing (activated partial thromboplastin time and prothrombin time) and fibrinolysis markers (D-dimers, quantitative fibrinogen), infectious disease screening, and thoracic and abdominal imaging were within normal limits, establishing a diagnosis of primary immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (ITP). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed minimally expanded, bilateral crescent-shaped, extra-axial fluid accumulations overlying both cerebral hemispheres. Based on T1-weighted and T2-weighted hyperintensities and peripheral susceptibility artifact on T2*-weighted gradient-recalled echo (GRE) imaging, a late subacute subdural intracranial hemorrhage was diagnosed. Despite initial uneventful anesthesia and recovery, the dog experienced acute neurological deterioration and suffered cardiopulmonary arrest, suspected due to ongoing hemorrhage or brain herniation. This report describes a rare neurological manifestation of primary ITP in a dog. While canine ITP generally carries a favorable prognosis, life-threatening secondary intracranial hemorrhage can occur. Primary ITP should be considered as a differential diagnosis for an acute, progressive neurological presentation until a normal platelet count is confirmed.

papers.title: Effects of transient intravascular volume overload on endothelial glycocalyx thickness in healthy anesthetized cats.
papers.authors: Yozova ID, Thomson N, Irie M, Owen R, Munday JS
papers.abstract: Previous studies suggest that the endothelial glycocalyx is damaged by volume overload. This study assessed the effects of transient intravascular volume overload on estimated endothelial glycocalyx thickness in healthy cats, using sidestream dark field videomicroscopy and the Glycocheck™ software. This was a prospective blinded cross-over single-center experimental study on twenty healthy cats. Cats were randomized to either receive 30 mL/kg/10 min of Hartman's solution (volume overload group) or no fluids (control) with a washout of 7 days. Sublingual mucosa videomicroscopy images were acquired at T0 (baseline), T1 (immediately after intervention), T2 (3 h after end of intervention) and T3 (24 h after end of intervention) with three measurements performed per timepoint under propofol anesthesia. The perfused boundary region (PBR), an inverse estimate for endothelial glycocalyx thickness, for vessels with diameter of 5-25, 5-9, 10-19 and 20-25 μm, respectively, was then automatically calculated with the Glycocheck™ software. Packed cell volume (PCV) was measured at each timepoint. Data normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test and visual inspection. Linear mixed-effects regression modelling, with cat as a random effect, analyzed interactions between GlycoCheck™ and other parameters. PBR 5-25 μm, 5-9 μm and 10-19 μm increased over time, reaching significance at T2 ( p = 0.001 , p = 0.017 and p = 0.008 , respectively). A significant group x timepoint interaction was identified for PBR 5-9 with decreased values at T2 ( p = 0.028 ) and T3 ( p = 0.010 ) in the volume overload group. Decreases in PCV were significantly associated with increases in PBR 5-25 μm ( p = 0.003 ) and PBR 10-19 μm ( p = 0.001 ). This study did not demonstrate decreases in estimated endothelial glycocalyx thickness after transient volume overload in healthy cats. The PBR did increase over time, suggesting potential anesthetic effects. Changes in PCV affected GlycoCheck™ parameters and this finding should be further explored. Further studies designed with understanding of feline volume kinetics are required to investigate the effects of IV fluids on the feline endothelial glycocalyx.

papers.title: Rapid test performance for the diagnosis of canine visceral leishmaniasis using blood, serum, and saliva.
papers.authors: Lamattina D, Sánchez-Fernández C, Depasquino AF, Laiño MA, Siccardi FM, Salomón OD
papers.abstract: A key aspect of controlling canine visceral leishmaniasis (CVL) is the availability of accurate diagnostic tools capable of reaching most of the population. In endemic areas with socially vulnerable populations, facilitating rapid CVL diagnosis by reducing sampling difficulties and diagnostic costs could provide substantial benefits. This study evaluated the performance of the Kalazar Detect™ Canine Rapid Test for CVL diagnosis using blood, serum, and saliva samples, and compared the results among sample types and with PCR detection in lymph nodes. Samples were collected from 100 dogs. Prevalence detected by the rapid diagnostic tests (RDT) was 21% using blood and serum and 17% using saliva, whereas PCR detected a prevalence of 46%. Agreement between serum and blood-based RDTs was 100%, while comparison between serum/blood and saliva showed a kappa index of 0.87, indicating almost perfect agreement. Using PCR as the reference standard, RDTs on serum and blood showed a sensitivity of 0.39 and specificity of 0.94, whereas saliva-based RDT showed a sensitivity of 0.33 and specificity of 0.96. The low sensitivity of the RDTs currently used by the National Leishmaniasis Program indicate that an additional diagnostic method should be incorporated into CVL surveillance in endemic areas. Nevertheless, our results suggest that saliva may be a suitable sample for the Kalazar Detect Canine Rapid Test, as it is easy to collect, less expensive, and less invasive. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate the performance of this RDT for CVL diagnosis using saliva samples.

papers.title: Medial Tympanic Membrane Displacement in Five Dogs Resembling Tympanic Membrane Retraction in Humans.
papers.authors: Botelho CB, Ferreira TS, Gmyterco VC, Alves C, Nuttall T, de Farias MR, Fernandes JI
papers.abstract: Five dogs with head tilt, ataxia, incoordination or deafness without a history of otitis externa (OE) were diagnosed with otitis media by computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Otoendoscopy showed possible tympanic membrane retraction with opaque, fibrotic membranes and advanced imaging showed middle ear involvement. The clinical significance requires further investigation.

papers.title: Effects of a gluten-free hydrolyzed diet in dogs with paroxysmal dyskinesia: a prospective cohort study.
papers.authors: Okonji S, Del Baldo F, Garuti E, Vecchiato CG, Di Carlo A, Costantini G, Cauduro A, Di Paola A, Falzone C, Gallucci A, Tartari I, Baroni M, Poli F, Bianchi E, Buffagni V, Valentini A, Gagliardo T, Gandini G
papers.abstract: Paroxysmal dyskinesia (PD) is an episodic movement disorder in dogs. Gluten-sensitive etiology has been suggested, but prospective studies in different breeds are lacking. Investigate whether a gluten-free hydrolyzed diet (GFHD) decreases PD episode frequency and gastrointestinal (GI) signs, and evaluate associations with serum anti-gliadin peptide immunoglobulin G (AGA IgG) and anti-transglutaminase-2 immunoglobulin A (TG-2 IgA) titers. Twenty-three client-owned dogs with PD. Prospective cohort study with 3 time points: baseline (T0), 90 days (T1), and 180 days (T2). Dogs were fed a GFHD. Episode frequency, GI signs and AGA IgG and TG-2 IgA titers were assessed at each time point. Response to GFHD was classified as excellent (episode disappearance), good (≥50% decrease), fairly good (<50% decrease), or poor (no change or increase). Median number of episodes decreased from 6 (range, 2-60) at T0 to 2 (range, 0-10) at T2 (P = .0003). At T2, 17/23 dogs were responders (5 excellent, 12 good). Gastrointestinal signs were present in 15/23 dogs at T0 and in 6/23 dogs at T2, with significant decreases in vomiting and diarrhea (P = .01). No significant correlation was found between episode frequency and AGA IgG or TG-2 IgA titers at any time point (P > .1). Antibody results did not significantly change between T0 and T2. The GFHD was associated with a significant decrease in PD frequency and GI signs in most dogs. The AGA IgG and TG-2 IgA titers were not predictive of dietary response, suggesting limited value as biomarkers.

papers.title: Outcomes of a 42-day course of molnupiravir in cats with feline infectious peritonitis: a prospective descriptive study.
papers.authors: Hishinuma K, Inoue A, Fukushima K, Sato M
papers.abstract: Antiviral therapy for cats with feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) has traditionally been administered for 84 days, although the optimal duration of molnupiravir treatment remains unknown. To evaluate the efficacy of a 42-day course of molnupiravir, orally (PO), for naturally occurring FIP in cats. Nineteen client-owned cats with newly diagnosed FIP. Prospective pilot study. Cats received molnupiravir, PO, q12h for 42 days at a median dosage of 11.5 mg/kg (IQR, 10.2-12.5 mg/kg). Cats with ocular or neurological involvement were excluded. Clinical assessments were performed during treatment and for 6 months after treatment cessation. Nineteen cats were enrolled. Two cats failed to complete treatment because of death or persistent clinical signs. Fourteen of 19 cats (74%; 95% CI, 49-91) achieved sustained remission on an intention-to-treat basis. Each non-completer failed on day 5 or 10, respectively, within a window common to 42- and 84-day protocols, and therefore do not inform the question of treatment duration; among the 17 cats reaching day 42, 14 (82%; 95% CI, 57-96) remained in remission for at least 6 months. Three cats relapsed after treatment cessation; all responded to retreatment with molnupiravir at the same dosage extended to 84 days. This prospective study suggests that a shortened course of molnupiravir is feasible in selected cats with non-ocular, non-neurological FIP. : (FIP) にするウイルスは 84 されてきたが、モルヌピラビルのなはらかではない。 : FIP のにするモルヌピラビル 42 のをすること。 : たに FIP とされた19。 : きパイロット。モルヌピラビルを 12 ごとに 42 した。のは 11.5  mg/kg (、 10.2-12.5  mg/kg) であった。またはをするはした。および 6 か、をった。 : 19 をした。 2 はまたはのによりをできなかった。 Intention-to-treat では 19 14 (74 %； 95% 、 49-91) がをした。の 2 はそれぞれ5および10にとなり、いずれも 42 および 84 のプロトコルにするであったため、のにはしなかった。 42 までをした 17 のうち 14 (82% ； 95% 、 57-96) はなくとも 6 かをした。 3 はにしたが、がのモルヌピラビルによる 84 のにした。 および: きパイロットのから、およびをわない FIP のでは、モルヌピラビルのがであるがされた。. Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is a serious disease in cats caused by feline coronavirus. Antiviral treatment is commonly given for 84 days, but the best treatment duration for molnupiravir is unknown. In this prospective pilot study, 19 cats without eye or neurological involvement received molnupiravir by mouth for 42 days. Seventeen cats completed the 42-day course. Fourteen of the 19 enrolled cats remained in remission for at least 6 months after treatment. Three cats relapsed after completing treatment. All 3 responded when molnupiravir was restarted at the same dose and continued for approximately 84 days. Two cats did not complete the initial treatment course because of death or persistent clinical signs early in treatment. These findings suggest that a 42-day course of molnupiravir can be feasible for selected cats with FIP, although this study was small and did not directly compare 42-day and 84-day treatment courses.

papers.title: Changes in flea and tick infestation following topical fipronil, permethrin, piperonyl butoxide, and pyriproxyfen in naturally infested dogs: an exploratory uncontrolled field study.
papers.authors: Romero-Núñez C, Heredia-Cárdenas R, Flores-Ortega A, Bautista-Gómez LG, Gaxiola-Camacho SM, Torres-Cruz JD
papers.abstract: Flea and tick infestations impair canine welfare and may have public-health relevance in rural settings. To describe temporal changes in ectoparasite infestation and associated clinical signs after a single topical application of fipronil, permethrin, piperonyl butoxide, and pyriproxyfen (PROTECH) in naturally infested dogs. This prospective, uncontrolled exploratory field study enrolled 44 privately owned dogs in Tahdziú, Yucatán, Mexico. Dogs received one topical application at Day 0 and were reassessed on Days 15 and 30. An approximately 5-min whole-body examination documented ectoparasite presence or absence. Field-recorded numerical skin-lesion and pruritus scores and observed adverse events were summarized. Among dogs with flea-only infestation ( n = 18), positivity decreased from 18/18 at Day 0 to 0/18 at Days 15 and 30. Among tick-only dogs ( n = 11), positivity decreased from 11/11 to 0/11 and 1/11, respectively. In mixed infestations ( n = 15), positivity decreased from 15/15 to 3/15 and 2/15. Mean lesion and pruritus scores also declined in all subgroups. No adverse reactions were observed. A single application was followed by marked temporal reductions in ectoparasite positivity and clinical signs through Day 30. Because the study lacked a comparator and used non-validated clinical scores, the findings are descriptive and exploratory; they do not establish a causal treatment effect or comparative efficacy.

papers.title: Prospective multicenter study of murmur localization and stage-associated murmur grading in dogs with echocardiographically diagnosed cardiac diseases: the LISTEN study.
papers.authors: Wess G, Häggström J, Stadler J, König L, Kraszewska K, Bittenecker D, Domenech O, Santamarina G, Van den Noortgate G, Bjerknaes MB, Eberhard J, Kriström K, Vatne L, Gajewski M, Schinner-Peters C, Tater G, Torti M, Schummer C, Ljungvall I
papers.abstract: Cardiac auscultation remains fundamental in dogs with suspected cardiac disease, but large prospective datasets describing clinician-recorded murmur localization and intensity across echocardiographic diagnoses are limited. This study aimed to characterize point of maximal intensity (PMI) patterns in dogs with echocardiographically diagnosed cardiac abnormalities and to evaluate the association between murmur grade and disease stage in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). This prospective international multicenter observational study included 6,996 client-owned dogs examined by 50 cardiology-trained veterinarians. Dogs underwent standardized cardiac auscultation at four predefined thoracic locations and transthoracic echocardiography during the same clinical visit. PMI localization was described across cardiac diagnoses, and murmur grade was evaluated in relation to disease stage in MMVD and DCM. Dogs with MMVD and DCM predominantly had a left apical PMI, whereas congenital outflow tract diseases and patent ductus arteriosus were predominantly associated with a left basilar PMI. Tricuspid regurgitation and ventricular septal defect were more commonly associated with right apical and right basilar PMIs, respectively. In MMVD, murmur intensity increased with advancing disease stage ( p < 0.001), and dogs with a murmur greater than soft had higher odds of being in stage B2 or C/D than B1 (OR 35.9, 95% CI 27.6-46.6). In DCM, 25.8% of dogs had no audible murmur. Although murmur grade distribution differed across DCM stages ( p = 0.03), intensity did not show a consistent stage-associated increase. Clinician-recorded four-point auscultation identified characteristic regional PMI patterns across several canine cardiac diseases. Murmur grade was strongly associated with disease stage in MMVD but provided limited stage-related information in DCM. Auscultation may support initial clinical assessment and prioritization of differential diagnoses, but echocardiography remains essential for definitive diagnosis and staging.

papers.title: Case report: long-term clinical remission of food-responsive enteropathy in a dog fed a yellow mealworm-based diet.
papers.abstract: Food-responsive enteropathy (FRE) is the most common form of canine chronic inflammatory enteropathy.
