Novel protein diets constitute first-line therapy, and many dogs have already been exposed to "novel" meat alternatives. Edible insects are a novel, highly digestible, and sustainable protein source. In the present study, a five-year-old male York-shire Terrier with chronic FRE and gallbladder sludge was transitioned to a diet with a 35% inclusion level of Tenebrio molitor larvae meal. Clinical indices improved from "severe" (CIBDAI = 9 and CCECAI = 11) to "clinically insignificant" (CIBDAI = 0 and CCECAI = 2) within 3 weeks and remained stable for 24 months. Body weight normalized (from 5.4 to 4.0 kg), coat quality improved, and the ultrasound examination revealed that gallbladder sludge was eliminated. A brief interruption of the insect-based diet coincided with the recurrence of sludge and gastrointestinal signs, both of which resolved after the reintroduction of T. molitor larvae meal. Hematological and serum biochemical parameters remained within the reference ranges. The mealworm-based diet led to long-term remission of FRE and elimination of gallbladder sludge without adverse effects. Insect protein is a viable hypoallergenic option for canine elimination diets and may convey additional gut and hepatobiliary benefits.

papers.title: Application of a convolutional neural network for automatic cytological diagnosis of 7 common canine tumors on whole slide images: a proof-of-concept.
papers.authors: Attini M, Newing E, Oikonomidis IL, Tsouloufi TK, Ressel L
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence may help improve speed and consistency of diagnostic veterinary cytology, but validated tools remain limited. To develop and evaluate a convolutional neural network (CNN) for automatic classification of 7 common canine tumors on cytology whole-slide images (WSIs). Ninety-one May-Grünwald Giemsa-stained canine cytology cases were selected, representing carcinoma, histiocytoma, lymphoma, mast cell tumor, melanoma, plasma cell tumor, and soft tissue sarcoma, together with a background class. Slides were tiled into 22,577 image patches (512 × 512 pixels) and manually labeled and split using a case-wise 3-fold design to avoid data leakage. An ImageNet-pretrained Inception-v3 CNN was fine-tuned for 8-class classification. Performance was assessed at tile level, Grad-CAM was used for qualitative interpretability analysis, and majority-vote prediction was further evaluated at ROI level using attention-guided inference and at WSI level using attention-free whole-slide inference. Mean test accuracy at tile level was 86.3%, with mean macro balanced accuracy of 92.0% and mean macro F1-score of 85.6%. Grad-CAM showed attention focused predominantly on cytologically relevant cellular regions. At ROI level, attention-guided inference achieved 100% Top1 accuracy (28/28 cases). At WSI level, attention-free whole-slide inference achieved 92.9% Top1 accuracy (26/28 cases), and the correct diagnosis was included within the top 3 predictions in all cases. Inception-v3 achieved high diagnostic performance on canine cytology WSIs. The results support the feasibility of both AI-assisted ROI-based decision support and fully automated whole-slide inference in veterinary cytology. These findings are proof-of-concept evidence from a curated, single-institution cohort of typical, well-differentiated cases and require validation on diagnostically challenging and external cases before clinical use.

papers.title: Phenotypic comparison of idiopathic epilepsy in English Springer Spaniels and Cocker Spaniels using a validated owner-completed questionnaire.
papers.authors: Dose JC, Matz MS, Harmas T, Hytönen M, Hakanen E, Lohi H, Parmentier T, Volk HA, Nessler JN, Bhatti SFM, De Risio L, Mandigers P, Ito D, James FMK, Jokinen TS, Ricketts S, Steffen F, Wielaender F, Eschenberg A, Fischer A, Tipold A
papers.abstract: In response to the recurring identification of medication-resistant idiopathic epilepsy (IE) in English Springer Spaniels (ESS), the objective of this retrospective questionnaire-based observational study was to delineate the phenotypic characteristics of IE in this breed in comparison to a cognate breed, the English Cocker Spaniel (ECS), employing a novel, validated, owner-completed multilingual online questionnaire. Owners of 49 ESS and ECS with seizures completed the questionnaire, of which 16 ESS and 14 ECS fulfilled the inclusion criteria and were subsequently included in the study cohort, while the remaining questionnaires were excluded due to incomplete or inconsistent information or because the criteria for IE were not fulfilled. At the time of the survey 43.3% of the dogs had died, including five that died in association with epilepsy. The median age at seizure onset was 2.5 years in ESS and ECS (range: 0,5-9 years; IQR 2.0-4.0 years). Notably a high proportion of dogs in both breeds had experienced ≥1 cluster seizure and ≥1 status epilepticus. In ECS a significantly higher rate of marked reduction in seizure severity following initiation of anti-seizure therapy compared to the ESS ( p = 0.009) was observed. Both breeds exhibit a moderate to severe disease course, with ESS showing a comparatively poorer response to antiseizure drugs. Furthermore, 43.3% of dogs with suspected IE also had affected relatives. The owner-reported occurrence of IE in related dogs may suggest a potential hereditary component in both breeds.

papers.title: Prognostic significance of EGFR-1 and VEGF-A expression in feline cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.
papers.authors: Linhares LCM, Rangel MMM, de Oliveira KD, Fonseca-Alves CE, de Moura FBC, Bispo GA, Queiroga FL, de Nardi AB
papers.abstract: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) is a prevalent malignancy in cats, and advanced cases remain challenging to manage due to their high potential for local invasion and recurrence. Epidermal growth factor receptor 1 (EGFR-1) and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) have emerged as promis- ing prognostic biomarkers in epithelial tumors, given their roles in proliferation, invasion, and angiogenesis. This study aimed to evaluate EGFR-1 and VEGF-A immunoexpression in cats with cSCC treated with electrochemotherapy (ECT) and their associations with clinicopathological variables and survival outcomes. Immunohistochemical expression of EGFR-1 and VEGF-A was evaluated in tumor samples from 33 cats with cSCC enrolled prospectively (n = 24) and retrospec- tively (n = 9). Associations between immunoexpression scores and clinicopatho- logical variables, overall survival time (OST), disease-free interval (DFI), and time to progression (TTP) were assessed using appropriate statistical tests. EGFR-1 positivity was detected in 78.8% (26/33) of cases and was significantly associated with shorter OST, perineural invasion, and intense inflammatory infiltrate. VEGF-A immunoexpression was detected in 71.9% (23/32) of cases and was significantly associated with previous history of cSCC, perineural invasion (PNI), and tumor invasion beyond the subcutaneous fat. These findings suggest that EGFR-1 and VEGF-A immunoexpression are associated with clinicopathological variables linked to aggressive tumor behavior in feline cSCC, supporting their potential role as prognostic biomarkers in this species and warranting further investigation in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Pyelonephritis in cats and dogs - a scoping review.
papers.authors: Pelander L, Ekstrand C, Scahill K
papers.abstract: There is a lack of consensus regarding the diagnosis and treatment of bacterial pyelonephritis (PN) in dogs and cats. The aim of this scoping review was to increase knowledge by describing published scientific literature on the subject, specifically to collate definitions and diagnostic criteria, antimicrobial regimens, reported outcomes, and to identify knowledge gaps. A structured search was performed of the bibliographic databases Biosis, CAB Abstracts, Medline, Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus. We included 176 original studies written in English or German that reported on any aspect of spontaneous PN (risk factors, signalment, history, clinical findings, diagnostic criteria, treatment, prognosis, and outcome) in cats or dogs. Three types of PN were identified in the literature: histologically diagnosed PN, clinically diagnosed PN, and pyonephrosis. Multiple information gaps regarding clinical aspects of PN in dogs and cats were detected. There were no universally accepted clinical criteria for clinical diagnosis of PN and no clinical trials evaluating antimicrobial or other treatment options. Information about short-term outcomes for dogs and cats with PN was scarce, and there were no data regarding long-term outcomes. More information regarding all aspects of clinical PN in dogs and cats is needed.The study protocol was registered prospectively in 2023 ( https://syreaf.org/protocols/ ).

papers.title: Seventeen Cases of Fungal Otitis Externa in Dogs and Cats.
papers.authors: Tang X, Luo X, Liu X, Zhao B, Wang F, Han HS
papers.abstract: Otitis externa (OE) is common in dogs and cats. Fungal OE (FOE) caused by non-Malassezia species fungi is relatively uncommon. Comprehensive information on clinical manifestations, risk factors and breeds or species predispositions remains sparse. In this case series, we describe 17 companion animals in China with FOE. To describe the clinical signs, potential risk factors and treatment of FOE in dogs and cats. Seventeen cases: four dogs and 13 cats. Retrospective review of medical records of cases presented to dermatology specialty practices for OE between 2022 and 2024 was performed. Records with positive fungal culture results were included. Case demographic, diagnostic and treatment information was extracted. Aspergillus spp. was isolated from 13 animals (three dogs, 10 cats), Microsporum canis from one dog and two cats, and one cat had a mixed infection with M. canis in the left ear and Aspergillus spp. in the right. The most common clinical signs were excessive cerumen and pruritus. Of 16 cases that received antifungal treatment, 13 received combined oral and topical therapy, and three received only oral therapy. Aspergillus spp. or dermatophyte infection should not be overlooked in cases of chronic or recurrent OE. Cytological examination of exudates and fungal culture are useful for establishing the diagnosis of FOE. Larger prospective studies are needed to elucidate risk factors and appropriate treatment for FOE.

papers.title: Efficacy of Heat-Killed Lactobacillus plantarum L-137 Supplementation in Treatment of Canine Atopic Dermatitis.
papers.authors: Kiewsiri C, Patumcharoenpol P, Kovitvadhi A, Chermprapai S
papers.abstract: Canine atopic dermatitis (cAD) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease and has been associated with gut dysbiosis. To evaluate the efficacy of heat-killed Lactobacillus plantarum L-137 (HK L-137), a postbiotic supplementation in managing cAD. Twelve client-owned dogs with cAD. A randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blinded crossover trial. Dogs were divided into two groups (n = 6) and received oral HK L-137 or placebo once daily for 12 weeks. After a 2-week washout period, they received the alternative treatment. Oral oclacitinib (0.4-0.6 mg/kg once daily) was permitted throughout the study. Clinical severity was assessed with the 4th iteration of the cAD Extent and Severity Index (CADESI-04) and owner-evaluated pruritus Visual Analog Scale (PVAS) and faecal scoring at 0, 12, 14 and 26 weeks. Serum concentrations of C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin (IL)-4, interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and C-C motif chemokine ligand 17 (CCL17), and haematological and biochemical findings were analysed at the same time points. Faecal microbiota composition (genomic DNA) was assessed at 12 and 26 weeks. PVAS scores mildly improved in both groups, with greater reduction in the HK L-137 group, yet this was not statistically significant. Serum CRP concentrations increased significantly in the control group (p = 0.02). Serum CCL17 concentrations decreased significantly in the HK L-137 group (p = 0.01). No significant changes were observed in CADESI-04, IL-4, IFN-γ or faecal scores or faecal microbiota diversity and composition. HK L-137 represents a potential, well-tolerated adjunctive therapy for dogs with cAD. Therapy was associated with reduced CCL17. Further studies with fewer variables are indicated.

papers.title: Diagnostic and stewardship considerations in fungal lower urinary tract infections of dogs and cats.
papers.authors: Prior C, Sykes JE, Barrs VR, Rautemaa-Richardson R, Klingspor L, Cornely OA, Gull T, Allerton F, Govender NP, Weese JS
papers.abstract: Fungal cystitis in dogs and cats presents a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge, with implications for antifungal stewardship in veterinary medicine. Unlike bacterial cystitis, diagnostic pathways for fungal infection are less well-defined, and antifungal therapy is often empirical. This article discusses key considerations for the diagnosis and management of fungal urinary tract infections, including the interpretation of urine cytology, the potential role and limitations of fungal culture, and the value of species-level identification and antifungal susceptibility testing. Clinical, laboratory, and pharmacokinetic factors that influence treatment decisions are highlighted, alongside the effect of confounding host and iatrogenic risk factors. The article also explores current gaps in evidence, variability in laboratory capabilities, and opportunities for strengthening antifungal stewardship in veterinary practice. Rather than providing prescriptive recommendations, this work aims to raise awareness, facilitate informed decision-making, and guide future research and consensus-building efforts to improve outcomes for animals while contributing to broader antifungal stewardship initiatives. Fungal infections of the urinary tract are uncommon in dogs and cats but can be difficult to diagnose and treat. Unlike bacterial urinary infections, there is less agreement about the best way to confirm a fungal infection and choose appropriate treatment. This article discusses how veterinarians can interpret findings from urine examination and fungal culture, and how identifying the fungal species and testing its response to antifungal drugs might help guide treatment decisions. It also considers factors related to the animal, laboratory testing, and medications that can affect diagnosis and treatment. The article highlights important gaps in current knowledge and differences in laboratory capabilities and emphasizes the need for careful use of antifungal drugs. Rather than providing specific treatment recommendations, this work aims to improve understanding of fungal urinary tract infections, support informed clinical decision-making, and identify priorities for future research and development of veterinary antifungal stewardship.

papers.title: Intestinal angioleiomyoma in a dog.
papers.authors: Nivy R, Bruchim Y, Eley T
papers.abstract: Angioleiomyoma is a rare, smooth muscle tumor of vascular origin, which primarily affects the skin. A 9-year-old, castrated male dog presented for transient ataxia. Abnormalities were not detected on physical examination, but blood tests revealed a mild, severely microcytic anemia and transferrin saturation of 2.5% (reference interval, 27%-66%). An exhaustive diagnostic work-up ensued but failed to find the cause of the severe iron deficiency in laboratory, imaging, and endoscopic studies. Severely microcytic anemia had persisted for 6 months, despite iron-dextran injections, and in the absence of clinical signs, until intussusception developed. The abnormal jejunal segment was removed and diagnosed as angioleiomyoma, based on characteristic histological features, positive immunolabeling with α-smooth muscle actin and CD31, and negative S100 and c-Kit/CD117 staining. Hitherto unreported in dogs, intestinal angioleiomyoma was associated with protracted, occult, asymptomatic intestinal blood loss, until intussusception developed. Prognosis appears favorable with full excision, based on clinical behavior in other organs, and the present case.

papers.title: Chondroprotective Effect of PCSO-524 (Green-Lipped Mussel Extraction) Application Evaluated by Ultrasonography in Pomeranian and Chihuahua With Medial Patellar Luxation Grade II.
papers.authors: Soontornvipart K, Sathienbumrungkit R
papers.abstract: This research evaluated the chondroprotective efficacy of PCSO-524 in dogs with osteoarthritis (OA) secondary to medial patellar luxation (MPL) using ultrasonography - a non-invasive technique recommended for early OA detection. Animals: 25 dogs total (21 with MPL grade II, 50 stifle joints evaluated) divided into three groups, including control group: 10 dogs receiving placebo, treatment group: 11 dogs receiving PCSO-524 (50 mg daily) and normal group: 4 healthy dogs (reference) Duration: 16 weeks Evaluations: Lameness scores, blood profiles, ultrasonographic findings, radiographic assessments and owner questionnaires at baseline, weeks 2, 4, 8, 12 and 16. The treatment group showed significant improvement in lameness scores within 8 weeks. The cartilage lesions improved within 4 weeks of PCSO-524 administration. Synovial fluid scores decreased significantly by week 4 in the treatment group. Radiographic OA scores improved mildly at 12 weeks in the treatment group versus progression in the control group. Owners observed better gait and quality of life by week 2. No adverse effects on blood chemistry or organ function. PCSO-524 demonstrates effective cartilage protection in dogs with OA secondary to MPL, with improvements in clinical signs, ultrasonographic findings and radiographic outcomes. For dogs that cannot undergo surgical correction, PCSO-524 supplementation combined with quadriceps muscle training and environmental management is recommended for improved quality of life.

papers.title: Occurrence and antimicrobial resistance of Acinetobacter baumannii in cats, veterinary hospital environments and medical wastes in Bangladesh.
papers.authors: Hasan M, Lira SA, Islam A, Miti AA, Rahman A, Suchy SA, Jahan I, Ali SB, Parvin MS, Islam MT
papers.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii presence in veterinary hospitals and companion animals is still poorly investigated despite its significance. The present study aimed to investigate the prevalence, antimicrobial resistance patterns, and resistance genes of A. baumannii in cats, veterinary hospital environments, and veterinary medical wastes in Bangladesh. Samples were collected from oral, rectal, and wound swabs of cats (n = 100) attending ten veterinary hospitals, as well as from environmental surfaces (n = 111) and wastes (n = 61) generated within these facilities. Isolates were identified by PCR targeting 16S rRNA (genus) and bla OXA-51-like (species) genes; antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by disk diffusion and broth microdilution following CLSI standards, and resistance genes (bla OXA-23-like , bla NDM-1 ) were screened by PCR. A high prevalence of A. baumannii was observed in cats (37%), while 26.1% in environmental samples and 21.3% in waste samples. Apparently sick cats had significantly higher prevalence (p = 0.049) than apparently healthy cats. All isolates were imipenem resistant, consistent with carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB). High resistance was also observed against cefotaxime and ceftriaxone. Multidrug resistance (MDR) was detected in 26.7%, 37.9%, and 30.8% of isolates from cats, environmental, and waste sources, respectively. The bla OXA-23-like gene was detected in only two cat isolates, whereas bla NDM was identified in one cat isolate and one environmental isolate. In conclusion, these findings identify cats, which live in close proximity to humans, as a possible CRAB reservoir, and veterinary hospital environments and waste as potential sources of persistence and dissemination, raising concern for zoonotic spread and underscoring occupational and public health risk.

papers.title: EXPRESS:Management of Distal Hindlimb Injuries in Cats Using an Exvet External Skeletal Fixation System: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Uygur S, Dogan A, Yardımcı C, Ulusan S, Beale BS, Immler M, Vidoni B, Schnabl-Feichter E
papers.abstract: To evaluate the clinical use of an Exvet external skeletal fixation (ESF) system applied using minimally invasive techniques for the management of distal hindlimb injuries in cats. Cats with distal hindlimb injuries treated using the Exvet Tarsal Fixator (ETF) at four institutions between September 2022 and January 2026 were included. Data collected included fracture type, surgical approach, postoperative complications and additional treatments, time to first limb use, time to fixator removal, radiographic findings, and clinical outcome. Of 73 cats evaluated, 35 cats with 36 distal hindlimb injuries met the inclusion criteria. Twenty-four cats (68.6%) were managed with a closed reduction, while 11 cats (31.4%) were managed with a limited open surgical fashion. Thirty-two of 35 cats (91.4%) started weight bearing immediately after surgery. Complications were recorded in 7 of 35 cases (20.0%), of which 5 cases (14.3%) were classified as minor and 2 cases (5.7%) as major complications. At a mean ESF removal time of 34 days (median: 28 days; range: 21-56 days), a full functional outcome was achieved in 25 of 35 cases (71.4%), while 10 cases (28.6%) showed an acceptable functional outcome. The ETF is an anatomically designed ESF implant specifically developed for feline distal hindlimb injuries. The findings of this multicenter retrospective study support its safe and effective use for the management of feline distal hindlimb injuries.

papers.title: EXPRESS: BENEFITS OF CONTRAST-ENHANCED COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY OVER PLAIN COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY FOR HEAD TRAUMA IN 41 CATS.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Mariaud V, Arinal P, Masson A, Mortier J
papers.abstract: The aim of this study is to evaluate whether contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) provides clinically useful information beyond Plain computed tomography (PCT) in cats with head trauma, and whether this benefit is influenced by the radiologist's level of experience. Forty-one cats that underwent head CT with both pre- and post-contrast sequences were included. Images were independently reviewed by three radiologists with different experience levels, assessing extracranial soft tissue injuries, bone fractures, and intracranial abnormalities. Intra- and interobserver agreements were analyzed using Cohen's kappa statistics. Substantial to almost perfect agreement was obtained for extracranial soft tissue injuries and bone fractures. The most commonly fractured sites were the temporomandibular joints, hard palate, mandibular bones, and pterygoid bones. For intracranial lesions such as hemorrhage and cerebral edema, intra- and interobserver agreements were low and variable, regardless of contrast use or reviewer experience. There was no significant difference found between PCT and CECT for any of the three categories. These results suggest that contrast medium injection is not useful for assessment of bone fractures and extracranial soft tissue and that computed tomography of the head is poorly reliable for intracranial lesions in cats presented for trauma.

papers.title: Feline viral infections: current perspectives on diagnosis, treatment and prevention.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Hosie MJ

papers.title: Effect of oral gabapentin administered in-hospital on behavioral stress, compliance, and physiologic stress markers: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Canosa C, Summers SC
papers.abstract: The aim of the study was to determine whether post admission oral gabapentin improves stress indices and handling tolerance in hospitalized cats. In this double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-design trial, healthy client-owned cats were enrolled. After the initial examination, cats received a 100 mg gabapentin or placebo capsule. At 90 min, a second examination, venipuncture, and brief dorsal positioning were performed. Five stress behaviors (struggling, vocalization, repelling, hypersalivation, mouth breathing), compliance, and enclosure activity score (1, sedate; 5, very active) were recorded; blood glucose, lactate, serum cortisol, and lymphocyte count were measured. Serum gabapentin concentrations were obtained 90 min after the capsule. A total of 30 cats (15 cats/group) were included in analysis. In the 15 cats who received gabapentin, the median gabapentin dose was 21.7 mg/kg (range 14.3-28.1), yielding a median serum concentration of 16.4 µg/ml (range 1.3-24.5). Most gabapentin-treated cats exhibited fewer stress behaviors (n = 13/15, 87%) and better compliance for handling during examination (n = 11/15, 73%) at 90 min post-capsule compared with 3/15 (20%) and 4/15 (27%), respectively, in placebo cats. Between-group differences were not detected for behavioral or compliance scores during venipuncture or dorsal positioning. Enclosure activity scores in the gabapentin group decreased from median 3 at baseline to 2 from 90-360 min post-dose (120, 240, and 300 min; P <0.05, respectively), consistent with mild sedation. Blood lactate and cortisol concentrations were lower in the gabapentin group than the placebo group ( P  = 0.002 and P  = 0.04, respectively). A 100 mg oral dose of gabapentin provides modest improvement in stress behaviors during examination and favorably alters select physiologic stress markers within 90 min of administration, with sustained reductions in kennel activity. Findings support incorporating gabapentin within a multimodal, low-stress approach for cats presenting without preappointment medication, while maintaining contingency plans for additional sedation as needed. Giving gabapentin in the hospital can modestly calm cats for examinations within 90 minutes Many cats become stressed during veterinary visits, which can make examinations and simple procedures difficult. Because some visits are unplanned, cats may arrive without any anxiety-reducing medications on board. We studied whether giving a single oral dose of gabapentin (a commonly used calming medicine) after admission could help. In total, 30 healthy pet cats were enrolled. Each cat first had a brief examination. Then cats received either a 100 mg gabapentin capsule or an inactive placebo pill by mouth. About 90 min later, we repeated the examination and carried out routine handling (a blood draw and brief positioning on the back). We scored each cat’s behavior and how easy the cat was to handle. We also noted how active the cat was while resting in the kennel for several hours. Blood tests included measures linked to stress (cortisol and lactate). Cats who received gabapentin showed modest improvements during the second examination: they struggled less and were easier to handle. Their blood tests also suggested lower stress (cortisol and lactate were lower) compared with cats who received the placebo pill. In their kennels, cats given gabapentin were less active for several hours, consistent with mild calming. However, we did not see clear differences between groups during the more uncomfortable steps (the blood draw and brief positioning). Giving gabapentin in the hospital can help with routine examination and gentle handling within about 90 min, especially for moderately stressed cats. It is best used as part of a broader, low-stress approach (quiet space, gentle handling, towels/pheromones) and may not be enough on its own for more invasive procedures. Responses varied between cats, likely because absorption of a single capsule can differ.

papers.title: Feline-Derived Lactiplantibacillus plantarum -Aloe Vera Polysaccharide Hydrogel as a Topical Control Strategy for Staphylococcus pseudintermedius -Infected Wounds.
papers.authors: Chen Q, Dong H, Wang W, Wang H, Yao J, Ma M, Zhu S, Zhu L, Du Z, Xia Z, Xiong W
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (SP) is an important opportunistic pathogen in companion animals, and the increasing prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant strains highlights the need for alternative approaches to local infection control. This study evaluated a topical hydrogel containing feline-derived Lactiplantibacillus plantarum ZYpet-014 and Aloe vera polysaccharides (AVEs) for the treatment of SP-infected wounds. AVEs promoted LP growth and organic-acid production and improved short-term LP viability within the carbomer hydrogel. The LP+AVE-hydrogel inhibited planktonic SP growth and biofilm formation in vitro and caused pronounced morphological disruption of SP cells. Therapeutic efficacy was further evaluated using a full-thickness murine wound model challenged with SP. LP+AVE treatment accelerated wound closure, reaching 95.75% by day 14, while qualitative histological observations suggested improved tissue organization and differences in collagen-associated staining patterns. Treatment was also associated with reduced TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 levels and increased IL-4, IL-10, TGF-β1, and serum VEGF concentrations. In wound tissues, LP+AVE treatment decreased CD80 and increased CD206 immunoreactivity, consistent with a shift in macrophage-associated responses toward a reparative profile. Moreover, 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed reduced relative abundance of Staphylococcus and increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus in treated wounds. Together, these findings demonstrate antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against SP in vitro, accompanied by improved wound healing, modulation of inflammatory responses, and changes in wound microbial composition in vivo, although direct reduction in SP burden in wound tissue remains to be established.

papers.title: Exploratory Evaluation of Refractometric, Biochemical, and Body Weight Change Parameters for Diagnosing Failure of Passive Transfer in Puppies.
papers.authors: Kara H, Şenel Y, Kaya U, Güven M, Şenol A
papers.abstract: Failure of passive transfer (FPT) is an important determinant of survival in neonatal puppies. Practical indirect indicators that could serve as alternatives to measuring serum immunoglobulin G (IgG) have not yet been adequately characterized. In this exploratory study, 76 Turkish Kangal puppies aged 48 ± 4 h, born to 12 dams (mean age 40.2 months) were evaluated. Serum IgG measured by ELISA was the reference method, with values below 2.3 g/L classified as FPT. Whole-blood, fresh-serum, and frozen-thawed serum Brix values were evaluated together with serum total protein, albumin, globulin, gamma-glutamyl transferase, canine parvovirus antibody levels, and percentage change in body weight from birth to sampling, using receiver operating characteristic analysis. FPT was identified in six puppies (7.9%). The area under the curve (AUC) values for total protein, globulin, and percentage change in body weight were 0.986, 0.981, and 0.948, respectively, with the associated cutoffs considered exploratory; each detected all six cases with 82.9-94.3% specificity. Fresh-serum Brix showed moderate discrimination (AUC: 0.771), whereas whole-blood Brix was inconclusive (AUC: 0.432). Total protein, globulin, and early body weight change are promising screening indicators for detecting FPT. However, because of the limited number of cases, their cutoffs should be validated in larger populations, including other breeds, before clinical use.

papers.title: Cardiac Vagal Decoupling in Canine Anesthesia: A Physiological Concept for Graded Vasopressor Titration.
papers.authors: Nagahama S
papers.abstract: During general anesthesia in dogs, vasopressor-induced increases in mean arterial pressure (MAP) may be partly opposed by reflex sinus slowing. Subsequent administration of atropine or another antimuscarinic may cause an abrupt increase in sinus rate; when vascular tone is already elevated, this increase may in turn contribute to an abrupt or excessive MAP rise. This article examines cardiac vagal decoupling, defined as reduced vagally mediated muscarinic restraint at the sinoatrial node, as a physiological concept for graded vasopressor titration. The hypothesis is that reducing this restraint before substantial vasopressor escalation, followed by MAP-guided dose adjustments, may permit more graded pressure control: reaching and maintaining a specified MAP range with fewer abrupt or excessive pressure increases. Canine studies support muscarinic control of sinus rate, baroreflex responses during anesthesia, and modification of vasopressor responses by prior antimuscarinic administration. These findings support components of the proposed concept, but whether it improves graded MAP titration has not been directly tested. The article contrasts the two hemodynamic patterns, evaluates the supporting evidence, and considers the limits of the hypothesis. Effects of such titration on cardiac output, tissue perfusion, and clinical outcomes require separate evaluation.

papers.title: CT-Clinical Dissociation and Focal Obstruction in Feline Chronic Rhinosinusitis: A Pilot Study.
papers.authors: Lee G, Chang J, Lee J, Song KH
papers.abstract: Feline chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is common and difficult to manage, and the relationship between computed tomography (CT) findings and clinical severity remains unclear. This exploratory retrospective pilot study included 10 cats with chronic upper respiratory signs for at least 4 weeks that underwent CT of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses at a single referral hospital. Newly developed, unvalidated semiquantitative scores graded CT severity (0-12) and clinical severity (0-12), and cats were grouped into four provisional clinicoradiologic patterns using integrated CT, clinical, and cytologic findings and, where available, microbiologic findings. CT scores ranged from 2 to 10 (median 8.0) and clinical scores from 4 to 11 (median 6.5), without a consistent monotonic association (Spearman r s = 0.250, 95% bootstrap confidence interval (CI) -0.558 to 0.885, p = 0.486). The provisional patterns were active/exudative ( n = 2), structural/remodeling ( n = 4), obstructive ( n = 3), and immune/mucosal ( n = 1). Focal obstruction defined both the obstructive pattern and the conceptual surgical candidacy categories, so their overlap is by design; of interest is that cats with the highest CT scores did not necessarily have focal obstruction. No cat underwent surgery. These hypothesis-generating findings require validation in larger prospective studies with validated scores.

papers.title: Regulatory Science for Veterinary Therapeutic Innovation: A Comparative Analysis of Drug Development Incentives Within the One Health Framework.
papers.authors: Hong S, Lee SM
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in antiviral therapeutics, targeted biologics, RNA medicines, and precision veterinary medicine are generating unprecedented scientific opportunities for veterinary healthcare, yet translation of these innovations into approved veterinary products remains disproportionately slow. This review employs a comparative regulatory science framework to identify the regulatory and economic determinants of this innovation gap across four jurisdictions-FDA-CVM (US), EMA-CVMP (EU), PMDA/MAFF (Japan), and APVMA (Australia)-and to compare existing incentive instruments and identify the regulatory gaps between them. Two illustrative case studies, GS-441524 for feline infectious peritonitis and canine osteosarcoma therapeutics, illustrate how the absence of breakthrough pathways, limitations in the practical translation of Minor Use/Minor Species (MUMS) eligibility, and unresolved intellectual property barriers can suppress development investment. The multi-jurisdictional analysis indicates that this innovation gap is evident across the jurisdictions examined and is consistent with differences in the availability and strength of regulatory incentives, though scientific and market factors likely also contribute. Policy reforms are proposed, including a Veterinary Breakthrough Drug Designation, a One Health Innovation Designation with enhanced exclusivity, adaptive regulatory pathways, and strengthened VICH harmonization. Additionally, the regulatory preparedness for advanced veterinary therapeutics-including gene therapies, mRNA-based vaccines, and cell-based products-is examined as a critical frontier. The analysis highlights the role of regulatory science in translating emerging veterinary therapeutics into clinical practice within the One Health framework.

papers.title: Dietary Pieris japonica Leaf Powder Enhances Hepatic Antioxidant Capacity, Modulates Cecal Microbiota, and Improves Eggshell Thickness in Laying Hens.
papers.authors: Wu Y, Chen J, Chen F, Liu Y, Lian J, Tang Y, He B, Lin Q
papers.abstract: Oxidative stress and intestinal health are critical factors that are closely linked to the production performance and physiological status of laying hens. This work assessed how dietary incorporation of Pieris japonica leaf powder (PJP) shapes egg quality attributes, hepatic antioxidant defence, gut tissue morphology, and cecal microbial community profiles in layers. A total of 360 healthy 56-week-old Hy-Line Brown layers were randomly assigned to four treatments, each containing six replicate pens housing 15 birds apiece. Animals received basal feeds containing 0.00% (control), 0.05%, 0.10%, or 0.20% PJP throughout the 10-week experimental run that including a 2-week adaptation period. Relative to the control group, diets with 0.05% PJP significantly increased eggshell thickness ( p < 0.05). Hepatic total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC), catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) were significantly elevated in PJP-supplemented groups ( p < 0.05). The 0.10% PJP addition improved duodenal villus-height-to-crypt-depth ratio (V/C). Regarding cecal microbiota, 0.10% PJP reduced the Simpson index while elevating Collinsella relative abundance ( p < 0.05). Noticeably, the 0.20% supplementation exerted adverse effects on egg-related indices. Correlation analysis indicated that cecal microbiota was closely associated with hepatic antioxidant indices and eggshell-related indicators. In summary, dietary PJP inclusion may improve the eggshell thickness of eggs from laying hens by enhancing host antioxidant defense, reshaping the composition of cecal microbial communities. It was reported that 0.10% PJP supplementation yielded the most favorable comprehensive responses under the conditions adopted within this trial.

papers.title: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia with Secondary Pseudomonas aeruginosa Infection in a Dog: Endoscopic and Diagnostic Findings.
papers.authors: Maggi G, Pirgher F, De Lorenzi D, Aresu L, Marchesi MC
papers.abstract: A 7-month-old, 3.6-kg, intact male Dachshund was presented with a lifelong history of chronic respiratory signs. Multiple courses of antimicrobial therapy resulted in partial or complete clinical improvement, followed by recurrence after treatment discontinuation. To investigate the underlying cause of the persistent respiratory disease, rhino-tracheobronchoscopy was performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid and respiratory mucosal biopsy specimens were collected for cytological, histopathological, and ultrastructural evaluation. Cytological examination of BAL fluid revealed septic neutrophilic inflammation, and bacterial culture yielded P. aeruginosa. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) identified ultrastructural abnormalities of the ciliary axoneme in 50% of the examined respiratory cilia. Based on these findings, primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) was diagnosed. PCD is a rare congenital disorder characterized by structural and functional abnormalities of motile cilia, resulting in impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent respiratory infections. This case highlights the diagnostic value of a detailed clinical history, endoscopic examination, and TEM in dogs with suspected PCD.

papers.title: Pulmonary Neoplasms with Pleuropulmonary Blastoma-like Features in Two Young Labrador Retrievers: Clinicopathological, Molecular and Comparative Characterisation.
papers.authors: van der Weyden L, Francis BA, Olson DR, Schultz KAP, Di Palma S, Ryan T, Kamieniarz K, Miguel-Garces M, Thompson L, Jones R, Nix C, Haugland S, Ortiz AL
papers.abstract: Pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB) is a rare, paediatric, mesenchymal, pulmonary neoplasm that can be highly aggressive. To date, there are only two reports of PPB in animals. We describe the finding of pulmonary neoplasms with PPB-like features in two unrelated Labrador Retrievers. Both dogs presented with acute dyspnoea, pneumothorax and pulmonary lesions. Treatment consisted of emergency thoracostomy tube placement followed by lung lobectomy. At follow-up, one dog experienced no recurrence 20 months post-surgery, whereas recurrence developed in the second dog 2 years postoperatively. Histopathological examination revealed spindle-shaped neoplastic cells with blastematous-to-sarcomatous appearance, associated with cystic spaces lined by non-neoplastic respiratory epithelium. Immunohistochemistry showed that the neoplastic cells were positive for mesenchymal markers but negative for epithelial and neuroendocrine markers, with some tumour cells showing desmin positivity, supportive of myogenic differentiation, possibly compatible with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Genome profiling revealed a heterogeneous somatic landscape. No pathogenic somatic or germline DICER1 variants were found. We compared these findings with those reported in human PPB. This is the first comprehensive analysis of pulmonary neoplasms with PPB-like features in animals, and reveals parallels with PPB in humans, further supporting the 'One Medicine' approach.

papers.title: Prostaglandin-Endoperoxide Synthase 2 (PTGS2) Expression Is Increased in Chronic Asymptomatic Orchitis in the Dog.
papers.authors: Packeiser EM, Körber H, Morawietz J, Goericke-Pesch S
papers.abstract: Chronic asymptomatic orchitis (CAO) in dogs lacks effective treatment options. To elucidate the involvement of prostaglandin endoperoxide synthase 2 (PTGS2), associated with inflammation and physiological steroidogenesis, testicular PTGS2 and StAR gene (via RT-qPCR) and protein expression (via immunohistochemistry) were analyzed in 11 canine CAO samples and compared to five normospermic control group (CG) samples. The percentage of immunopositive area (PIA) and mean gray scale (MGS) intensity were evaluated in the interstitial and tubular compartments. In CAO, PTGS2 and StAR gene expression levels were significantly increased compared to CG ( p < 0.001 and p = 0.0034). Leydig cells and some peritubular cells stained immunopositive for PTGS2 and StAR and Sertoli cells positive for PTGS2. PIA and MGS for PTGS2 differed significantly between groups in the interstitial (PIA: p < 0.0001; MGS: p = 0.0051) and tubular (PIA: p = 0.0006; MGS: p = 0.0413) compartments. For StAR, PIA, but not MGS, was significantly higher in CAO ( p = 0.0010). Except for PTGS2 gene expression, higher degrees of spermatogenetic impairment correlated with more prominent expression changes. This study demonstrates an association between increased PTGS2 expression and CAO. Further research is needed to investigate potential clinical benefits of selective PTGS2 inhibitors.

papers.title: Perioperative Glycemic Changes Following Partial Pancreatectomy for a Pancreatic Islet Cell Neoplasm in a Dog: A Case Report.
papers.authors: Choi CH, Kim JW, Park MS, Cho JS, You DH, Kim JH, Eom KD, Kim HY, Kim JM
papers.abstract: Canine insulinomas are functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors that typically cause hypoglycemia, but blood glucose may fluctuate before surgery and increase after resection. This report describes the diagnostic evaluation, surgical treatment, and perioperative glycemic course of a 12-year-old female Miniature Schnauzer with a pancreatic islet cell neoplasm considered clinically consistent with insulinoma. Intermittent low or low-normal blood glucose concentrations ranging from 54 to 72 mg/dL were documented before surgery, and the blood glucose concentration on the day of surgery was 73 mg/dL. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography identified a mass in the left pancreatic limb, and partial pancreatectomy was subsequently performed. Blood glucose reached 416 mg/dL 2 h after pancreatic mass removal while surgery was ongoing, then initially declined without insulin administration. Recurrent postoperative hyperglycemia was treated with regular insulin on postoperative days (PODs) 2 and 3, whereas subsequent decreases in blood glucose were treated with dextrose supplementation. Blood glucose continued to fluctuate on POD 4; no additional insulin was administered after POD 3. Histopathologic examination identified a pancreatic islet cell neoplasm. Although a paired serum insulin concentration during documented hypoglycemia was not available and immunohistochemical staining for insulin or other neuroendocrine markers was not performed, the clinical, imaging, glycemic, and histopathological findings were considered consistent with a clinicopathologic diagnosis of insulinoma. Blood glucose was 150 mg/dL on POD 7; subsequent recorded concentrations through POD 150 ranged from 107 to 133 mg/dL. Serial glucose monitoring helped characterize the perioperative course and guide postoperative insulin and dextrose treatment.

papers.title: Cytologically Suggested Vulvar Involvement in a Dog with Multicentric Lymphoma After a Nodal Response to CHOP-Based Chemotherapy, with Discordant Clonality Results: A Case Report.
papers.authors: Roh T, Song K
papers.abstract: Involvement of the female reproductive tract is rare in canine lymphoma. A 9-year-old spayed female Maltese dog was presented with generalized lymphadenopathy. Cytology of a mandibular lymph node aspirate indicated large cell lymphoma, whereas PCR for antigen receptor rearrangement (PARR) of the same sample was polyclonal. Splenectomy confirmed splenic large cell lymphoma, classified as World Health Organization clinical stage IVa. After 12 cycles of a CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone)-based protocol, restaging computed tomography showed a marked reduction in all measurable lymph nodes, whereas gastric and subcutaneous nodules persisted. On Day 181 (168 days after the start of chemotherapy), vulvar swelling was noticed and progressed despite antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory treatment, together with inguinal lymphadenopathy. Disease progression was diagnosed by inguinal lymph node cytology, and rescue chemotherapy was started; however, the dog developed acute dyspnea and died two days later. Results reported after death showed a mixed monoclonal and polyclonal immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) pattern in the inguinal lymph node and a clonal IgH rearrangement in the vulvar aspirate, which was cytologically consistent with lymphoma. In dogs treated for lymphoma, vulvar swelling may reflect neoplastic infiltration, and PARR results may differ between samples obtained at different sites and time points.

papers.title: A Salivary Conglomerate with a Substantial Organic Component Mimicking a Mineral Sialolith in the Mandibular-Sublingual Gland Complex of a Dog.
papers.authors: Schidu D, Zelinschi V, Hrițcu OM, Acomi ȘM, Ștefănescu RA, Șindilar EV, Burtan LC, Solcan G
papers.abstract: Solid lesions of the mandibular-sublingual salivary gland complex are rare in dogs. We report the case of an 11-year-old, 5 kg, intact female Maltese dog that presented with a non-painful, 2-3 cm left cervical swelling, soft at the surface and firm in depth. Fine-needle aspiration yielded clear, sero-mucous fluid. Radiographs revealed a well-defined, ovoid radiopaque structure measuring 3.1 × 2.9 cm in the cranial cervical region. Mandibular and monostomatic sublingual sialoadenectomy via a ventral approach revealed a large, heart-shaped, solid conglomerate within the glandular complex. Histopathological examination confirmed glandular atrophy, fibrosis and sialoadenitis. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometry of the submitted fragments indicated a substantial organic, protein- and lipid-rich component, with additional bands suggesting a possible minor mineral component. The dog healed completely, with no recurrence detected at the 2-week examination. Limitations include the absence of cross-sectional imaging and elemental analysis and the limited clinical follow-up. This case shows that protein-rich solid conglomerates should be included in the differential diagnosis of cervical swellings in dogs, that radiopacity alone does not establish mineral composition, and that complete surgical excision was associated with a favourable short-term outcome.

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of the Fatty Acid Profiles of Hypoallergenic Veterinary Diets, Commercial Dog Foods, and Oral Fatty Acid Supplements Available on the Hungarian Market.
papers.authors: Tóth Z, Fébel H, Wágner L, Buránszki B, Lajos A, Vida K, Tarpataki N
papers.abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), particularly the long-chain n-3 PUFAs (eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA)), are integral to the dietary management of canine atopic dermatitis (CAD). However, the fatty acid profiles of commercially available canine products on Hungarian markets have not been systematically characterised, and the present study aimed to address this gap. A total of 35 products selected from those available on the Hungarian market at the time of sampling were analysed by gas chromatography with flame ionisation detection (GC-FID): 8 hypoallergenic veterinary diets (HVD), 22 commercial dog foods (CD), and 5 oral fatty acid supplements (FS). FS1-FS4 are complementary feeds under Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. FS5 is a food supplement under Directive 2002/46/EC. FS5 was included for comparative reference only. Fatty acid composition is expressed as % of total peak area. The n-6/n-3 ratio differed substantially across categories (HVD mean 6.16, range 2.65-10.71; CD mean 9.94, range 2.68-18.16; FS1-FS4 mean 18.08, range 0.29-63.49 (FS5 excluded as human product)). Combined % of EPA + DHA was lower in dietary products (HVD mean 0.94%, range 0.16-2.10%; CD mean 0.19%, range 0.09-0.34%) than in marine-based supplements (FS3 7.52%, FS4 24.19%). Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) was the predominant n-3 fatty acid in 29 of 30 dietary products. Pronounced inter-product heterogeneity was observed among supplements, including one plant-based product with an n-6/n-3 ratio of 63.49. These findings indicate that commercial and hypoallergenic diets contain low proportion of EPA, and that marine-based oral supplementation provided substantially higher proportions of EPA and DHA than any dietary product evaluated.

papers.title: Transosseous Suture Fixation of an Inverted Palatal Mucoperiosteal Flap to Residual Buccal Alveolar Bone for Oronasal Fistula Repair in a Dog.
papers.authors: Lee JH, Lee S, Cho JS, Park C, Park BJ, Yoon S, Jeongwon L, Kim J, Kim HY, Kim JM
papers.abstract: Advanced periodontal disease can compromise the recipient tissues available for flap fixation during oronasal fistula repair. This report describes double-layer repair of an acquired periodontal oronasal fistula in an eight-year-old castrated male Beagle. Radiographs and computed tomography (CT) identified regional bone loss and residual alveolar bone adjacent to the defect. Following extraction of the left maxillary canine and second premolar and debridement of the fistula margins, an inverted hard palatal mucoperiosteal flap was anchored to residual buccal alveolar bone through four transosseous bone holes created with an 18-gauge needle. Transosseous suture fixation used 4-0 polydioxanone simple interrupted sutures. A buccal mucosal advancement flap covered the inverted flap and palatal donor site; no interpositional graft was used. Healing without clinically evident dehiscence was documented on postoperative day 18, and nasal discharge had resolved by day 45. At 555 days, visual oral examination revealed an intact repair, with concordant CT findings obtained for an unrelated otologic indication. This case illustrates the use of residual buccal alveolar bone for palatal flap attachment when periodontal tissue loss limits gingival recipient margins, with maintained closure documented at late clinical and imaging reassessment.

papers.title: Dietary Curcumin Protects Common Carp ( Cyprinus carpio ) Against Potassium Permanganate-Induced Toxicity: Hematological, Immunological, Oxidative, and Molecular Docking Evidence.
papers.authors: Eroğlu M, Mişe Yonar S, Tanrıkulu D, Uslu H, Yonar ME
papers.abstract: Potassium permanganate treatment can adversely affect fish physiology despite its usefulness in aquaculture. This study evaluated the protective effects of dietary curcumin against potassium permanganate-induced disturbances in common carp (Cyprinus carpio). Fish were fed a basal diet or diets supplemented with 1%, 2%, or 4% curcumin for eight weeks, with or without subsequent exposure to potassium permanganate at 2 mg/L for 30 min daily for seven days. Hematological and immune parameters and oxidative status in the liver, kidney, spleen, and gill were assessed. Potassium permanganate exposure altered blood and immune parameters, increased lipid peroxidation, and weakened antioxidant defenses. Curcumin supplementation alleviated these effects, with protection evident at 1%, the lowest dietary inclusion level tested, and further improvements in selected parameters at 4%. Inclusion levels below 1% were not evaluated, so the minimum effective level remains unknown. Molecular docking predicted interactions between curcumin and the antioxidant enzymes SOD, CAT, GPx, and GST at structurally plausible binding sites. These computational findings were interpreted alongside the biological results as supportive, hypothesis-generating evidence rather than confirmation of functional effects on these enzymes in vivo. Overall, dietary curcumin showed potential to reduce the physiological disturbances associated with repeated potassium permanganate exposure. Further dose-response studies should evaluate inclusion levels below 1% to identify effective and economically viable supplementation rates and determine whether curcumin affects the antiparasitic or antibacterial efficacy of potassium permanganate.

papers.title: Clinical Diagnostic Assessment of Serum Testosterone in Intact and Castrated Tomcats.
papers.authors: Tekin K, Pereira M, Pimazzoni L, Bonsembiante F, Zucchini P, Romagnoli S
papers.abstract: Basal serum testosterone may help determine reproductive status in tomcats with an uncertain surgical history, but interpretation of a single result is limited by episodic secretion and reduced analytical precision at very low concentrations. We evaluated the analytical performance and diagnostic accuracy of an automated fluorescence enzyme immunoassay (FEIA) in 80 male cats (40 intact and 40 castrated). Within-run and between-day precision and dilutional recovery were assessed using pooled feline serum, and diagnostic performance was evaluated by receiver operating characteristic analysis. Testosterone concentrations were significantly higher in intact than castrated cats ( p < 0.001), although overlap occurred at low concentrations. ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.773 (95% CI, 0.665-0.859). The Youden-derived threshold > 0.124 ng/mL had 60.0% sensitivity (95% CI, 43.3-75.1%) and 90.0% specificity (95% CI, 76.3-97.2%). No castrated cat had a concentration > 0.271 ng/mL; this cohort-specific rule-in threshold had 47.5% sensitivity (95% CI, 31.5-63.9%) and 100% observed specificity (95% CI, 91.2-100.0%). Therefore, clearly elevated basal testosterone can support the presence of functional testicular tissue, but concentrations ≤ 0.271 ng/mL cannot exclude intact status. Low or equivocal results require integration with clinical examination and, when indicated, GnRH stimulation and/or anti-Müllerian hormone measurement. Independent validation is required before broad clinical application.

papers.title: Hematologic Responses to Molidustat in Cats with Anemia of Heterogeneous Etiology: A Retrospective Descriptive Study.
papers.authors: Lee G, Lee J, Song KH
papers.abstract: Molidustat, an oral hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, is approved for nonregenerative anemia associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in cats but is also used for anemia of other causes. This retrospective, single-center study described the hematologic response to molidustat in 39 cats with anemia of heterogeneous etiology and identified factors that complicate attribution of improvement to the drug. Response was defined as a hematocrit (HCT) increase of ≥4 percentage points from baseline at the complete blood count closest to day 28 (days 14-45), without transfusion to treat anemia. Molidustat was used outside the approved indication in 33 cats (84.6%). Seventeen cats (43.6%) had a response-window measurement; they had a longer treatment span and differed in etiology and concurrent treatment from non-evaluable cats. Among these 17 cats, 12 (70.6%; 95% CI 46.9-86.7%) met the response criterion; sensitivity analyses specified before formal analysis gave 70.6-75.0% and post hoc attribution analyses 29.4-50.0%. In 7 of the 12 responders, darbepoetin or transfusion preceded the qualifying measurement, or it was obtained more than 7 days after the last dose. These data describe clinical use but do not establish effectiveness outside CKD-associated anemia.

papers.title: Detection of Zoonotic Protozoan Enteropathogens in Stray and Owned Dogs with Diarrhea in Trabzon Province Using Microscopic and Molecular Methods.
papers.abstract: Zoonotic protozoan parasites in dogs represent a significant public health concern because of their ability to infect humans. This study aimed to detect and determine the prevalence of zoonotic protozoan infections, including Balantidium coli , Entamoeba histolytica , Giardia duodenalis , Cryptosporidium spp., Sarcocystis spp. and Cystoisospora spp. in stray and owned dogs with diarrhea in Trabzon Province, Türkiye. Fecal samples were obtained from 450 dogs of various ages, sexes, and breeds. Samples were preserved in 70% alcohol for molecular analysis and incubated in 2.5% potassium dichromate for microscopic examination. Parasite DNA was analyzed using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and identified by restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP). Microscopic examination identified the Cystoisospora ohioensis group, Cystoisospora canis , and Sarcocystis spp. in 56 samples (12.44%). Specifically, Cystoisospora spp. and Sarcocystis spp. were detected in 36 (8.00%) and 20 (4.44%) of the samples, respectively. A mixed infection involving C. canis and the C. ohioensis group was observed in one sample. Molecular analyses detected Cystoisospora spp. DNA in 36 samples (8.00%) and Sarcocystis spp. DNA in 20 samples (4.44%). RFLP analysis confirmed that all detected Cystoisospora spp. DNA belonged to C. ohioensis , while Sarcocystis spp. could not be differentiated at the species level. This study reports the first microscopic detection of Sarcocystis spp. and C. ohioensis in dogs in Trabzon Province and constitutes the first molecular identification of C. ohioensis in Türkiye.

papers.title: MicroRNA Regulation of the Estrogen Receptor Alpha 3'UTR in Canine Mammary Tumor (CMT28) Cells.
papers.authors: Goyal D, Bird RC
papers.abstract: Reduced estrogen receptor alpha (ERα/ ESR1 ) expression is seen in canine mammary tumors, but the mechanisms involved are not fully understood. This study examined ESR1 , miR-18a, and miR-19a expression in canine mammary cell lines. Further CMT28, a canine mammary tumor cell line, was used to test whether these miRNAs can regulate the reporter activity through selected regions of the canine ESR1 3'UTR containing predicted miR-18a and miR-19a binding sites. ESR1 mRNA expression was measured by RT-qPCR, and miR-18a and miR-19a expression was measured using LNA-based assays. ESR1 mRNA expression was much lower in CMT27, CMT28, and CMT47 compared with normal canine mammary epithelial cells, while CMT12 showed higher expression. miR-18a and miR-19a were increased to different levels across the tumor cell lines. Bioinformatic analysis identified predicted miR-18a and miR-19a seed-match sites in the canine ESR1 3'UTR. Luciferase reporter assays showed that both miR-18a and miR-19a significantly reduced activity of the reporter containing selected regions of the 3'UTR of ESR1 encoding predicted miR-18a and miR-19a binding sites. In contrast, neither miRNA significantly reduced activity of the mutant reporter containing deletions in the predicted miR-18a and miR-19a seed-match regions. Anti-miR-18a and anti-miR-19a also significantly increased reporter activity compared with the corresponding miRNA alone. These findings provide functional evidence that miR-18a and miR-19a can regulate reporter activity through selected regions of the canine ESR1 3'UTR. Further studies are needed to determine the role of this regulation in endogenous ESR1 expression and canine mammary tumor biology.

papers.title: Intra-Articular Autologous Conditioned Serum Alone or Combined with Oral Cannabidiol in Dogs Undergoing Tibial Plateau Leveling Osteotomy: An Exploratory Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.authors: Ardaum P, Kashemsant N, Wibulchan W, Pooliam J, Vijarnsorn M
papers.abstract: Autologous conditioned serum (ACS) contains anti-inflammatory mediators, whereas cannabidiol (CBD) may have analgesic and immunomodulatory effects. This exploratory randomized trial evaluated intra-articular ACS, alone or combined with oral CBD, after tibial plateau leveling osteotomy in dogs. Twenty-seven dogs were randomized to placebo, ACS, or ACS + CBD ( n = 9/group). Outcomes included C-reactive protein (CRP), peak vertical force, orthopedic assessment scores (lameness, joint mobility, pain on palpation, weight-bearing, and overall clinical condition), Canine Brief Pain Inventory, radiographic outcomes, and safety. CRP peaked on Day 1. In the linear mixed model using a heterogeneous first-order autoregressive covariance structure, treatment-group ( p = 0.001) and visit ( p < 0.001) effects were significant, whereas the treatment-group × visit interaction did not reach significance ( p = 0.053). Exploratory comparisons showed lower CRP in ACS + CBD than placebo on Days 3 (adjusted p = 0.007) and 5 (adjusted p = 0.001), with model-dependent sensitivity findings. No consistent treatment-group differences were identified in clinical or structural outcomes. One ACS-treated dog developed a surgical site infection, and alkaline phosphatase activity was higher in ACS + CBD on Day 28. The CRP findings remain hypothesis-generating, with uncertain clinical relevance.

papers.title: Sinonasal aspergillosis-associated pneumocephalus in a dog: recovery after endoscopic interventional debridement and antifungal treatment.
papers.authors: Costes MTA, Saunders JH, Rickerts V, Daminet S, Rösch S
papers.abstract: A 16-year-old Border Collie was referred for acute severe apathy and chronic nasal discharge. Computed tomography (CT) performed 2 weeks earlier was suggestive of sinonasal aspergillosis (SNA) with severe turbinate destruction and mucosal thickening in the left nasal cavity and frontal sinus. No treatment was initiated. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at presentation identified intrameningeal pneumocephalus, meningitis, frontal sinusitis with ventral focal frontal bone lysis of the cranial cavity. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable, suggesting pneumocephalus as the cause of apathy. Rhinoscopy confirmed fungal plaque (qPCR: Aspergillus spp.). Systemic antifungal treatment and endoscopic debridement were initiated. Despite frontal bone lysis, topical antifungal treatment also was administered. A 3-week follow-up MRI showed complete resolution of pneumocephalus. Final imaging identified scarring around the defect and no active infection. These findings indicate that intrameningeal pneumocephalus secondary to SNA can be reversible and should not preclude antifungal treatment. Endoscopic therapeutic intervention may enable full recovery.

papers.title: Prophylactic strategies to reduce cyclophosphamide-induced sterile hemorrhagic cystitis in dogs: a first-opinion practice retrospective study and a referral survey.
papers.authors: Ivanovs A, MacKenzie C, Wardle Z, Pinchbeck G, Grieve H, Noble PJ, Killick DR
papers.abstract: Cyclophosphamide occasionally causes sterile hemorrhagic cystitis (SHC) in dogs. Prophylactic coadministration of furosemide reduces SHC risk, yet the extent of the implementation in practice is unknown. To explore the frequency of cyclophosphamide and furosemide coadministration in first opinion practice (FOP) and referral settings. Small Animal Surveillance Network (SAVSNET) searches identified 106 dogs receiving cyclophosphamide, of which 72 met the inclusion criteria. This study was composed of: (1) electronic health record (EHR) review using the SAVSNET database, in which data regarding dosage, co-prescribed medications, preventative measures, and suspected SHC occurrence were collated (2014-2024); and (2) a survey of referral oncology practitioners and educators (2023-2024) exploring contemporary approaches to SHC prevention. Treatment approaches were evenly divided between maximum-tolerated dose cyclophosphamide (MTDC, 53%) and metronomic cyclophosphamide (MC, 47%). Furosemide was prescribed in 32% of cases, most commonly with MTDC protocols (53%). The overall frequency of suspected SHC was 15% (11/72); notably, no suspected SHC cases occurred in dogs receiving furosemide (P = .013). Survey results showed frequent use of prophylactic diuretics: 88% recommended furosemide for MTDC and 55% for MC protocols. Diuretic co-prescription with cyclophosphamide was inconsistent in FOP, which was unexpected given the prior evidence regarding reduction of risk of SHC. Greater standardization of guidance and improved dissemination of best-practice recommendations are necessary to optimize dog safety. Cyclophosphamide is a chemotherapy drug used to treat dogs with cancer. It can occasionally cause inflammation and bleeding in the bladder. Furosemide, a drug that increases urine production, can be given alongside cyclophosphamide to reduce this risk. This study investigated how often furosemide and other preventative measures were used in dogs receiving cyclophosphamide in general veterinary practice. Veterinary specialists and educators were also surveyed about their prevention practices, recommendations to general veterinary practitioners, and veterinary student teaching. Furosemide was used inconsistently in general veterinary practice, whereas specialists more commonly recommended its use. No suspected cases of bladder inflammation and bleeding occurred in dogs receiving furosemide, although the study had limitations that should be considered when interpreting this finding. More consistent guidance on preventative measures might improve the safety of dogs receiving cyclophosphamide.

papers.title: An observational retrospective study of online owner perceptions of diet-related health signs in dogs using social media listening.
papers.authors: Kaur JP, Hollands T, Clarke C, Tarrant G, Rai T, Street T, Wells K, Armstrong SK
papers.abstract: Dog owners increasingly link health to diet type, and the pet food market has diversified beyond kibble/canned diets (KC) to raw and fresh diets (FD; human-grade, gently/mildly cooked, and home-cooked). However, it remains unclear which owner-reported health-related signs (ORHS) are associated with dietary changes, including KC-FD transitions. Social media listening (SML) enables large-scale capture of naturally-occurring online owner discussions. Investigate owner perceptions of diet-related ORHS in dogs within online discourse using SML. None. Observational, retrospective study of 21 896 KC and 2336 FD online posts (>96% from Reddit) collected using Pulsar Platform™ (January 1, 2025 to July 3, 2025). After preprocessing and large language model (LLM)-based zero-shot filtering, 8040 KC and 924 FD posts were analyzed using LLM-assisted topic modeling and dictionary-based ORHS quantification. Topic modeling identified recurrent themes across KC (number of topics [k] = 7, coherence score [Cv] = 0.58) and FD (k = 6, Cv = 0.44) posts. Owners discussed diet as both the perceived cause and management strategy for gastrointestinal (GI), dermatologic, allergy/intolerance, appetite, and body condition ORHS, alongside decision uncertainties. Gastrointestinal (2286/8040, 28.4%; 282/924, 30.5%) and allergy/intolerance (1932/8040, 24.0%; 194/924, 21.0%) ORHS predominated within KC and FD posts, respectively; allergy/intolerance co-occurred with skin/coat (478/918, 52.1%; 57/114, 50.0%), and GI with allergy/intolerance (476/1,932, 24.6%; 68/194, 35.1%). Our study demonstrates the feasibility of SML-LLM-assisted analysis for capturing diet-related ORHS in online dog owner discourse. The study captured owner perceptions rather than clinically verified outcomes, highlighting the need for future studies to align ORHS with clinically validated endpoints to support veterinary nutrition discussions and informed owner decision-making.

papers.title: Efficacy and tolerability of a sequential COP and doxorubicin chemotherapy protocol for treatment of high-grade lymphoma in cats.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Neiderfer K, Iwaki Y, Donnelly LL, Bryant JE, Bryan JN, Henry CJ
papers.abstract: The aim of this study was to evaluate tolerability of a COP/DOX protocol, where cats received COP (vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and prednisolone) induction weekly for 6 weeks followed by doxorubicin (DOX) consolidation every 3 weeks for six doses. A secondary objective was to evaluate the efficacy of the COP/DOX protocol in this cohort of cats. Records were retrospectively reviewed for cats with high-grade lymphoma treated with the COP/DOX protocol between 2005 and 2024. Data collected included signalment, method of diagnosis, tumor location, staging, baseline diagnostics, drug dosages, adverse events, restaging diagnostics, and treatment response. Progression-free survival and survival time were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared across selected variables using log-rank test. In total, 27 cats met the inclusion criteria. Gastrointestinal lymphoma was the most common form, occurring in 33.3% of cats. The number of cats achieving a maximal response of clinical remission and partial remission throughout COP was 10 (37.0%) and 12 (44.4%), respectively. Of the five cats who had stable disease or progressive disease during COP, one achieved partial remission on DOX. Four cats (14.8%) did not respond to either the COP or DOX part of the protocol. The overall response rate at 6 weeks after initiation of COP/DOX was 77.7%. Median progression-free survival was 98 days (interquartile range 41-141) and median survival time was 154 days (interquartile range 102-546). The cats who had clinical remission at the completion of DOX had progression-free survival of 554.5 days and median survival time of 546 days. High-grade adverse events included grade 3 and 4 neutropenia (n = 3 for each) during COP. Lymphocyte:monocyte ratio and response at the completion of DOX were significantly associated with progression-free survival and median survival time. We conclude that the COP/DOX protocol was well tolerated by this population. Progression-free survival and median survival time were similar to previous reports. The COP/DOX protocol is an effective treatment approach for cats with lymphoma. Effectiveness and side effects of a sequential COP and doxorubicin chemotherapy plan for cats with aggressive lymphoma This study looked at how well cats with aggressive lymphoma tolerated and responded to a chemotherapy protocol that combined two types of treatment: COP and doxorubicin. The COP part used three drugs (vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and prednisolone) given weekly for 6 weeks. After that, cats received doxorubicin every 3 weeks for up to six treatments. Records from 27 cats treated between 2005 and 2024 were reviewed. Most commonly, lymphoma started in the intestines. After the first part of the treatment (COP), 37% of cats went into full remission, meaning no signs of cancer could be found, and 44% had their cancer shrink. Among cats who improved but did not reach full remission after COP, three later reached full remission after adding doxorubicin. Only four cats did not respond to either treatment. Overall, about 85% of the cats had some level of improvement. On average, disease progression occurred at approximately 3 months (98 days), and cats survived for about 5 months (154 days) after the initiation of treatment. Cats whose cancer went fully into remission after the full treatment lived much longer, around 1.5 years. The treatment was generally well tolerated. Some cats had temporary drops in white blood cell counts, but serious side effects were uncommon. In summary, this combined COP and doxorubicin treatment was safe and effective for many cats with aggressive lymphoma, offering similar outcomes to other chemotherapy options reported in previous studies.

papers.title: Comparative Effectiveness of COP and CHOP Chemotherapy Protocols in Feline Intermediate- to Large-Cell Lymphoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.authors: Lam YWS, Pimentel PAB, Nekouei O, Giuliano A
papers.abstract: Feline intermediate- to large-cell lymphoma is commonly treated with COP or CHOP chemotherapy, but the clinical benefit of adding doxorubicin (CHOP) remains controversial given its associated toxicity profile and cost. This systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis summarized response and survival outcomes reported for COP- and CHOP-based protocols in feline intermediate- to large-cell lymphoma. Searching PubMed, Scopus, and CAB Abstracts (2000-2024), we included 21 studies comprising 1054 cats. An exploratory random-effects meta-analysis utilizing Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) estimation was conducted to evaluate overall (ORR), complete (CR), and partial response (PR) rates. The overall pooled ORR was 81.0%. Subgroup meta-regression revealed no statistically significant differences between COP and CHOP for ORR (83.0% vs. 77.0%, p = 0.360), CR (57.0% vs. 49.0%, p = 0.350), or PR (28.0% vs. 22.0%, p = 0.468). Profound heterogeneity (overall I 2  = 85.4%-89.6%) persisted across all analyses, driven primarily by the pooling of diverse anatomical subtypes and uncontrolled confounding by Feline Leukaemia Virus (FeLV) status. Furthermore, inadequate variance reporting and a widespread lack of standardized response criteria (e.g., VCOG-RECIST) precluded a formal meta-analysis of survival outcomes. Descriptively, reported median survival times ranged broadly (COP: 108-610 days; CHOP: 62-973 days) without a clear advantage for CHOP. A custom weighted risk-of-bias assessment highlighted significant methodological deficiencies across the literature. In conclusion, current aggregate evidence does not demonstrate a statistically detectable difference in response rates between CHOP- and COP-based protocols. Severe methodological heterogeneity and retrospective selection bias prevent definitive conclusions regarding long-term survival, emphasizing the critical need for homogeneous, prospective randomized trials utilizing standardized reporting guidelines.

papers.title: Differences in DNA Methylation Status Between Epithelial and Mesenchymal Phenotypes in Canine Malignant Mucosal Melanoma.
papers.authors: Ishizaki T, Yamazaki J, Aoshima K, Kimura T
papers.abstract: Canine malignant mucosal melanoma is one of the common cancers with a high mortality rate. Pathologically, malignant melanomas show multiple morphological patterns including epithelioid, spindle and round, indicating that neoplastic cells change their morphology. Regarding morphological change, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) has been considered to be an important mechanism. EMT is a reversible biologic process being suggested the correlation with DNA methylation in human cancer. The aim of this study was to assess the difference in DNA methylation status between epithelial and mesenchymal phenotypes and correlation with EMT in canine oral malignant melanoma. Sixteen samples were classified into epithelial phenotype and eight samples were classified into mesenchymal phenotype based on E-cadherin expression using immunohistochemistry or western blotting. We analysed DNA methylation level of 46 673 cytosine-guanine dinucleotides (CpG sites) in all samples and compared average DNA methylation level between epithelial and mesenchymal phenotypes. In a comparison of average DNA methylation level at each site in CpG island promoters (3089 sites), 17 and 6 hypermethylated sites were identified in epithelial phenotype and mesenchymal phenotype, respectively. Finally, 10 out of 23 sites showed de novo hypermethylation, and two genes, NEUROG1 and ITGAV, which are associated with cell adhesion, were found to be hypermethylated in epithelial phenotype. This study revealed the difference of DNA methylation status between epithelial and mesenchymal phenotypes suggesting the influence of DNA methylation on EMT in canine malignant mucosal melanoma.

papers.title: Prospective evaluation of the prevalence and characteristics of heart murmurs and gallop sounds in anemic cats.
papers.authors: Robertson A, Boswood A, Luis Fuentes V, Lo EJY, Humm K
papers.abstract: Heart murmurs and gallop sounds are common in anemic cats; however, their association with underlying cardiac disease is unclear. Determine the prevalence of murmurs and gallops in anemic cats. Investigate the association of auscultatory abnormalities with anemia severity and heart disease. Investigate whether change in anemia severity affects the audibility of murmurs and gallop sounds. Sixty-four anemic cats (packed cell volume [PCV] below 30%) presenting to a referral hospital. Single-center prospective observational study. On presentation, cats were examined and had PCV measurement. Each cat underwent echocardiography. Cats had PCV checks and daily auscultation to document heart sounds. Fifty-eight percent (37/64) had a murmur and 23% (15/64) had a gallop. Mean PCV at enrollment was 18% (±6). Lower PCV was associated with the presence of a murmur (P = .03) and gallop (P = .016). Cardiac disease was present in 34% (22/64) of cats. After adjusting for anemia severity, murmur presence showed no statistically significant association with cardiac disease (P = .636 (OR: 1.31, 95% CI, 0.43-3.95)). A gallop sound was associated with greater odds of cardiac disease (P = .037 (OR: 3.97, 95% CI, 1.09-14.5)). Murmur intensity (P = .001) and likelihood of a gallop sound (P = .022) were lower in individuals when their PCVs increased. Murmurs and gallop sounds are common in anemic cats with and without cardiac disease. Anemic cats with gallops are more likely to have underlying cardiac disease than anemic cats without gallops.
