Abnormal heart sounds, known as heart murmurs and gallop sounds, can occur frequently in cats with a low red blood cell count (anemia). Murmurs and gallops are also common in cats with heart disease. Whether the abnormal heart sounds are due to anemia or if anemic cats have underlying heart disease causing the murmur or gallop is unknown. This study aimed to determine how many anemic cats had abnormal heart sounds, if murmurs or gallops were associated with heart disease or red blood cell count, and if change in red blood cell count over time affected the presence of abnormal heart sounds. In this study abnormal heart sounds were common in anemic cats. Lower red blood cell count was associated with having a murmur or gallop. Heart disease was frequently present in our cats. Having a heart murmur was not associated with having heart disease, but a gallop sound was associated with having heart disease. When individual cats’ red blood cell count increased, the severity of their heart murmur and likelihood of a gallop sound were lower.

papers.title: Correction to "A Rare Case of Cutaneous Infection by Corynascus verrucosus in a Shih Tzu Dog: Molecular Identification and Phylogenetic Analysis".
Hemodynamic responses to clinical dosages of dopamine and dobutamine in dogs with hypotension under isoflurane anesthesia.
papers.authors: Seki D, Kusu H, Fujimoto T, Kitagawa H, Goya S, Yamaya Y, Teshima K
papers.abstract: While dopamine and dobutamine are widely used in anesthetized dogs, clinical evidence supporting their use remains limited. We aimed to compare the hemodynamic responses to clinical dosages of dopamine and dobutamine in dogs with hypotension undergoing elective orthopedic surgery under fentanyl-isoflurane anesthesia. The pressor effects at clinical dosages (2-8 µg/kg/min) of dopamine (n = 15) and dobutamine (n = 15) for hypotension were compared and confirmed using the ramped-rate infusion protocol in 30 dogs. The following hemodynamic parameters measured by invasive arterial blood pressure and transesophageal echocardiographic monitoring were analyzed: heart rate (HR), systolic (SAP), mean (MAP), diastolic arterial pressure (DAP), stroke volume index (SVI), cardiac index (CI), and systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI). The proportion of dogs that achieved the treatment goal (MAP: 70-89 mmHg) was 93% (dopamine responders, 14/15 dogs) in the dopamine group and 53% (dobutamine responders, 8/15 dogs) in the dobutamine group, with a significantly higher probability in the dopamine group (P = 0.035, a risk difference of 40% [95% confidence interval: 8.2-63.9%]). In dopamine responders, significant increases were observed in SAP, MAP, DAP, SVI and CI, whereas no significant changes were observed in HR and SVRI. In conclusion, the pressor effect was more likely to be observed at the clinical dosage of dopamine than that of dobutamine for treating hypotension in isoflurane anesthetized dogs. This study was approved by the Nihon University Animal Medical Center Research and Trial Ethics Committee (approval number: 1-007; approval date: September 29, 2022).

papers.title: Demographic and environmental factors associated with canine cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma development in Australia: a retrospective matched case-control analysis.
papers.authors: Zhang JJ, Dejene H, Granados-Soler JL, Henning J, Allavena R
papers.abstract: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) is a common canine skin tumour that occurs more frequently in high ultraviolet (UV) environments. Despite Australia's consistently high UV exposure, large-scale epidemiological studies on canine cSCC are limited. This study investigates the frequency of canine cSCC in Australia, its geographic patterns relative to UV index, and its association with animal-level risk factors. A matched case-control study was conducted using records from the VetCompass database from 1st January 2014 to 31st December 2023. In total, 295 histopathologically confirmed cSCC cases and 1,180 matched controls were included. Frequency statistics of cSCC and animal-level risk factors associated with cSCC were analysed and spatial patterns were mapped. The highest proportions of cases were recorded in Queensland (39.7%) and New South Wales (39.3%), with increased frequency along coastal areas of both states. cSCC cases occurred most frequently on body regions caudal to the thorax (54.9%), in senior dogs (58.6%), in desexed males (45.1%), and in dogs with white mixed coat colour (43.7%). In the final multivariable model, senior (seven to 11 years old) and geriatric (12 + years old) dogs had significantly higher odds of cSCC than mature (two to six years old) dogs (odds ratio = 7.4 and 4.8, respectively; p ≤ 0.001). Risk was also markedly elevated in Dalmatians, bulldogs, Staffordshire terriers, and schnauzers compared with mixed breeds. Dogs with white or white mixed coats had higher odds of cSCC than dark-coated dogs (p ≤ 0.001). cSCC demonstrated anatomical and geographic patterns consistent with chronic UV exposure, with age, breed, and coat pigmentation emerging as risk factors.

papers.title: Histomorphometric characterization of cardiac nodes in cattle, ponies, and cats.
papers.authors: Gómez-Torres F, Ballesteros-Acuña L, Ruíz-Saurí A
papers.abstract: The sinoatrial node (SAN) and atrioventricular node (AVN) are essential components of the cardiac conduction system and play a critical role in initiating and propagating the electrical impulse. To characterize these cardiac nodes across different species, we examined the hearts of ten cattle, ten cats, and five male ponies without evidence of cardiac disease using conventional histological and immunohistochemical techniques. Morphometric parameters of the nodes and their constituent cells were quantified at different magnifications. The SAN displayed an oval morphology in all species. Its diameter was 888.58 ± 6.36 μm in cats, 2143.17 ± 199.13 μm in ponies, and 2033.28 ± 939.44 μm in cattle. Mean nodal density was significantly higher in ponies than in cattle (p = 0.011). Pacemaker (P) cells of the AVN were significantly larger in ungulate species than in cats (p < 0.001). Heart bone (os cordis) was identified in all ten cattle hearts and in one cat heart, showing typical features of compact bone and bone marrow. Cartilaginous metaplasia was observed in all pony hearts and in 60% of cat hearts and was associated with reduced AVN size and cellularity in cats. These findings highlight important interspecies differences and contribute to the understanding of conduction system pathology in veterinary cardiology. The structural changes in the cardiac nodes in these species warrant more in-depth functional research, given the lack of functional cardiac assessment and the small sample size.

papers.title: Echocardiographic description of pulmonary vein stenosis in a cat with atrioventricular septal defect.
papers.authors: Seyednejad F, Locquet L, Ardehali P, Astaraki N
papers.abstract: A 2.5-year-old, intact female British Shorthair cat was referred for cardiology evaluation owing to intermittent panting and a heart murmur identified on cardiac auscultation before elective surgery. Physical examination revealed a left parasternal grade II/VI systolic murmur without arrhythmia. Thoracic radiographs showed cardiomegaly without pulmonary infiltration. The echocardiography was prompted by auscultation, history and radiological findings. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated marked right atrial enlargement and eccentric hypertrophy of the right ventricle. Echocardiography revealed a partial atrioventricular septal defect characterised by a large ostium primum defect (0.79 cm) and an anterior mitral valve cleft, resulting in a left-to-right shunt (estimated Qp:Qs ≈ 2.2). Doppler interrogation of the left pulmonary vein entering the lateral wall of the left atrium demonstrated focal turbulence and increased peak velocity (1.08 m/s), corresponding to a pressure gradient of approximately 4.7 mmHg, findings consistent with suspected unilateral pulmonary vein stenosis. Tricuspid regurgitation velocity (2.2 m/s) did not reflect increased afterload. Elective surgery was postponed owing to uncertainty regarding peri-anaesthetic haemodynamic risk. Medical treatment with enalapril and clopidogrel was initiated. At the 9-month follow-up, the cat remained clinically stable and echocardiographic findings were unchanged. Pulmonary vein stenosis is rarely reported in cats. This report describes the concurrent presence of partial atrioventricular septal defect and suspected unilateral pulmonary vein stenosis. These findings highlight the detection of a congenital heart defect in a young cat, despite the low-grade murmur. A rare congenital heart condition in a British Shorthair cat A 2.5-year-old, female British Shorthair cat was referred for a heart check after intermittent panting and a heart murmur were noticed before planned elective surgery. Examination confirmed a mild heart murmur and chest radiography showed an enlarged heart. Heart ultrasound revealed a congenital heart defect called a partial atrioventricular septal defect. This means there was an abnormal opening between the upper chambers of the heart, together with an abnormality of the mitral valve. These changes caused increased blood flow from the left side of the heart to the right side, leading to enlargement of the right side of the heart. The ultrasound also showed abnormal blood flow in one of the pulmonary veins, raising suspicion of narrowing of that vein. Because of the heart findings and possible anaesthetic risk, the planned surgery was postponed. The cat was started on medical treatment and remained stable after 9 months, with no worsening of the heart ultrasound findings. This case is important because pulmonary vein stenosis is rarely reported in cats, especially alongside this type of congenital heart disease. It also shows that even a mild heart murmur in a young cat can be associated with significant underlying heart abnormalities.

papers.title: Development and Validation of a New Online Tool for Monitoring Clinical Signs of Canine Atopic Dermatitis.
papers.authors: Harvey N, Watson A, Laxalde J, England G, Gow D
papers.abstract: The aim of the study was to develop a simple, reliable and validated patient-reported outcome tool for use in monitoring the severity of clinical signs in dogs with confirmed or suspected atopic allergies and recurrent otitis externa. The tool is called the Dog-Orientated Severity of Atopy Scale (DOSAS). The human Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure (POEM) was adapted for relevance to the owner-observable clinical signs of canine atopic dermatitis (cAD). Refinements were made via consultation with dog owners and veterinary surgeons to ensure applicability and ease of use. Relevant features of reliability (including internal consistency, intrarater reliability and test-retest reliability) were evaluated. The tool was then tested by owners and clinicians for performance against established clinical sign assessment methods. The DOSAS was shown to be both reliable and valid with psychometric properties above acceptable guidelines for the development of such tools. Guidelines are presented for score creation and stratification of the score to enable interpretation. When compared to how severity assessment scores from Canine Atopic Dermatitis Extent and Severity Index, 4th iteration (CADESI-04) and pruritus Visual Assessment Scale (PVAS) responded to change, the DOSAS performed particularly strongly, although it performed less well when compared to the 0-3 Otitis Index Score (OTIS-3). The DOSAS is presented as a supplementary tool for use in veterinary practice and clinical research programmes alongside existing clinical measurements such as CADESI-04, providing a focus on the disease as it is experienced by the dog and their owner. Unlike clinical measurement, the DOSAS is accessible and interpretable for dog owners, which is important for the management of chronic pruritic conditions, and will enable dog owners to be more actively involved with their dog's disease management.

papers.title: The use of cold-stored platelets to provide hemostasis in dogs with thrombocytopenia.
papers.authors: Monaco SA, Haines JM, Guess SC, Fiedler SM, Wardrop KJ
papers.abstract: Platelet transfusion can be lifesaving in dogs with severe thrombocytopenia and hemorrhage, but platelet products are limited by short shelf life and contamination risk. Cold-stored platelets (CSP) may provide a practical alternative, but in vivo hemostatic efficacy in dogs is unknown. Evaluate the clinical hemostatic efficacy and safety of CSP transfusions in thrombocytopenic dogs. Twenty-four thrombocytopenic dogs from a veterinary teaching hospital population that received CSP transfusions between March 2022 and October 2024. Retrospective cohort study. Medical records of dogs receiving platelet concentrate stored at 4 °C for up to 21 days were reviewed. Hemorrhage severity was assessed using a modified Daily Canine Bleeding Assessment Tool (DOGiBAT) score before transfusion and at 1 and 4 h post-transfusion. Primary outcomes included change in bleeding score, clinical response, transfusion reactions, and survival to discharge. Twenty-four dogs received 27 CSP transfusions. Mean pre-transfusion platelet count was 23 × 103/μL (range, 2-107 × 103/μL) and mean post-transfusion count was 28 × 103/μL (range, 2-100 × 103/μL; P = .84). Mean DOGiBAT score decreased from 3.15 ± 2.4 at baseline to 2.21 ± 2.1 at 4 (mean change, -0.94; P = .002). Clinical improvement occurred in 19 of 27 transfusions (70%). No transfusion reactions were documented. Nineteen of 24 dogs (79%) survived to discharge. Cold-stored platelets were well-tolerated and associated with decreased bleeding severity in thrombocytopenic dogs, supporting CSP as a practical platelet transfusion option for clinical hemostatic support.

papers.title: Serological response to field rabies vaccination in owned dogs in the immune belt of Peninsular Malaysia.
papers.authors: Noorazmi MSN, Ahmad Yunus AF, Che Rose FZ, Ballakrishnan N, Mohd Ziadi MZ, Ismail MAR, Razali MA, Rajeendran A, Abd Aziz MR, Wan Omar Bakri WN, Zainun Z, Merawin LT, Mohd Saeid FH
papers.abstract: Rabies vaccination is conducted along the northern border of Peninsular Malaysia, but paired field serological data are limited. We analysed routine programme data from 154 owned dogs sampled immediately before vaccination and 30-83 days later (median, 43 days). Rabies virus-neutralising antibody levels were measured using the fluorescent antibody virus neutralisation test. Paired levels in IU/mL were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and benchmark proportions were compared using the exact McNemar test. The proportion with levels ≥ 0.5 IU/mL increased from 72.7% (112/154; 95% confidence interval [CI], 65.2-79.1%) to 98.1% (151/154; 95% CI, 94.4-99.3%; p < 0.001). Three dogs remained below the benchmark. Median levels increased from 1.98 IU/mL (interquartile range [IQR], 0.38-5.92) to 13.5 IU/mL (IQR, 4.5-13.5); the median paired increase was 5.45 IU/mL (bootstrap 95% CI, 3.31-7.25; p < 0.001). Levels increased in 128 dogs, were unchanged in 19 and decreased in seven. Eighty follow-up values equalled the dataset maximum of 13.5 IU/mL, suggesting possible upper-end censoring. Vaccination history identified 99 previously vaccinated dogs and seven recorded as receiving their first vaccination, limiting comparison of these groups. Nearly all dogs retained at follow-up met the serological benchmark. Convenience sampling, incomplete follow-up and uncertain measurement limits restrict inference to this cohort and preclude estimates of population immunity or clinical effectiveness.

papers.title: Attitudes and practices of veterinarians regarding feline pain management in Western vs Eastern Europe.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Bukhari SSUH, Marangoni S, Almendros A, Luna SPL, Steagall PV
papers.abstract: This study aimed to report and compare attitudes and practices of veterinarians regarding feline pain management in Eastern and Western Europe. A questionnaire was developed and divided into demographic data, drug availability/administration, and pain management practices. The questionnaire went through content and face validity and was translated into several languages. An internet-based survey was created, and responses were collected using a convenience sampling method. Data were analyzed using multiple correspondence analysis. In total, 833 participants from Europe were included. Most respondents indicated good knowledge of acute pain assessment and recognition (n = 478, 57.4%). The Feline Grimace Scale was the most commonly used instrument to assess acute pain (n = 346, 41.5%). Chronic pain scoring instruments were not used by 48.5% (n = 404) of participants. Meloxicam and robenacoxib were the most used non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for chronic pain management. Limited knowledge of pain assessment, non-use of NSAIDs in cats undergoing surgery, and postoperative use of opioids were more closely associated with Eastern than Western Europe. Reported good knowledge of pain management, pre- and intraoperative use of NSAIDs, use of pain scales and preoperative opioids, having a specialty diploma, and working in a cat-friendly practice were associated with Western Europe compared with Eastern Europe. Important regional differences were found regarding feline pain management across Europe. Continuing education, wider implementation of validated pain assessment tools, and improved access to analgesics may help reduce regional disparities and improve feline welfare.

papers.title: Retrospective Application of the Current International Myeloma Working Group Disease Definitions in 20 Cats With Immunoglobulin Secreting Neoplasms.
papers.authors: Jeffries CM, Harris RA, Vickery K, Avery PR, Rao S, Moore AR
papers.abstract: Studies describing feline myeloma related diseases (MRD) are limited and reported prognostic indicators are inconsistent. Cats more commonly exhibit visceral plasma cell tumours (PCTs) than marrow-predominant disease, suggesting that diagnostic approaches adapted from the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) criteria, incorporating extramedullary involvement and myeloma defining events (MDEs), may better capture clinically relevant disease. We sought to evaluate cats with serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) and immunofixation (IF) confirmed M-proteins using IMWG-adapted criteria, determine how often cases satisfy IMWG-adapted versus classic multiple myeloma (MM) definitions, compare outcomes, characterize clinical and laboratory findings and assess prognostic indicators. A retrospective cohort of 20 cats with SPE/IF-confirmed M-proteins and clinical data was included in the study applying IMWG-adapted and classic MM criteria using available clinical records, laboratory data and cytologic or histologic findings. Survival was evaluated using the log-rank test. 14/20 cats met IMWG-adapted MM criteria, whereas 7 cats met classic criteria. Median survival time did not differ between classic MM (226.5 days) and IMWG-reclassified MM (141 days; p = 0.99). Visceral organ involvement was common; splenic PCTs occurred in 71.4% (10/14) and hepatic PCTs in 87.5% (7/8) of sampled organs. Lytic bone lesions were infrequent (3/14). IgG M-proteins predominated (71.4%). No clinicopathologic variable was significantly associated with survival. IMWG-adapted criteria reclassified MM without altering survival, supporting their diagnostic utility in feline MRD. The predominance of visceral PCTs and infrequent bone involvement highlights species-specific disease patterns and the diagnostic value of extramedullary sampling. Larger prospective studies should refine feline-specific biomarkers and validate MDEs.

papers.title: Proactive Treatment of Canine Allergic Otitis Externa With Hydrocortisone Aceponate: A Retrospective Observational Study.
papers.authors: Maina E, Rigert JC, Filippini C, Cao R, Oliveira A
papers.abstract: Allergic otitis externa is common in dogs and recurrence may lead to repeated consultations and antimicrobial use. Long-term data on proactive topical corticosteroid maintenance are limited. To describe 12-month relapse frequency in dogs with allergic otitis externa receiving proactive hydrocortisone aceponate maintenance therapy and compare consecutive-day and non-consecutive-day schedules. Medical records of client-owned dogs prescribed hydrocortisone aceponate ear spray were retrospectively reviewed. Maintenance started after clinical and cytological remission. Only dogs with confirmed continuation, stable concomitant allergy management and complete 12-month outcome data were included. Relapse was defined as recurrent otitis externa requiring veterinary examination, cytology and additional otic treatment. Dogs were grouped by schedule: Protocol 1, two consecutive days; and Protocol 2, two non-consecutive days weekly. Outcomes were compared using Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests. Seventy-one dogs were included; 36 in Protocol 1 and 35 received Protocol 2. During 12 months, 50/71 dogs (70.4%) had no relapse, 12/71 (16.9%) had one relapse and 9/71 (12.7%) had multiple relapses. At least one relapse occurred in 9/36 dogs (25.0%) in Protocol 1 and 12/35 (34.3%) receiving Protocol 2 (p = 0.443). Multiple relapses occurred in 2/36 (5.6%) and 7/35 (20.0%) dogs, respectively (p = 0.085). Relapse counts did not differ significantly between protocols (p = 0.290). Most dogs had no relapse or only one relapse during proactive hydrocortisone aceponate maintenance. No statistically significant difference was detected between schedules, but equivalence or non-inferiority cannot be concluded.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Experimental Evaluation of the Immunogenicity of Feline Erythrocyte Antigen 6 (FEA 6) in Transfusion-Naive FEA 6-Negative Cats.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Bangash MY, Blais MC
papers.abstract: ObjectivesFeline Erythrocyte Antigen 6 (FEA 6) is a newly identified red blood cell (RBC) antigen in cats discovered following an unintentional sensitization event, suggesting it can be immunogenic. Its ability to consistently induce alloimmunization remains unknown. This prospective study evaluated FEA 6 immunogenicity in transfusion-naive, FEA 6-negative cats by assessing anti-FEA 6 alloantibody production and plasma levels. A secondary objective was to bank polyclonal anti-FEA 6 antibodies.MethodsFifty-three cats underwent AB and extensive blood typing for FEAs 1-6, naturally occurring alloantibody (NOAb) screening, and compatibility testing to select donor-recipient pairs. FEA 6 prevalence was assessed in 82 type A cats. Two transfusion-naive, FEA 6-negative cats received FEA 6-positive, otherwise compatible RBC transfusions and were monitored for anti-FEA 6 alloantibody production by gel column agglutination. Repeat transfusions were performed if alloantibodies became undetectable. Agreement between recipient-derived and reference anti-FEA 6 alloantibodies was evaluated in 51 type A cats using kappa statistics.ResultsFEA 6 prevalence among type A cats was 75.6% (62/82); NOAb were detected in 10.3% of screened type A cats, but none were directed against FEA 6. Both recipients developed anti-FEA 6 alloantibodies. Recipient 1 responded after two sensitizations, whereas recipient 2 responded after a single transfusion. Both reached peak titers of 1:8, with alloantibodies detectable through days 372 and 200, respectively. Recipient-derived anti-FEA 6 alloantibodies showed substantial agreement with the reference anti-FEA 6 antibody (κ = 0.64-0.78, P < .001) and almost perfect agreement with each other (κ = 0.87, P < .001).Conclusions and relevanceTransfusion of FEA 6-positive RBCs induced anti-FEA 6 alloantibodies in all transfusion-naive, FEA 6-negative recipients, supporting FEA 6 immunogenicity and its likely contribution to unexplained post-transfusion alloantibodies in cats. The resulting polyclonal antibodies may support FEA 6 typing and transfusion research, although more durable reagents remain needed.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Mineral Analysis of Feline Treats: Unrecognized Sources of Phosphorus and Calcium in the Management of Chronic Kidney Disease.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Harris AN, Harris T, Vaden S
papers.abstract: Dietary phosphorus restriction is a cornerstone of chronic kidney disease (CKD) management in cats. While therapeutic renal diets are formulated to limit phosphorus intake, treats also contribute to total dietary phosphorus and calcium intake. The objective of this study was to quantify the phosphorus and calcium content of some feline purée-style treats and evaluate their potential contribution to dietary mineral intake in cats with CKD. A convenience sample comprising four flavors of commercially available Inaba Churu purée treats and three flavors of Weurva low-phosphorus purée treats were analyzed. Phosphorus and calcium concentrations were quantified using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry and reported descriptively as milligrams per sachet and milligrams per 100 kcal. Phosphorus content varied widely across products, ranging from 9 to 36 mg per sachet (64-600mg/100kcal). The evaluated Churu treats contained higher phosphorus concentrations (29-36 mg/ sachet) than the evaluated Weruva low-phosphorus formulations (9-10 mg/sachet). Calcium concentrations ranged from 0.14 to 4.06 mg per sachet (2.3-67.7 mg/100 kcal), with corresponding calcium-to-phosphorus (Ca:P) ratios ranging from 0.004 to 0.119. Phosphorus and calcium content, including Ca:P ratios, varied substantially among the products evaluated. These differences should be considered as part of the overall dietary management of cats with CKD, particularly when treats are administered routinely.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Assessment of an educational social media campaign on improving feline osteoarthritis pain awareness and knowledge among cat owners.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Wong WS, Alcântara H, Bukhari SSUH, Murrell J, Steagall P
papers.abstract: Objectives - Feline osteoarthritis (OA) is highly prevalent but often underdiagnosed, largely owing to owners' difficulty recognising subtle clinical signs. This study evaluated the effects of an evidence-based, peer-reviewed educational social media campaign on cat owners' knowledge and awareness of feline OA.Methods - A prospective, interventional study was conducted with a convenience sample of adult, non-veterinary cat owners recruited via social media. Participants completed a validated online survey assessing knowledge and attitudes about feline OA before and after viewing an evidence based social media campaign (i.e., the intervention) covering 4 domains (introduction, clinical signs, diagnosis, management). Paired non parametric tests compared pre- and post-intervention total knowledge scores, individual knowledge items and Likert scale attitude items.Results - A total of 53 participants completed both surveys. Mean total knowledge scores increased from 19.9 ± 3.1 to 23.6 ± 2.8 (p < 0.001). Correct identification of OA as non-curable increased from 49.1% to 83% (p < 0.001), and the misconception that OA only affects senior cats decreased from 13.2% to 0% (p = 0.02). Recognition of key risk factors improved: neutering after 6 months of age (9.4% to 60.4%, p < 0.001) and outdoor access (28.3% to 73.6%, p < 0.001). Recognition of scratching posts as an option for environment changes increased from 24.5% to 60.3% (p <0.001). The owners' confidence in their ability to contribute to diagnosis increased (Hodges-Lehmann shift +0.99, p = 0.04), knowledge of environmental modifications increased (+1.49, p <0.001), and stress about lifelong management decreased (-0.99, p = 0.01). Most participants (≥91%) found the intervention materials enjoyable and useful; 96% would share the content with others.Conclusion and relevance - An evidence-based educational social media campaign significantly improved cat owners' awareness and knowledge regarding feline OA, suggesting a scalable platform to complement traditional veterinarian-client communication.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Allogeneic Mesenchymal Stromal Cells Versus Lokivetmab in Mild-To-Moderate Canine Atopic Dermatitis: A Single-Blind Randomised Study.
papers.authors: Pasikowska M, Ciszewska-Ceran J, Cekiera A, Gocek E, Grzesiak J, Reniewicz P, Popiel J, Szczepanik M, Wilkołek P
papers.abstract: Canine atopic dermatitis (cAD) is a chronic allergic inflammatory skin disease that requires multimodal management. Allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) have emerged as a potential therapeutic option. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of an investigational allogeneic adipose-derived MSC product (PK/CM-1) in dogs with cAD. Dogs with mild-to-moderate cAD were enrolled in a single-blind, randomised study and allocated in a 2:1 ratio either to an experimental group (receiving a single intravenous dose of PK/CM-1) or a control group (receiving three monthly subcutaneous doses of lokivetmab). Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Canine Atopic Dermatitis Extent and Severity Index, 4th iteration (CADESI-04) and pruritus Visual Analog Scale (PVAS) scores on Day (D)28 (primary end-point) and D7, D56 and D84. Safety assessments included haematological and biochemical analyses on D84, along with monitoring for adverse events. Thirty-two dogs were included. By D28, both CADESI-04 and PVAS scores had significantly decreased from baseline in both groups. No significant differences between groups were observed on D28 (p = 0.696 and p = 0.088, respectively). Clinical improvement was sustained up to D84. In the experimental group, CADESI-04 and PVAS scores were lower on D84 than on D28 (p = 0.0074 and p = 0.0015, respectively). Two adverse events (one severe and one mild) occurred during PK/CM-1 administration. No clinically significant haematological or biochemical abnormalities were observed. PK/CM-1 demonstrated comparable efficacy and safety to those of lokivetmab over a 3 month period. Careful monitoring is recommended during intravenous administration of PK/CM-1.

papers.title: Use of plasma chromogranin a epitopes vasostatin and catestatin as biomarkers for catecholamine-producing tumours in dogs.
papers.authors: Prabert J, Hanson J, Ishigaki K, Asano K, Höglund K, Stridsberg M, Höglund OV
papers.abstract: Differentiation of catecholamine-producing tumours from other adrenal tumours remains difficult. Chromogranin A (CgA) is a marker for catecholamine secretion in the body. An assay for quantification of the CgA epitopes vasostatin and catestatin has been validated for use in dogs but not yet evaluated in dogs with catecholamine-producing tumours. The aims were to evaluate the assays foranalysis of plasma concentrations of the CgA epitopes vasostatin and catestatin in dogs with adrenal tumours and to compare concentrations between catecholamine-producing tumours and adrenocortical tumours in dogs that were subjected to adrenalectomy. Twelve dogs with histopathologically confirmed catecholamine-secreting tumours (eleven pheochromocytomas (PCCs), one extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglioma (PGL)) and twelve with adrenocortical tumours were included in the study. Plasma concentrations of the CgA epitopes vasostatin and catestatin were determined byradioimmunoassay (RIA), before adrenalectomy in 23 out of 24 dogs and after adrenalectomy in six of the dogs with catecholamine-secreting tumours (five PCC, one PGL). Tumour diagnosis was made by histopathology in all cases. Overall, median plasma concentration of the CgA epitopevasostatin in dogs with catecholamine-secreting tumours was 0.82 nmol/L (interquartile range (IQR) 0.52 to 1.60 nmol/L), which was significantly higher(Wilcoxon rank sum exact test, P= 0.0374) than the vasostatin concentration in adrenocortical tumours (median 0.50; IQR 0.34 to 0.59 nmol/L). A subsetof dogs (5/12) with catecholamine-secreting tumours had elevated plasma vasostatin concentrations preoperatively. After successful surgery, thepreoperatively elevated plasma vasostatin concentrations decreased numerically, however without reaching statistical significance. Catestatin concentrationdid not differ between tumour types. Elevated plasma concentration of the CgA epitope vasostatin showed potential as a biomarker for asubset of catecholamine-secreting tumours.

papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Nelson CT, Moorhead A, Ames MK

papers.title: Spontaneous tumors in dogs and cats in Algeria: a dual-source descriptive study of practitioner-reported patterns and histopathology-submitted cases.
papers.authors: Bouchoukh AS, Boukhechem S, Bougherara H, Chaabi AZ
papers.abstract: Algeria has no documented national companion-animal cancer registry, and limited information is available on tumors encountered in veterinary practice or reaching histopathological confirmation. This dual-source descriptive study combined two independently analyzed components: a histopathology-based descriptive case series of diagnostic tumor submissions from dogs and cats, and a cross-sectional questionnaire survey of veterinarians practicing in Algeria. The first component characterized tumors reaching histopathological confirmation, whereas the second examined practitioner-reported tumor patterns, perceived diagnostic-resource availability, and self-reported preparedness. The histopathology-based case series comprised 86 tumor submissions from 81 animals accrued between March 2022 and March 2025. Mammary tumors were the largest category (43/86; 50.0%), followed by cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors (20/86; 23.3%); 80 tumors (93.0%) were classified as malignant. Among 162 questionnaire responses collected between October 2024 and May 2025, 111 respondents selected "dogs and cats" as their main animal group. Mammary tumors were reported by 109 respondents (98.2%), cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors by 79 (71.2%), and canine transmissible venereal tumor (CTVT) by 54 (48.6%); multiple categories could be reported. The most frequent self-reported preparedness rating was "Moderately prepared" (52/111; 46.8%), while 99 of 110 respondents with valid data (90.0%) rated diagnostic resources as either "Insufficient" or "Not at all satisfactory." Mammary and cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors ranked first and second in both sources, whereas the rankings of the remaining categories differed. Because the sources represented different populations, analytical units, denominators, and diagnostic pathways, the comparison was restricted to an exploratory descriptive assessment and was not interpreted as evidence of differences in population-level tumor occurrence. This study provides an initial structured account of companion-animal tumor documentation in Algeria. The partial agreement between the two sources, together with unfavorable diagnostic-availability ratings, suggests potential gaps between clinical recognition, histopathological confirmation, and systematic recording. Standardized submission and coding procedures, improved specimen-transport and formal pathology-referral pathways, broader geographic participation, and progressive development of companion-animal cancer registration are needed to strengthen the national evidence base.

papers.title: Molecular evidence of Bartonella spp. in wild felids from Brazil.
papers.authors: Dias CM, Lee DAB, da Silva JVDSA, Nunes LB, May Júnior JA, Baggio-Souza V, Peters FB, Favarini MO, Albano APN, Segui SD, Terra SR, Tirelli FP, Cherem J, Morzele HB, Tortato MA, Lagos AR, Manzano FV, de Oliveira Tourinho TC, Machado RZ, Soares JF, André MR
papers.abstract: Among Felidae, domestic cats play a role as reservoirs for Bartonella henselae, Bartonella clarridgeiae, and Bartonella koehlerae. Despite the well-known relationship between Bartonella spp. and domestic cats, to date, there is still a paucity of reports on Bartonella spp. in wild felids. The aim of this study was to molecularly detect and characterize Bartonella spp. in blood and tissue samples from wild felids sampled in Brazil. Among 291 DNA samples (211 blood, 77 spleens and three livers), 3.09% (9/291) were positive in the Quantitative Real-Time PCR (qPCR) assay for Bartonella spp. based on the nuoG gene: 1/44 Leopardus pardalis, 3/61 Leopardus geoffroyi, 1/66 Panthera onca, 1/3 Herpailurus yagouaroundi, and 3/32 Leopardus wiedii. In the phylogenetic analyses, while the gltA sequence detected in L. wiedii grouped with Bartonella henselae, the gltA and ftsZ sequences detected in L. geoffroyi clustered within the same subclade as Bartonella sp. sequences previously identified in wild rodents and associated fleas. These findings reinforce that besides harboring Bartonella species associated with cats, wild felids also may act as accidental hosts for Bartonella species associated with wild small mammals, possibly as a consequence of predation.

papers.title: Doxorubicin-induced Cardiotoxicity in Dogs: A Narrative Review.
papers.authors: Sunpongsri S, Roos T, Gerhing R, Zandvliet M, Santarelli G
papers.abstract: Doxorubicin, an anthracycline widely used in both human and veterinary oncology, is highly effective against a variety of malignancies in dogs, including lymphomas, sarcomas and carcinomas. Despite its efficacy, doxorubicin exposure can be associated with cardiotoxicity, which may present acutely or chronically, potentially leading to severe cardiac arrhythmia and congestive heart failure. Mechanisms underlying cardiotoxicity are multifactorial, including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage via topoisomerase IIβ, inflammation and dysregulated cell death pathways such as apoptosis, pyroptosis and ferroptosis. In dogs, known risk factors include higher cumulative dose, breed predisposition to idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, and higher body weight. Cardiac biomarkers, electrocardiography, echocardiography and other advanced imaging techniques have been employed to detect cardiac changes that can be seen also in the absence of clinical signs. However, current evidence is predominantly derived from experimental and retrospective research, highlighting the need for large prospective clinical studies to strengthen recommendations for monitoring and prevention. A deeper understanding of doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity in dogs is needed to identify factors influencing individual susceptibility, clarify the progression from subclinical damage to clinical cardiac dysfunction, and guide future research. Emerging approaches, including advanced echocardiography, microRNAs, proteomic biomarkers and pharmacokinetic modelling, may help improve early detection and guide more individualised dosing to minimise toxicity.

papers.title: Rabies surveillance in the United States during 2024.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Keshavamurthy R, Boutelle C, Bonaparte S, Gigante CM, Condori RE, Earnest R, Kirby JD, Nelson KM, Orciari LA, Ross Y, Wallace RM
papers.abstract: Describe the epidemiologic landscape of rabies and rabies testing in the US during 2024. Animal rabies testing results from approximately 130 public health, agriculture, and academic laboratories are collected by the US National Rabies Surveillance System (NRSS) each month. Data reported in 2024 were analyzed to examine temporal and geographic trends in animal rabies cases by rabies virus variant (RVV). In 2024, 3,834 cases of animal rabies were reported to the NRSS (4.2% of 90,343 samples submitted), representing a 2.0% increase from 2023. Of positive samples, 331 (8.6%) were domestic animals, and 3,503 (91.4%) were wildlife. The most commonly found rabid domestic animal was cats (243 positive [1.3% positivity]), and the most commonly found wildlife were bats (1,376 positive [5.7% positivity]) followed by raccoons (1,080 [10.1% positivity]). Two nonenzootic RVVs gained entry into the US in 2024. Four people died from rabies, including 2 who experienced bat exposures that were left untreated and 1 person whose case involved international travel. The expansion of the historical range of enzootic RVVs can lead to substantial public health and animal health burden. Domestically acquired human rabies cases in 2024 underscore the need for continual public education on the risks of rabies exposures to ensure timely and effective administration of postexposure prophylaxis. The internationally acquired human rabies case demonstrates that the US remains vulnerable to human and animal rabies importations. The NRSS plays a crucial role in protecting public and animal health by monitoring rabies trends in the US.

papers.title: Large language models demonstrate variable diagnostic performance and a systematic risk of undertriage in surgical triage of feline metacarpal and metatarsal fractures.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Okur S, Özkalipçi Ç, Baykal B, Kartal T, Şenocak MG, Bedir AG, Yanmaz LE
papers.abstract: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of multiple large language models (LLMs) against expert consensus in determining surgical intervention needs for feline metacarpal and metatarsal fractures. In this retrospective study (December 2023 to February 2025), 73 clinical cases of feline metacarpal and metatarsal fractures were evaluated. Two board-certified veterinary orthopedic surgeons established a reference standard for surgical versus conservative management. Five LLMs (ChatGPT, version 5.2 [OpenAI Inc]; Gemini, version 3 Pro [Alphabet Inc]; Grok, version 4.1 [SpaceXAI]; Qwen, version 3.5 [Alibaba Cloud]; and Claude Sonnet, version 4.5 [Anthropic PBC]; and Claude Sonnet, version 4.5 [Anthropic PBC]) assessed anonymized case summaries using a standardized zero-shot prompt. Model recommendations were compared with the reference standard to calculate accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and the Cohen κ. The reference standard classified 49 cases (67.1%) as surgical and 24 (32.9%) as conservative. ChatGPT achieved the highest performance (accuracy, 84.9%; sensitivity, 79.6%; specificity, 95.8%; κ = 0.69). Other models showed lower performance; Qwen and Claude Sonnet failed to identify any surgical cases (0% sensitivity). A systematic bias toward conservative management was observed across all models, causing high false-negative rates (undertriage). LLMs demonstrate highly variable diagnostic performance and a systematic risk of undertriage in feline fracture assessment. While top-performing models approach expert-level agreement, others fail in critical clinical scenarios. Independent LLM use for surgical decision-making in feline orthopedics is not recommended due to undertriage risks. These tools require strict clinician oversight for preliminary triage.

papers.title: Medetomidine-vatinoxan (Zenalpha) results in reduction of systolic function, blood pressure, and heart rate with prolongation of electrocardiographic intervals in healthy dogs.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Forsyth KK, Hogan DF, Dos Santos LFN, Weng HY
papers.abstract: To determine the effects of medetomidine-vatinoxan (Zenalpha; MVZ) on echocardiographic parameters, blood pressure, and cardiac rhythm in healthy dogs. Healthy, client-owned dogs were eligible for enrollment in this prospective, pretest/posttest study. Exclusion criteria included preexisting cardiac disease or medications that could alter the measured study parameters. Echocardiography, blood pressure, and 1-hour Holter monitor were performed at baseline and after sedation with MVZ per the manufacturer's guidelines. Multiple echocardiographic parameters, blood pressure, and arrhythmic burden score were assessed with pairwise comparisons between baseline and sedation. 21 dogs were enrolled in the study. Compared to baseline, MVZ resulted in significant reduction in multiple echocardiography-derived systolic function parameters (including ejection fraction, fractional shortening, end-systolic volume index, stroke volume index, and fractional area change), blood pressure, and heart rate, along with prolongation in PR and absolute QT intervals; there were nonsignificant increases in corrected QT interval and arrhythmic burden scores. Thirteen of 21 dogs (62%) developed or had worsening of atrioventricular nodal conduction on Holter monitor, while 2 of 21 (9.5%) developed or had worsening atrial or ventricular ectopic activity. Of all measured echocardiographic systolic function parameters, 15 of 21 dogs (71.4%) had 2 or more parameters below reference range with MVZ sedation. Sedation with MVZ resulted in significant changes to multiple cardiovascular and hemodynamic parameters. The cardiovascular effects of MVZ should be considered prior to sedation in dogs with, or being screened for, cardiovascular disease.

papers.title: Abnormal modified Insall-Salvati index values are associated with increased odds of medial meniscal tears in dogs with cranial cruciate ligament tears.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Zayas JP, Steurer JA, Dixon BC, Newman RJ
papers.abstract: To evaluate the association between patellar height, as measured by the modified Insall-Salvati (IS) index, and medial meniscal tear in dogs with cranial cruciate ligament tears (CCLTs). Medical records from dogs treated for CCLT were reviewed. Preoperative patellar height was measured on mediolateral radiographs with the use of the modified IS index. Craniomedial stifle mini-arthrotomy documented the presence or absence of medial meniscal tears. Statistical analysis, adjusted to control for confounding variables, assessed whether abnormal IS index values were associated with meniscal injury. The study included 229 stifles. Abnormal modified IS index values were found in 12.6% (29 of 229) of stifles, of which 44.8% (13 of 29) had a concurrent medial meniscal tear. Among the dogs with a normal modified IS index (87.4% [200 of 229]), only 24.5% (49 of 200) had a concurrent medial meniscal tear. Dogs with an abnormal IS index had 3 times the odds of a medial meniscal tear (95% CI, 1.2 to 7.3) compared to those with a normal index. There was no statistically significant difference in the distribution between complete and partial CCLT between the normal IS index and abnormal IS index groups. Abnormal patellar height, as measured by the modified IS index, is significantly associated with increased risk of secondary medial meniscal tear in dogs with CCLT. Preoperative measurement of the modified IS index may help identify dogs at increased risk for meniscal tearing, supporting surgical planning and client communication.

papers.title: Ultrasonographic evaluation of the canine gracilis, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus muscles.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Huguet E, Repac J
papers.abstract: To describe a practical technique for ultrasonographic evaluation of the gracilis, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus muscles in dogs. 2 clinically healthy client-owned German Shepherd Dogs were used for this tutorial. Owner consent and approval from the University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine IACUC were obtained prior to participation. Dogs were clipped, sedated, and placed into dorsal recumbency in a relaxed position with bilateral coxofemoral abduction. A stepwise ultrasonographic approach was demonstrated with a high-frequency linear transducer. The image was optimized by adjustment of depth, focal zone placement, gain, and time-gain compensation. Scanning was performed in both transverse and longitudinal planes to assess muscle origin, body, and insertion. Normal anatomic relationships of the gracilis, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus muscles were identified to facilitate consistent evaluation. Ultrasound allowed clear identification of the gracilis, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus muscles on the basis of location, shape, echogenicity, and fiber orientation. The gracilis was identified in a transverse plane as a superficial, flat adductor muscle, with the semimembranosus located deeper and the semitendinosus positioned more caudally with a rounded contour. Standardized scanning planes enabled consistent visualization of muscle architecture and tendon attachments. Ultrasonography is a valuable, accessible tool for evaluating the gracilis, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus muscles in dogs. Familiarity with normal anatomy and scanning techniques is essential for the diagnosis of conditions such as fibrotic myopathy, facilitating earlier intervention.

papers.title: An anatomic plate provides successful outcomes for stabilization of periprosthetic femoral fractures and greater trochanteric osteotomies in dogs undergoing total hip replacement.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Lotsikas PJ, Fink OT, Murphy S, Lirtzman RA, Kim SE, Lu M, Rochat M
papers.abstract: To report the clinical and radiographic outcomes of a locking proximal femoral anatomic bone plate in the management of periprosthetic femoral fractures (PFFs) and greater trochanteric osteotomies (GTOs) in dogs undergoing total hip replacement (THR). Medical records from August 2023 to February 2026 were reviewed for dogs with THR that developed PFF or underwent planned GTO and were subsequently stabilized with a locking proximal femoral anatomic bone plate. Cases involving a second plate, preexisting surgical site infection, or THR implant removal at the time of surgery were excluded. Eleven dogs were included-8 with PFF and 3 with GTO. The median age of dogs that sustained a femoral fracture was 7.5 years (range, 2 to 12.5 years). Three fractures occurred intraoperatively, and 5 occurred < 30 days postoperatively. The median age of dogs that underwent GTO was 2 years (range, 1 to 9 years). Of the 3 cases, 1 was a revision of a previously failed pin and tension-band repair of a GTO, and the other 2 were the primary repairs of the GTO. Radiographic bone healing and full function were achieved in all PFF cases. Two cases of GTO completely healed, and 1 was a delayed union but stable at12 weeks; all achieved full or acceptable function. One major complication occurred in the PFF group and was successfully revised with a larger plate. A locking proximal femoral anatomic bone plate provided adequate fixation and successful outcomes in dogs with PFF or elective GTO in dogs undergoing total hip replacement.

papers.title: Is annual Dirofilaria immitis antigen testing at preventive renewal proportionate to the residual infection risk in documented-compliant dogs?
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Horvath M
papers.abstract: Current American Heartworm Society guidelines characterize prescribing macrocyclic lactone preventives in the absence of antigen testing as "NOT RECOMMENDED," regardless of compliance history or geographic prevalence. Number Needed to Screen, an established human preventive medicine framework applied here as a novel veterinary screening tool, has not previously been used to evaluate this guideline. Using county-level Companion Animal Parasite Council prevalence data and the compliance-gap distribution as a proxy, we derive geographically stratified Number Needed to Screen estimates varying approximately 25-fold across US states. A risk-stratified approach calibrated to local prevalence and compliance history merits prospective evaluation.

papers.title: Use of phenylephrine-soaked gauze following staphylectomy does not reduce the need for reintubation or temporary tracheostomy in brachycephalic dogs.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Strain W, Reed RA, Grimes JA
papers.abstract: To determine whether application of phenylephrine-soaked gauze (PG) against the soft palate following staphylectomy reduces the incidence of reintubation and temporary tracheostomy. Electronic medical records for dogs that underwent staphylectomy from January 2023 through December 2024 were reviewed. Data collected included signalment, stage of laryngeal collapse, whether PG was used or not, and incidence of reintubation and temporary tracheostomy. Normally distributed data were analyzed with a Student t test; nonnormally distributed data were analyzed with a Wilcoxon test. Categorical data were analyzed with a Fisher exact test. 96 dogs were included (PG group, n = 56; no PG [NPG] group, 43). Dogs in the NPG group were more likely to have stage I versus stage II laryngeal collapse compared to those in the PG group. No other variables differed between groups. In the PG group, 19.6% (11 of 56) underwent reintubation and 7.1% (4 of 56) underwent temporary tracheostomy. In the NPG group, 22.5% (9 of 43) underwent reintubation and 5.0% (2 of 43) underwent temporary tracheostomy. There was no difference in reintubation or temporary tracheostomy between PG and NPG. The use of PG placed against the soft palate did not reduce reintubation or temporary tracheostomy rates among brachycephalic dogs undergoing staphylectomy. Veterinarians performing staphylectomy for brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome should not expect PG to reduce reintubation and temporary tracheostomy rates among patients; other methods to reduce soft palate swelling after staphylectomy should be evaluated.

papers.title: Teleneurology video recordings and live streams provide reliable neuroanatomic lesion localization in dogs and cats.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Shinn R, Connolly B, Parker R, Togawa G, Rossmeisl J
papers.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the reliability and accuracy of teleneurology consultation for neuroanatomical lesion localization in client-owned dogs and cats. This prospective cross-sectional study was conducted from June to July 2023. Fifty-five client-owned dogs and cats presenting to an academic teaching hospital neurology service were enrolled. Animals were pragmatically allocated into 2 groups to undergo neurologic examination performed by veterinary students; group 1 underwent neurologic examination via prerecorded video, and group 2 was live streamed. A separate, in-person neurologic examination by a blinded board-certified neurologist or neurology resident served as the baseline assessment. The Cohen κ statistic was used to assess agreement between the neuroanatomical localization for each group. In total, 30 animals were evaluated in group 1 and 25 animals in group 2. Both teleneurology modalities demonstrated strong agreement with the in-person neuroanatomic localization. For group 1, κ was 0.84 (95% CI, 0.69 to 0.98). For group 2 (live stream), κ was 0.85 (95% CI, 0.66 to 1.00). Discrepancies in neuroanatomic localization were observed in 4 cases (13%) from group 1 and 3 (12%) from group 2. Teleneurology consultation shows promise as a reliable method for neuroanatomical localization in small animals. The observed high agreement suggested the potential utility of teleneurology consultation for nonemergent consultations, recheck appointments, and surgical follow-ups, particularly when a thorough examination with a dedicated videographer is ensured. Further standardization of protocols could enhance its widespread application.

papers.title: Retrospective evaluation of canine parvovirus monoclonal antibody supports faster clinical recovery in shelter dogs with naturally occurring canine parvovirus.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Welton M, Hadden H, Herron M, Winston JA
papers.abstract: To retrospectively evaluate the clinical efficacy and safety of the canine parvovirus monoclonal antibody (CPMA) administered with standardized supportive care for naturally occurring canine parvovirus (CPV) in a shelter setting. Electronic medical records from CPV-positive dogs treated at Gigi's Parvovirus Treatment Center between June 2020 and May 2024 were reviewed. All dogs received a standardized standard-of-care (SOC) algorithm. Dogs treated prior to August 2023 received SOC alone (n = 49), while those admitted thereafter received CPMA (0.2 mL/kg, IV) plus SOC (63). Primary outcomes were hospitalization duration, mortality, and time to isolation release criteria (2 consecutive negative CPV ELISA tests [SNAP; Idexx Laboratories Inc]). Secondary outcomes included modified clinical severity scores, medication scores, and total cost of care. Dogs receiving CPMA with SOC had significantly shorter hospitalization (median, 2 vs 4 days) and reached isolation release criteria sooner (median, 5 vs 6.5 days) compared with SOC alone. Mortality did not differ significantly (17% vs 22%). Maximum medication scores and overall cost of care were not statistically different, although CPMA-treated dogs showed a real-world median cost reduction of $978.50. One CPMA-treated dog experienced an anaphylactic reaction and recovered with supportive care. CPMA administration in combination with SOC accelerated clinical recovery and time to release from isolation compared with SOC alone. CPMA appears clinically effective and safe for naturally occurring CPV infections in a shelter environment. By reducing isolation time, CPMA may improve welfare, reduce behavioral risk associated with prolonged isolation and medical trauma, and support earlier adoption.

papers.title: A single-layer, full-thickness, simple continuous suture pattern is safe for hysterotomy closure in dogs undergoing cesarean section.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Goldblatt BH, Burns JG, Marvel SJ
papers.abstract: To evaluate short-term complications for single-layer, full-thickness, simple continuous appositional closure (AC) of the uterus in dogs undergoing cesarean section (CS). Additional objectives included comparing the complication rates with dogs that underwent an inverting closure (IC) and reporting the litter size in dogs with subsequent pregnancies. A medical record review for dogs undergoing CS between May 2014 and February 2025 was performed at Colorado State University. Data retrieved included signalment, reason for CS, uterine closure pattern, anesthesia and surgery time, litter size, complications, and subsequent CSs. The study population included 77 dogs that underwent 89 CSs (70 AC, 19 IC). Postoperative complications were noted in 6 of 89 cases (6.7%). Closure pattern was not found to be a risk factor for development of postoperative complications. No dogs required intervention related to hysterotomy closure, and all dogs survived the 14-day follow-up period. One dog developed paralysis following epidural use at the time of CS. Twenty-four dogs had subsequent pregnancies: 19 of 24 (79.2%) after AC and 5 of 24 (20.8%) after IC. Full-thickness AC was not a significant risk factor for short-term postoperative complications. Both single- and double-layer, full-thickness hysterotomy closures were compatible with subsequent successful whelping and CSs. Single-layer, full-thickness, simple continuous appositional and double-layer full-thickness closures are safe for hysterotomy closure.

papers.title: Automated acute pain assessment in brachycephalic cats with ocular pain using the Feline Grimace Scale.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Steagall PV, Li J, Marangoni S, Bukhari SSUH
papers.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and limitations of an AI-powered Feline Grimace Scale (FGS) pipeline for acute pain assessment in brachycephalic cats with ocular pain. A total of 200 facial images of brachycephalic cats with ocular pain were used for model training and evaluation. A landmark localization model was used to predict facial landmarks. Pain prediction was performed with regression models from a machine-learning library (XGBoost; XGBoost Developers); 5 independent submodels were trained, each corresponding to 1 of the 5 FGS action units-ear position, orbital tightening, muzzle tension, whiskers change, and head position. Three configurations were applied to input variables: without muzzle tension and whiskers change, without whiskers change and head position, and all geometric descriptors retained. The landmark localization performance was assessed via normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), whereas pain prediction was assessed via mean absolute error, Pearson correlation, and R2 values. Facial landmark detection showed reduced accuracy in brachycephalic cats (NRMSE, 19.96%) compared with previous reports in predominantly mesocephalic cats (NRMSE, 16.76%). Pain prediction models demonstrated poor generalizability, showing the best results for without muzzle tension and whiskers change (mean absolute error, 0.168; R2, 0.115; Pearson correlation, 0.374). Automated landmark detection and pain prediction using an AI-powered FGS pipeline is possible in brachycephalic cats. However, cautious interpretation is needed due to limited annotated data, which precludes robust predictive performance estimates. Conformation-specific datasets are required before this AI-powered FGS pipeline can be used for pain assessment in brachycephalic cats.

papers.title: Development of a predictive model for estimation of postoperative risk following brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome surgery.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Ruzics EA, Reynolds PS, Morse Z, Shipman J, Ham KM
papers.abstract: To identify risk factors for postoperative death and complications in dogs undergoing brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS) surgery and utilize this information to develop a predictive model for risk estimation. Records of dogs undergoing BOAS surgery at a veterinary teaching hospital between 2012 and 2023 were reviewed. Predictor variables were categorized into domains, including signalment, history, clinical signs, underlying pathology, acuity status, and surgeries performed. Outcomes were categorized as death, major complications, or minor complications. The association between outcomes and predictors was modeled by logistic regression. Results were reported as ORs and regression coefficients with 95% CIs. A predictive model was created to estimate risk of mortality and complications following BOAS surgery. 297 cases were included. Twelve dogs (4%) died prior to discharge. Major complications (airway interventions and pneumonia) were reported for 29 dogs (10%). Major complications were strongly associated with emergent presentation (OR, 7.45; 95% CI, 2.70 to 20.59), female sex (OR, 2.78; 95% CI, 1.11 to 6.67), high-grade laryngeal collapse (OR, 4.28; 95% CI, 1.56 to 11.79), and history of regurgitation/vomiting (OR, 2.16; 95% CI, 0.87 to 5.38). Risk factors for postoperative death and complications were identified. A predictive model was developed, allowing estimation of postoperative risk based on individual patient factors. A multivariable predictive model may be useful in clinical practice to obtain individualized postoperative risk predictions to contribute to prognostication, decision-making, and triage. However, as this model has not been externally validated, calculated risk should be utilized with caution and consideration for the clinical picture of each patient.

papers.title: Pretreatment with phenoxybenzamine improves short-term survival and hemodynamic stability in dogs undergoing adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Wund Z, Monnet E
papers.abstract: To evaluate indices of hemodynamic instability (HDI) in dogs and evaluate the effects of phenoxybenzamine (PBZ) on HDI and short-term survival in dogs undergoing adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma. A retrospective medical record review of all dogs that underwent adrenalectomy at a single institution between 1996 and 2024. Dogs were included if the mass was confirmed to be a pheochromocytoma on histopathology and excluded if they received α antagonists other than PBZ, had incomplete medical or anesthetic records, or were treated with laparoscopy. 52 dogs met the inclusion criteria. Thirty-five dogs that did not receive PBZ were entered in the NPBZ group, and 17 that received PBZ were entered in the PBZ group. The mean dosage of PBZ was 1.1 mg/kg/d (0.4 to 1.7 mg/kg/d) administered for a mean length of time of 13.4 days (9.3 to 17.4 days) before surgery. Indices of HDI including systolic blood pressure > 200 mm Hg seemed to be more appropriate for dogs with pheochromocytoma. Six of the 22 dogs in the NPBZ group that required cavotomy experienced HDI compared to 0 of 17 in the PBZ group. The 14-day survival rate was 94.1% in the PBZ group and 62.9% in the NPBZ group. Pharmacologic α-adrenergic blockade with PBZ prior to adrenalectomy improved short-term patient survival. Indices of HDI that include systolic arterial pressure above 200 mm Hg seem to be more appropriate for dogs. PBZ should be considered as an effective pretreatment strategy to reduce the effects of HDI during adrenalectomy in dogs undergoing adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma.

papers.title: Serological response to extralabel use of parenteral rabies vaccines in 28 mammalian species.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Wallace RM, Müller T, Freuling C, Seetahal JFR, Slavinski S, Brown C
papers.abstract: To evaluate immunogenicity, persistence of antibodies, survival after challenge, and anamnestic response following extralabel parenteral rabies vaccination across mammalian species compared with benchmarks from on-label canine vaccination. Mammals described in published studies of extralabel parenteral rabies vaccination. A structured literature review (1980 to 2025) identified studies reporting serologic or challenge outcomes after extralabel parenteral rabies vaccination. Extracted data included taxonomic family; vaccine type and schedule, timing of serum collection, antibody titers, survival after experimental challenge, and response to booster vaccination. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted by family and overall. Pooled proportions were compared with the World Organisation for Animal Health benchmark of 88% survival and with canine benchmarks for primary seroconversion (88.1%), antibody levels 6 to 12 months after primary vaccination (72.9%), and booster response (96.8%). 32 articles describing 41 studies met inclusion criteria, representing 2,630 animals from 28 species in 17 families. After primary vaccination, 84.4 ± 4.1% achieved titers ≥ 0.5 IU/mL, with 14 of 16 families noninferior to the canine benchmark. At ≥ 6 months, 63.7 ± 10.6% maintained titers ≥ 0.5 IU/mL. Among 79 vaccinated animals challenged with rabies virus, 89.0 ± 9.8% survived. Booster vaccination produced adequate titers in 89.1 ± 8.0% of 275 animals, with reduced responses in the families Elephantidae and Ursidae. Modern-day rabies vaccines generate strong antibody responses across diverse mammalian families, with nondomestic canids responding similarly to domestic dogs. These findings support recognizing extralabel vaccination as biologically protective and can inform public health and animal management policies.

papers.title: Ethanol ablation guided by sonographic appearance of the nodule is effective for treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism in dogs.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Schindler S, Lane M, Woodard M, Baron-Chapman M
papers.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of a modified percutaneous ultrasound-guided ethanol ablation technique for the treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism in dogs. This prospective observational study was conducted at a single veterinary referral center. Dogs with persistent ionized hypercalcemia, normal/increased parathyroid hormone concentrations, normal/undetectable parathyroid hormone-related protein concentrations, and ultrasonographic identification of ≥ 1 presumed hyperfunctioning parathyroid nodule (≥ 2.5 mm) underwent percutaneous ultrasonographically guided ethanol ablation, in which ethanol was administered until real-time diffuse intralesional hyperechogenicity was achieved. Dogs with alternative causes of hypercalcemia were excluded. Data collected from October 2018 through April 2023 included signalment, lesion characteristics, ethanol volume administered, complications, and biochemical outcomes. Resolution of hypercalcemia following ablation was the primary outcome measure. 49 dogs were enrolled, and follow-up data were available for 47. Hypercalcemia resolved in 42 of 47 dogs (89.4%). Complications occurred in 12 of 47 dogs (25.5%) and were classified as minor in 10 and major in 2. Dogs with resolution of hypercalcemia received a greater median volume of ethanol than dogs without resolution (0.60 mL [IQR, 0.30 to 1.00 mL] vs 0.15 mL [IQR, 0.09 to 0.37 mL]; P = .012). Ethanol volume was not associated with ethanol leakage severity or complication rates. Sonographically guided ethanol ablation was an effective treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism in dogs, achieving resolution of hypercalcemia in nearly 90% of cases with a low rate of major complications. Ultrasound-guided ethanol ablation based on real-time nodule hyperechogenicity may be a practical alternative to volume-based protocols while maintaining efficacy and safety.

papers.title: Cardiac etiology is the leading cause of feline chylothorax: 35 cases (2006-2022).
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Severac L, Juette T, Conversy B
papers.abstract: To identify the most frequent underlying causes of chylothorax in cats and to assess whether clinical and laboratory findings at presentation could predict etiology and outcome. Cats diagnosed with chylothorax were retrospectively enrolled in 2 veterinary centers between 2006 and 2022. Data collected for each case included signalment, history, physical examination findings, pleural effusion analysis, hematologic and imaging results, etiology, treatment (medical and/or surgical), and survival time. Descriptive statistics and multinomial logistic regression were used to identify markers of etiology. Associations with survival were assessed with the Cox proportional hazards models. 35 cats met the inclusion criteria. Cardiac disease was the most common etiology (57%), followed by idiopathic (31%), neoplasia (9%), and peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia (3%). Cats with neoplastic chylothorax were significantly older than those in other etiologic groups. Cats with cardiac chylothorax had a higher left atrial-to-aortic ratio (median, 2.4) than cats in other etiologic groups (< 1.4). Median survival times for cardiac, idiopathic, neoplastic, and peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia etiology were 172, 416, 38, and 27 days, respectively. Regardless of the chylothorax etiology, survival was negatively correlated to older cats and low rectal temperature on initial arrival to the hospital. Cardiac disease was the predominant cause of chylothorax. All cats with a left atrial-to-aortic ratio > 1.4 had a cardiac etiology. All cats aged over 14 years had a neoplastic etiology. Felines with a cardiac etiology had a poorer prognosis than idiopathic cases. Neoplastic cats had the shortest survival time. An echocardiogram should be considered for all cats diagnosed with chylothorax.

papers.title: Biological response stability of refrigerated cosacthen after opening and non-hormonal effects of ACTH stimulation testing in healthy dogs.
papers.authors: de Oliveira MC, Nogueira TB, Gouvêa FL, Oliveira JM, Trevizan L, Pöppl ÁG
papers.abstract: The adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test (ACTHST) is widely used to evaluate adrenal reserve in dogs. This study assessed the effects of refrigerated storage of tetracosactide (Cosacthen) after opening for up to three weeks and investigated hematological, biochemical, and electrolyte changes following ACTH stimulation. Ten healthy beagle dogs (five males and five females) were enrolled. Each dog received tetracosactide (5 μg/kg, IV) at vial opening (T0) and at 7-day intervals over 3 weeks (T1 to T3), using aliquots from the same vial stored at 2-8°C. Blood samples were collected before and 1 hour after ACTH administration to measure cortisol, hematology, biochemistry, and electrolytes. Clinical monitoring was performed after each test. Cortisol concentrations increased significantly after ACTH administration at all time points (T0-T3). Delta-cortisol was higher at T1 than at T0 (P = 0.0104) and lower at T2 than at T1 (P = 0.0059), with no differences among T0, T2, and T3. After ACTH administration, red blood cell count, hematocrit, hemoglobin, albumin, alkaline phosphatase, triglycerides, cholesterol, potassium, and total calcium decreased significantly, whereas glucose increased. All values remained within reference intervals, and no adverse effects were observed. Refrigerated storage of Cosacthen after opening did not alter cortisol responses. Post-ACTH changes in laboratory variables should be considered when interpreting results.

papers.title: Polarization Sensitive Optical Coherence Tomography for Surgical Margin Assessment for Canine Soft Tissue Sarcoma.
papers.authors: Patel N, Fontes G, Dornbusch J, Biggo M, Erickson A, Jurcak N, Mignucci JS, Shen YF, Weaver H, Jennings R, Selmic LE
papers.abstract: Soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) and skeletal muscle both appear high scattering on spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) imaging, which resulted in instances of misclassification by observers in prior soft tissue sarcoma margin assessment studies. Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an extension of OCT that provides additional information about tissue polarization contrast. In this prospective study we wanted to evaluate whether PS-OCT improves tissue differentiation and diagnostic accuracy compared to spectral-domain OCT (SD-OCT) alone. PS-OCT images from surgical margins of 10 resected STS were compared with histopathology to identify characteristic features of normal and neoplastic tissues. Then, six observers of varying OCT image interpretation experience assessed surgical margins from 30 resected STS using SD-OCT alone and SD-OCT combined with PS-OCT. PS-OCT images demonstrated distinct birefringence (optical patterns), corresponding to tissue organization: skeletal muscle exhibited alternating high and low birefringence bands, fascia showed variable birefringence and STS had uniformly low birefringence. Overall diagnostic accuracy was high for both modalities [correct classification rate: SD-OCT alone 93.7% (95% confidence interval (CI): 90.1, 96.0) vs. SD-OCT combined with PS-OCT 92.6% (95% = CI: 89.3, 95.4)]; adding PS-OCT did not significantly improve accuracy across all observers (p = 0.82), though expert observers benefited significantly (p = 0.0018). Interobserver and intraobserver agreement ranged from substantial to near perfect. These findings suggest PS-OCT can be interpreted reliably after brief training and may enhance accuracy for experienced users. Further research should explore structured training and real-time applications for comprehensive surgical margin evaluation.

papers.title: Clinical Characteristics of Hair Cycle Arrest in Toy Poodles: A Retrospective Comparison With Pomeranians.
papers.authors: Ueyama A, Amatuji H, Iyori K, Hsiao YH
papers.abstract: Hair cycle arrest (HCA), known as alopecia X, is an alopecia disorder most commonly reported in Nordic breeds-particularly Pomeranians. Toy poodles (TPs) also are frequently affected, yet their clinical characteristics have not been reviewed systematically. The aim of this retrospective case series was to compare the clinical characteristics of HCA in TPs and Pomeranians. Medical records of client-owned dogs diagnosed with HCA between 2018 and 2024 were reviewed. Signalment, including age of onset and age at diagnosis, clinical features, skin barrier function (transepidermal water loss [TEWL], stratum corneum hydration [SCH]) and treatment outcomes were analysed. Fifty dogs (19 TPs, 31 Pomeranians) met the inclusion criteria. TPs were significantly older than Pomeranians both at disease onset and at the first presentation (p = 0.003 and p = 0.001, respectively). Both breeds exhibited similar bilateral symmetrical alopecia presentations; however, Pomeranians mainly presented with a single alopecic site, while nearly half of the TPs had multiple affected sites (p = 0.032). Pruritus and superficial pyoderma were common in both breeds. TEWL and SCH values frequently deviated from reference ranges (increased TEWL and decreased SCH), indicating impaired skin barrier function. TEWL was significantly higher in TPs with pyoderma than in those without (p = 0.025). Regarding outcomes, > 70% of patients showed partial or complete regrowth, despite various treatment regimens. HCA in TPs closely resembles that in Pomeranians, despite genetic divergence, suggesting a conserved pathogenesis across their breeds. Frequent pruritus and pyoderma, together with abnormal TEWL and SCH, indicate secondary skin barrier dysfunction. Clinical management should address both hair regrowth and restoration of skin barrier function.

papers.title: Ultrasonographic Features of Pleural Thickening in Cats With Pulmonary Carcinoma and Pleural Effusion: A Retrospective Descriptive Study.
papers.authors: Toshima A, Fulkerson CV, Murakami M
papers.abstract: Pleural involvement is an important but poorly described manifestation of feline pulmonary carcinoma. Thoracic ultrasonography may identify pleural abnormalities and accessible targets for cytologic sampling in cats with pleural effusion. To describe ultrasonographic features of pleural thickening in cats with pulmonary carcinoma and pleural effusion and summarise cytologic findings from pleural effusion and ultrasound-guided lesion sampling. Medical records from one referral hospital were retrospectively reviewed for cats with pulmonary carcinoma or metastatic epithelial neoplasia consistent with pulmonary origin, pleural effusion, and stored thoracic ultrasound images. Images were reviewed in consensus by three observers for distribution, location, shape, maximal thickness, echogenicity, homogeneity, and suspected intercostal muscle invasion. Twenty-two cats were included. Pleural thickening was recorded in all cats. Thickening was classified as diffuse in 12 cats, focal in 6, and multifocal in 4; however, scanning was not systematic across all thoracic regions. The representative or measured pleural abnormality was in the cranial pleural region in 18 cats. Maximal pleural thickness was 5.6 ± 3.3 mm (median, 4.9 mm; range, 1.2-16.2 mm). Suspected intercostal muscle invasion was recorded in eight cats. Neoplastic cells were identified in pleural effusion cytology in 15/20 cats. Six cats underwent ultrasound-guided lesion sampling; cytologic or histopathologic findings were supportive of carcinoma in all 6, including 1 confirmed by biopsy. In this selected cohort, thoracic ultrasonography identified pleural thickening with variable morphology.
